translations.text: The First Book of Eusebius of Caesarea on the Divine Manifestation.

Those who say of this entire ordered creation, this great and beautiful universe, and of the intricate, richly composed structure of heaven and earth, that it has neither a beginning nor a governor, that it has no master and is without providential care, and that idly, vainly, and through some senseless chance that happened to occur,
it arose by itself—let them be regarded as thoroughly wicked and godless. For this reason let them be driven away from godly people and from our holy temples;

let them be completely excluded. For they themselves cannot even construct a house without planning and care, nor can a ship be properly fitted together with its timbers without a shipwright, nor a garment
be woven without the craft of weaving, nor a city be built without the skill of a master builder. Yet, while admitting these things, through what madness of mind I do not know, they fail to perceive

the courses of the sun in their established form, the changes of the moon in their order, the arrangements of the stars in their proper places, the revolution of the vaults of heaven, the return of the appointed times, and the succession of the seasons.

And again, along with these, the [?] of the [?] of the mountains, the equal lengths of days and nights, the unhindered reproduction of living creatures, and the unchanging continuation of existence over a long period of time.

And the plants of every kind that sprout and flower from the earth, the nourishment suited to all living creatures, their distinctive senses, the body's limbs and its colors, beautifully arranged in their places—they see these with their eyes and touch them with their hands. This

is something they say is evident even to the blind. Yet with godless utterances and the wicked perversity of their minds, they supposed that it was not the work of wisdom, nor of the Word of God and providence, but a senseless encounter of chance that occurred idly and vainly, from whatever source.
Let these people, then, as thoroughly godless, be driven far away from the company of those who fear God and from divine instruction.
2. But the company of those who believe in many gods, drawn up on the other side against the first group, seems to me to represent an error

of another kind. Like children, they have gone astray in their thinking: they exchanged the worship of the maker of the universe and governor of all, God who is over all, for the things that came into being through him. The sun, the moon, the remaining parts of the universe, and the primary elements—earth, water, air, and fire—
they honored with the very same name as their maker and creator, calling these things gods. These things did not exist from eternity, nor would they have come into being or even been named, if

the maker of the universe, the Word of God, had not willed them to exist. They seem to me no better than people who disregard the master builder responsible for the excellence of the workmanship in royal palaces
and marvel at the [?], the porticoes, the pictures with their many colors and varied flowers, the ceilings inlaid with gold, and the stone carvings, and to these very things

ascribe the praise due to their craftsman's wisdom. They ought to attribute the cause of their wonder not to these visible things but solely to the one who is their master builder, and acknowledge that the works
are many works of wisdom, but that the wise one is he alone who caused these many things to exist. Thus they are absolutely no different from little children.

Nor are those who, in the case of seven-stringed lyres, admire the musical instrument itself rather than the inventor of its construction, the knowledgeable man himself and his wisdom; or those who disregard the man who is valiant
in battle and adorn his spear and shield with crowns of victory;
or those who give the same honor as they give to the great king responsible for the great royal city to its streets, squares, buildings, lifeless chambers,
and gymnasia. They ought to marvel not at columns or stones, but at the great maker of these skillful works himself and at the lawgiver.
3. In the same way, let us not assign the cause of this entire universe, which people see with their bodily eyes, to the sun [?], the moon, or any other heavenly body.
We ought to acknowledge that all these things are works of wisdom, but not to place on their level the one who, in turn, is known not through bodily eyes but only through a pure
and enlightened mind. Let us praise and worship that king of all, the Word of God, with all the love of our soul. For no one has ever regarded even the body of a wise and knowledgeable man
his eyes, or his head, or his hands, or his feet, or the rest of his body. Much less does he call the covering of his outer clothing wisdom, nor are the utensils in his house wise.
Nor are the implements used by philosophers wise. But everyone who has understanding marvels at that hidden, invisible thing—the mind that is in a human being.

4. In the same way, and even more, rather than these visible adornments, which are the bodies of this entire world, made from a single material, let us marvel at the hidden, invisible Word, the maker and arranger of the forms of everything, who is the only-begotten Word of God.
The Maker of all, who is beyond everything and above every substance, himself begot him from his own divinity, like a ray of light, and appointed him the governor and organizer of this universe.
5. For it was not fitting for this lowly bodily substance and this nature of rational beings, which had only just come into existence,
to approach God, the governor of all, because of its great deficiency in excellence. For he was the self-existent One, beyond and above everything, who cannot be
expressed, comprehended, or approached, who dwells in exalted light unlike any other, as the divine words tell us. This nature, however, had not existed.

He brought it into existence out of nothing, and it is very different and far removed from the nature of the self-existent One. Therefore God, the Lord of all, who is full of every good thing, rightly established as mediator the divine power
of his Only Begotten, who is sufficient for everything, who converses with his Father with exact understanding, surpassing excellence, and intimacy, and receives from within his hidden depths.
He humbly extends himself to become like those who are far removed from that supreme majesty, taking their form. For otherwise it was neither fitting nor right
that the One who is beyond everything and above everything should be mingled with perishable matter and with a body. For this reason the divine Word penetrated this whole universe, mingling with it,
and bound together the veins of everything by his divine, bodiless power. He leads and brings everything along, governing with all wisdom, as seems good to him.
6. The proof of this statement is clear. For if the parts of the world that we customarily call the primary elements of everything had come into existence by themselves—
earth, water, air, and fire—and had been constituted from a mingled nature, which we also see with our own eyes, and if there had been a single substance underlying everything,
which those skilled in these matters like to call the receptacle of everything, its mother and its nurse,

and it had been without form or appearance, and entirely without soul or reason, where, one might ask, did this world within it come from? Where did the separation of the elements come from? And where did the movement of opposing things toward equilibrium come from?
And who commanded this heavy element, earth, to ride above the watery substance?
7. And who reversed this nature of water, which flows downward, and raised it back up into the heights in clouds?
8. And who confined the power of fire so that it penetrates wood, and mingled it with things that are contrary to it in their nature?
9. Who mingled this cold air with a hot power, released them from their conflict with each other, and reconciled them in love?
10. Who made provision for the mortal race through successive generations and brought it into the lasting continuance of undying life?
11. Who thus fashioned the male and made the form of the female, joined the two in a single union, and devised a single beginning of reproduction for all living creatures?
12. Who transformed this lowly seed of reproduction from its perishable, senseless flow and made it bring forth living beings?
13. Who has continued to accomplish all these things, and myriads beyond them that surpass every wonder and every marvel, down to the present?
14. Who brings about their births and transformations every day and every hour, secretly and by an invisible power?

15. But the cause of all these things may rightly be called that worker of wonders, the Word of God. For truly the Word of God, glorious in everything through his almighty power, extended himself upward to the heights and downward

to the depths, stretching himself out without a body. He held the breadth and vastness of everything as though in his hands, gathering and enclosing this whole universe, and he himself established this vessel filled with every kind of compound thing.

And this substance of bodies, without reason, without form, and without visible appearance, he, with every kind of wisdom and rational power, beautifully joined together within these distinct dimensions
and fitted together. He governs the sun, the moon, and those lights in heaven by inexpressible commands, and directs them for the benefit of all.
16. This same Word of God also extended himself deep into the earth and established all the varied kinds of animals and all the forms of beautiful plants.
17. This same Word of God also plunged down to the depths of the sea and spread himself among those swimming creatures.
Here too he made countless myriads of forms and all the distinct kinds of living creatures.
18. He also brings to completion within the womb those conceived there, through the craftsmanship of nature, and fashions living beings. This same one also takes this watery substance,

flowing and heavy by nature, and makes it light, raising it upward to the heights. Then he changes it into sweetness and brings it down upon the earth in measured amounts, fulfilling his provision at appointed times,
like an excellent farmer who waters his land well and mixes moisture with dryness. And he varies it in every

form: sometimes with flowers, sometimes with shapes of every kind, sometimes with sweet fragrances, sometimes with fruits differing in their varieties, and sometimes he gives flavors of every delightful kind.
19. And why must I speak about the powers of the Word of God, speaking and discoursing about what cannot be expressed, when his visible work far surpasses all mortal thought?

20. Some, then, have called him the nature of the universe; others, the soul of the universe; others, [?]; and others have said that he is God who is beyond everything. I do not know how they confused things so widely separated.

They cast that governor of everything, the power of the Being who is above everything, down upon the earth, and mingled him in bodies with corruptible matter. They said that he moves about among irrational and rational living beings, both mortal and immortal. But these are their views.
21. Divine teaching, however, says that the one who is above all good things, the very one who is the cause of everything, is beyond all comprehension.
For this reason he cannot be expressed, spoken of, or named.
He is exalted not only above speech but also above all thought. He is not contained in a place, nor is he in bodies, nor in heaven, nor in the ether, nor in any one

of the parts of the universe. Rather, he is at once in everything and outside everything, preserved in the depth of hidden knowledge. The divine words teach us to acknowledge this one alone as the true God,
who is far removed from all bodily substance and has no part in any service of administration. For this reason it has been handed down to us that everything is from him, but not through him.

22. Rather, like a king, he sits within, concealed and hidden, where he cannot be comprehended, in the very height of his vision. By the power of his will alone he governs and orders everything. For whatever exists exists by his will, and if he does not will it, it does not exist.
He wills every good thing, because he himself is good in his own being.
23. But the one through whom everything exists, the divine Word, comes from above, from his good Father, as from a boundless spring
that flows continually and pours forth forever in inexpressible ways. He comes forth as a river, filled entirely for the common salvation of all.
To use an illustration drawn from ourselves: the mind within us is hidden and invisible. No human being has ever known what it is like or what it is in its own substance,
and like a king it sits concealed within its chambers and reflects upon actions. But a single word comes forth from it, as from a father, out of its hidden concealment.
He is begotten before everyone. He is the messenger of his Father’s purpose and openly proclaims [?] what his Father has conceived in secret.
He carries out that will in action, passing through the [?] of all; then these receive the help that comes from the Word.

He makes known the hidden, invisible one, the Father of the Word, whom no one has ever seen with eyes like these. That is, beyond all manifestations and likenesses, he is the perfect Word of God, the King of all, as his Father’s only-begotten Son.

He did not come into being through the force of an utterance, nor was his nature constituted by the pronunciation of names and words, nor by a sound produced through the striking of air. Rather, he is the living Word,

and the agent of God who is over all. In his own essence he is the power of God and the wisdom of God. He proceeds from his Father’s divinity and kingship, and he is the good offspring of a good Father and the Savior

of all alike. He gives everyone life, reason, wisdom, and light to drink, and pours out every good thing upon all from his own fullness. He gives drink not only to those who are before him and near him,

but also to those separated from him by distance, those on land and in the sea, and any other nature that exists anywhere. For all of them together he establishes boundaries, places, laws, and allotted inheritances.

With justice and the authority of his kingship, he provides for each one and gives what is fitting. He assigns some to the region above the universe, some to dwell in the heavens themselves, some to a dwelling in the ether, some in the air, and some on earth. Page 8[24*]
Then, turning from these, he again fittingly distinguishes everyone’s dwelling in another way, and variously apportions their customs and forms.
He cares for life and sustenance, not only for rational beings but also for animals without reason, for the use of rational beings.
24. To some he gives the enjoyment of mortal, temporary life,
and to others he grants a share in immortality. He does everything as the Word of God. While he is near everything and rules over everything with rational power, upward

he looks toward his Father. At his Father’s bidding, as the Savior of all, he guides the things below him that follow after him. In this way he mediates and brings this substance of created things near to the self-existent One.
He is the unbreakable bond, the Mind, the Word of God who stands between,
who binds together those that are separated and does not allow them to fall far apart. He is the providence that watches over all.
He is the one who orders everything. He is the power of God and the wisdom of God. He is the only-begotten Son of God,
God the Word, begotten of God. For in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,
and the Word was God. Everything came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being, as the glorious words of godly men teach.
25. He is the Savior of all alike, through whom the substance of everything flourishes and rejoices, constantly drinking his dew and constantly being refreshed by his presence.
He always gives it a beautiful appearance. He holds its roots firm and brings it to its proper order. At his Father’s bidding, he guides the great ship of this entire universe with his rudders. This
skilled craftsman, the only-begotten Son, was begotten as good fruit by God who is above all, as a good Father. He gave him to this world as an excellent gift, like a soul to a lifeless body.

He placed his Word within the nature of the body that lacked reason, and by the power of the divine Word he illuminated and gave life to this substance, which had no form, no appearance, no soul, and no color.
We too ought to know and worship him. He is always near matter and the elements of bodies, yet he is immaterial and bodiless, and is not wise as though he had learned wisdom from others. Page 9[26*]
Rather, he himself is wisdom, he himself is life, and he himself is light—the intelligent offspring of the ineffable light. He is one in his own essence,
since he comes from one Father, yet he possesses many powers within himself.
For we should not suppose that there are many powers merely because the parts of the world are many. Nor should we posit many gods merely because their works are many.
26. But human beings, like children in their souls, went astray into the bitter error of believing in many gods.
They made the parts of the whole world into gods and divided the one world into many.
It is as though someone were to take the eyes separately from the constitution of a single human being and say that these were a human being,
and that the ears were another human being, and likewise the head; and were to cut off the neck, chest, shoulders, feet, hands, and remaining limbs bit by bit, and divide the power of the senses
in speech, and say of one human being that there were many human beings. In the judgment of the wise, he deserves nothing more than the ridicule due to foolishness.
Such too is the person who establishes for himself myriads of gods from the parts of the one world, and takes the bodies within the universe, which by nature are moving and dispersed,
and are made from a single matter, and cuts them into many pieces, and then, in speech, makes them into gods for himself.

27. But far worse than this is the person who supposes that this entire created world, taken altogether as a whole, constituted from many parts, is God. He does not know that the divine nature has not [?]

been constituted from parts, nor is it composite, lest it require someone else to put it together. Nor is the divine made up of many parts. How, then, could it be constituted from dissimilar elements, inferior and superior?
For what is composite can also be dissolved, and what has many parts is necessarily [?]. But what is alike in every respect
and does not differ in any respect is simple and not composite. What is composite, however, is composed of dissimilar things, and what is dissimilar contains something inferior in comparison with
something superior. For if it were entirely superior, it would be uniform and alike. If it is so in every respect, it is alike throughout its entirety.
And thus it is simple in substance, without parts. But nature itself shows that this is not the case, when this visible
world is considered. For it is entirely perceptible to the senses, constituted from myriads of parts, and composite, differing within itself in its myriads of parts. And where this is so,
its nature also admits opposites. For this reason, this world shares in mortal and immortal things together, in rational and irrational things, and in substance that is cold, hot, wet,
and dry. God is free from all these things. For if God's nature is simple, without parts, and without composition,
he is beyond and very far removed from the entire order of this visible world. For this reason, this herald of truth proclaimed openly, saying: “The Word of God, who alone exists before all things,

is the Savior of all rational beings. But God, who is beyond all things, is the source of the Word's generation. He alone is the cause of all things and of his Only Begotten, and is truly called the Father of the Word.
But he acknowledges no other cause above himself. For this reason, he alone is God.
The Only Begotten came forth from him by a hidden, inexpressible will—the Savior of all, the Word of God, who is one and is present through all things.”
28. This perceptible world, then, is like a harp with many strings,
constituted from dissimilar strings: thin and thick, slack and taut, and those between these extremes, all fitted together beautifully by the art of music.

Like this harp, this world too, with its many aspects and many combinations, has been brought together into one composition: coldness [?] together with its opposite, heat, and the wetness and dryness of substance.
It is a great instrument and a work of the God of all. 29. But the divine [?] Word was not constituted from parts.
Nor is he composed of opposites. He is without parts and without composition, and beautifully and wisely resembles his Father in everything; and to the King of all, the praise that is owed to him and
is fitting, he returns. Just as myriads of parts, limbs, internal organs, and intestines are gathered together in one body, while the soul, though unseen, is one and extends throughout them all,
and the mind, without parts and without a body, is one, so it is also with this, which is constituted from many parts:

one world. Likewise, the Word of God, mighty in power and capable of everything, is one, extending throughout them all and invisibly spread over them all; and he is the cause of everything within them.
30. Do you not see with your own eyes that one heaven surrounds the whole world?

Myriads of ranks of stars dwell in it. Again, there is one sun, not many, and through the superiority of its light it eclipses the radiance of them all. So, then, just as there is one Father, his Word too,
being one, must be the good offspring of a good Father. But if someone objects, asking why there are not many sons, he must also raise the question of why there are not many suns, moons, and worlds,

and find fault with myriads of other things, in the manner of madmen, [?] to overturn the arrangements of nature that are right and good. But just as, among visible things, one sun illuminates the whole world perceived by the senses,

so also, among intelligible things, the one Word of God, full of all power, illuminates everything invisibly and without being seen by us. For why would many suns be needed when one is sufficient to bring everything to completion?
And why, again, are many sons of God needed when the one only-begotten Son is sufficient to accomplish his Father's wishes? For if there were many, they would either be alike or unlike.
If they were alike, their multiplicity would be pointless, because one who is perfect and capable of everything
is sufficient for the creation and ordering of everything. For the Word of God, the Wisdom of God, light, life, and the entire fullness of goodness, being one in his essence, makes the number

of their multitude useless, since they would share the same power pointlessly and to no good purpose. But if they were unlike, they ought not to exist. And what could be unlike one who is perfect and sufficient for everything,
except something imperfect and deficient in its nature? But no offspring of God is imperfect. Therefore God's only-begotten Son is perfect, and there are not many Words of God, but God from God,
sufficient for everything and glorious in his power over everything.

He is the one image of the light of his being, as the divine words teach. He was established as necessary for the benefit [?], ordering, and healing of all beings. In his own essence he is one, but manifold in his powers, so that he alone may suffice for the ordering of everything.
31. For perhaps even a human being has one soul and one rational power, yet it is capable of accomplishing many things at once. Whether it is to cultivate the earth, it is the same soul

that constructs [?], steers it, and builds, and learns and does many things. There is one mind and understanding in a human being, and over time it receives myriads of teachings. The very same mind plows the earth,
understands the courses of the stars, and masters the teachings of grammarians and rhetoricians [and rhetoricians].

It also becomes skilled in medicine through learning and the work of its hands. Yet no one has ever supposed that there are many souls in one body, nor imagined that there are many essences in a human being because of

his capacity to receive many kinds of instruction. And if someone [?] a shapeless lump of clay, then molds it with his hands and puts into it the forms of living creatures—a head in one shape, hands and feet in another,
and eyes in yet another—and fashions cheeks, ears, a mouth, nostrils, a chest, and shoulders through the art of modeling, it is not because many shapes and limbs have been made in one body
that we should suppose there are likewise many makers. Rather, let us give full praise to the sole craftsman of everything, who fashioned everything by one thought and one power.
32. So also, concerning this universe, which is one although constituted from many parts, we should not posit many creative powers, nor name many gods.

Rather, let us bless the one who is full of every kind of wisdom and every harmonious arrangement, who truly is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, who by one power and one excellence passes through [?], dwells throughout the whole world, sustains everything, and gives it life.
And for all of them together, and for each one of them individually among the bodies and elements in their various divisions, he provides different kinds of care from himself.

33. Likewise, the light of the sun is one, and by its single action it simultaneously illuminates the air, gives light to the eyes, warms the sense of touch, ripens the earth, makes plants grow, and establishes the seasons.
It goes before the stars, circles the heavens, shines upon the world, and visibly establishes everything by the power of God.
It accomplishes all these things through a single impulse of its nature. The nature of fire is likewise: it purifies gold and melts wax.
It dispels cold, dries clay, and burns forests. It does all these things through a single burning power.
34. Likewise, the Word of God is the king who extends through everything. He is in everything and passes over everything in heaven and on earth, governing both invisible and visible things.
He orders the sun itself, the heavens, and the whole world through powers that cannot be expressed.

Through his creative power, he is near everything and extends throughout everything. From his own springs he showers unfailing light upon the sun, the moon, and the stars, and the heavens as an image resembling his own greatness
he established and holds forever. And those beyond heaven and the world—the angelic powers and the essences of intelligent and rational spirits—with life, light, wisdom, and every

excellence of all beauty and all goodness, he fills from the treasury that is with him, all at once and through that same creative skill. He never fails to give substance to the elements, and into bodies themselves
he variously blends, at different times, combinations, mixtures, likenesses, appearances, forms, and countless works, in animals, plants, and rational and irrational souls.
He provides everything for them all together through a single power, and clearly displays not a lyre with seven strings or many strings, but one world with many components,
the work of the one Word, the maker of the world.

35. Such, then, is the common Savior of all, the Word of the God of all, concerning whom someone speaking about God says mystically: “He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him.”
For it had not known him previously, until he himself shone forth in the last days upon those who were held in the darkness
of evil. But he, the maker of the whole world, who is the common Savior of all, has rightly been revealed to us as such, and he gives all this assistance to this whole universe.
And this very universe, which is directed by one helmsman and is composed of heaven, earth, and what is in them—what nature of substance it has attained [?], not to speak in small terms.
36. This, then, participates in two natures: the superior essence, akin to the divine Word,
which is intelligent and rational, is seen by the mind and apprehended by reason; and everything superior to bodies can

be apprehended by it. And that which was necessarily supplied for its use is matter and the offspring of bodies, perceived by sense [?], which comes into being and perishes and never exists fully. I think this has been well stated.
But what is seen through bodily sensation reveals one world, this entire visible universe. The invisible, too, is rightly described in the same way as one family of

rational beings. Just as among visible things there is one bodily nature, and its individual things are distributed, some in heaven and the ether and among the things within them, and some in the air and on earth,
and the animals and plants seen in them, so also, in the invisible intelligent essence, the common class of them all is one.
The nature of the offspring of rational and intelligent powers is one, and within it there are countless differing distinctions.
37. This, then, which is made of matter and bodies, we are accustomed to call the perceptible world, composed of heaven, earth, and the things within them.
Let us make a comparison with a royal city containing tens of thousands of citizens, in which royal palaces and royal chambers are set apart from the rest.
There are the inner chambers, which few people enter or tread, and others in the outer areas belonging to the bodyguards, and still others farther away.
And the courtyard is left separately for the common people [?] and the crowds. There are many places in heaven,
and many below them, in the ether and in the air above the earth; and the dwelling place on earth, for those who walk upon it,
is this spacious place known to us all. But those places beyond heaven are beyond all thought. They too are set apart within the divine royal palace, and those who dwell near the King of all

and beside the divine Word [?] shine brightly. From the rays coming from him, as from inexhaustible springs of light, they draw and shine brightly; and from the rays coming from him, as from springs of light
that never fail, they draw and are illuminated, and stand filled with light and radiant in their voices. They occupy assemblies of incorporeal light and the ordered ranks of the places beyond heaven.
They honor God, the King of all, with lofty praises worthy of God. In between he set the great heaven, as a gateway [?] for those
outside the royal palaces, keeping them back. In this very place the bodyguards dwell, as at [?] the gate, holding the sun and moon as torches.
Those in heaven are clothed in light. They honor him who is beyond all, the King of all, and at his command and his word they illuminate those whose allotted place is the dark region
outside heaven, with lamps of light that never goes out.

This has fallen to the lot of the powers of the air, which are invisible to bodily eyes, and of earthly animals and other creatures, and of the human being, the head of them all, whose race was not foreign
to that invisible, intelligent, and rational substance. This human being was created to praise on earth the divinity and kingship of him who is the cause of all. By way of comparison,
on earth one and the same human race extends throughout the inhabited world. From it tens of thousands of nations have arisen, with dwellings of every kind, different forms of dress, customs,
and ways of life—not only those of barbarous and savage people, but also those of peaceful, well-mannered, and wise people. Among them are slaves and free people, poor and rich,
and those who differ even in their color, such as the Scythians and those whose lot it is to dwell in the far north, and the Indians who live where the sun rises,

and the Ethiopians who live where the sun sets, and the Greeks and others whose lot it is to dwell in the middle of the world [?]. Again, among all these, some exercise authority over portions of the nations,
while others submit as subjects. With the great king of them all, some are counted among his friends, and some rise to
great honors, while some are honored for their excellent deeds. Some fill the ranks of servants, and some surround him carrying spears and shields.
Again, some serve as military commanders in the cities, and some fulfill the duties of city government, while some have been admitted among the divisions of the common people [?].
Others are counted as enemies and adversaries. Yet they are all human beings, and there is one race common to them all.

Above them all there is one king, a sole ruler, clothed with his own authority over everyone. Attending him are the royal law and word. From above, the great king alone, its father and lawgiver, prescribes it; below, it runs through all, rulers and subjects alike.
He subjects the entire race under his hand to a single royal yoke. Some he raises to higher honor, and some he repays as they deserve.
38. In the same way as these, there is one generated substance [?], intelligent and rational, above all; and it is rightly said that these too constitute a single race.

They are all nothing more than brothers, having been made by one, as by their own father, the Word of God. Yet there are tens of thousands of nations and races, both of the better portion and of its opposite.
And differences arising from differing dispositions, which cannot be counted, and forms and ways of life and opposing positions—not differences of nature.
For the nature of them all is one, and their kind is one and the same. But through the difference in their wills, they have found many forms of distinct ways of life.

From this arise companies of angels and spirits and powers without bodies and invisible. Some of them are bright and radiant, illuminated by the rays of the divine Word; others are dark, blacker than all Ethiopians, with all rational light extinguished in them.
This numerous race has been assigned an intermediate share and is fully receptive to evil and virtue alike. But there is one king, one sole authority over everything: God.
He is the God of those in heaven and those above heaven, and likewise of those in the air and those on earth,
and of those beneath the earth, and of everything. He holds authority over all through the law and word of his kingdom. The law and the Word are one: he who lives in all, the active Word of God.

He is not like this mortal speech cast into the air from the mouths of mortals. Rather, as we have now learned from what he is able to do, he governs everything with complete power and wisdom. To everyone, fully and justly, as the Word

of God, he distributes suitable portions and gives each of them the places they deserve. He grants what leads to blessedness, and repays those who have fallen from virtue with the opposite, according to what they deserve.
And all alike are to dwell in distinct places, like those in [?].
Some are to rejoice beside the kingdom of heaven, some are to wait outside, and some are to dwell far away.

Yet all of them are to praise God, the king of all, with one voice, through their own teaching and learning. They are to carry this law in their hearts and in the disposition of their nature, and acknowledge together that he is the likeness of the royal image. This is

the only-begotten Word, who is the likeness of the invisible God, the firstborn of all created things—the only-begotten, who is the likeness of the invisible God, the firstborn of all created things, as the divine Scriptures teach in a mystery.
39. And in the honors paid to him, in all our houses and all our cities,

rulers and subjects alike have joined together—not with lifeless colors blended in pictures. Rather, the worship of his divinity is inscribed inwardly in the hearts of their rational faculty, as on tablets endowed with understanding.
In this way all who are under his authority worship, except those who have placed themselves among his enemies and foes: evil demons, spirits of wickedness, and rulers who hold sway over the world.
These fashioned a counterfeit royal image for themselves and put forward one writing after another—that is, myriads of
false inscriptions. They seized for themselves that name of power and that title established by law—indeed, a name that is above law.
They did this to cast the race of mortal human beings down upon the earth, among bodies and elements and the parts of the world. Because of
this, human beings revered and served created things rather than their Creator.
40. Again, they also called those powers that fight against God and rebel against him—having become so through their own conduct—gods, which they have never been. And rightly
they too were counted as enemies and foes. The law of truth commands us to flee from these and take refuge only in him who is the Word, the Savior of all. He also sowed the seed

that comes from him, not only in the heavenly places but also upon the earth, so that it might grow. He gave one and the same share in this race to those in heaven and those among the elements of the earth.

Thus the rational mind in human beings belongs to that incorporeal, intelligent substance and to the race of the divine Word who is in all. While it is still a child, it is brought up through its exercises on earth,

and is prepared and trained here beforehand for the passage to virtue. It learns to prepare in advance for its departure to those of its own kind. In this very respect, entirely because of its fellowship with the divine Word, it alone among

those on earth is worthy of the name of rationality. Yet a mind and a rational soul have necessarily been allotted a place on earth, as was stated a little earlier in the illustration of the great city of God.
A small image was to be established on earth, and throughout the whole kingdom of God not even the earthly region was to be deprived of this share. For the Word was not the common father of all [?]
so that in every region of the universe he might be praised by his offspring.

Thus not even the element of earth was deprived of a lasting share in rational life, so that not only from those beyond the world, those in heaven, and the rational beings in the air, but also from those dwelling on earth,

the praise due to the maker and father of all might be sent up. This is what the divine voice itself teaches when it commands everyone to sing the praise due to God in these words: “Praise God from heaven; praise him in the heights.
Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all the stars and light. Praise him, heaven of heavens.” And after these,

he listed the things on earth in this way: “Praise God from the earth,” and the other things, including this rational race of human beings, which [?] all this, and which he also divides into distinct groups and ranks in this manner:
“Praise him, kings of the earth and all nations, rulers and all judges on earth, young men and virgins, old people together with children. Let them praise the name of the Lord,
for his name alone is great, and his glory is on earth and in heaven.”

41. Thus, corresponding to those assemblies in heaven, he also led those on earth together with them to praise the king of all through these things. For it is truly him alone, and no other—God, who is far above every heaven—
that the assemblies above the vaults of heaven honor and praise with inexpressible praises: the hosts of angels and the spirits born of intellectual light bow to him,
their father. For him also the sun, moon, and stars, traveling a long course through the distant circuits of the universe, proceed along the racetracks of the ether and race for a crown for him.
And the invisible powers flying through the open expanse of the air offer the praise of blessing that is owed and fitting. 42. What, then, follows from this?
Was the element of earth alone to lack this provision for all, and was this nature, which produces all those fruits, to be excluded from praise, and the inhabited earth,

which bears fruits of every kind, to be barren of rational life? But this did not seem good to the maker of all, who is full of every kind of wisdom. For this reason he sowed intellectual and rational beings in this earthly region too,

and for their use he prepared the rest of the animals and the production of fruits and flowers. Thus, here too, he joined the praise offered by human beings to his father with that offered by the assemblies of the universe.

This had been fulfilled in this way from ancient times: together with the divine and rational assemblies, and in the ranks of the angels, the human being who had come into existence in the image of God
honored the Word, his father, with songs and praises. He did not distract his mind by fashioning lifeless idols, or by the enticements of demonic deception,
or by the fables of the error of many gods.
For these things appeared only later, newly invented in the fabrications of poets. But those earliest founders of our ancient race had not yet learned these crafts:
painting, carpentry, and carving. Nor were they concerned with this later craft of deeds

that were evil. In the simplicity of their souls and with their natural understanding, they called upon the maker of the whole universe and their Lord. Guided by their understanding, they acknowledged him alone as Lord and God of all. And just as those founders of our race acted,

so too did the Hebrew race, which had loved God from ancient times. Like a son receiving from his father, they received the good inheritance of a godly way of life. They honored nothing except the one God, the king who is above

all, and his Word, who is the savior of all, through a chaste life and godly conduct. For this reason they were found worthy of the revelation of the Word of God, of prophecy, and of instruction in righteousness.

43. Thus the Word of God, the maker of all, filled every place and every region beyond the world and in heaven, as well as the element of earth, with the seed of intellectual and rational being. But the seed that fell upon

earth, the seed of that intellectual and rational plant, is this human understanding, which is now enclosed amid abundant reeds and the straw of an earthly, perishable body, and surrounded by the many stars [?] of mortal life.

But if he accepts the work of watchfulness, is cleansed of the matter that corrupts him, recognizes his sower as the Word who is above heaven, praises him here, and, like a newborn child, studies his first teaching, then at the proper time

he will yield the ear of his virtue and the fully ripened fruit of his rational nature. As at harvesttime, at the very death of his mortal life he will lay aside the superfluous outer stalk and the earthly, perishable clothing of the body.
For he has made good use of them for the growth of the fully ripened fruit, and has rightly stripped them off at the proper time.

And he himself, having grown in virtue and gathered the powers of his virtue, is kept in the treasury of good things, perfected, having lived among the perfect. And to the sower of all and the cultivator
he will yield the fully ripened fruit of the praise due to God, because in this life he recognized him alone as his Father, his King, and his Lord, and acknowledged this one alone

as God, his maker and creator, in those bonds of kinship and brotherhood, and also in the place where the virtuous gather, so that they may exalt him and honor him with the honor fitting and due to him.

But he will not call anything else God when it does not deserve to be called God, but only the one to whom everything bears witness, whom the whole visible and invisible creation calls God and worships, since he alone is the cause of everything.
44. Such, then, are these matters. But let us return once more to the preceding part of the argument before us.
Those heavens, then, and the places in heaven that are perceived through the bodily senses, and the earth itself and the air, and this whole structure made from them,
which resembles a great city, is no different in its nature from those lifeless elements found in its parts: earth, water, air, and fire.
But we should not even think of calling the citizens of the great city material beings, nor should we say that there is one and the same seed
for the rational soul and the perishable body. For the mind, the word, and the rational soul,
and every intelligent nature, are rightly and precisely said to be the offspring of the Word, God, the creator of all.
They are not a portion of earth and air, nor do they come from cold and hot substance, but from powers nobler than these, which were deemed worthy of sharing
in virtue. For the first things became the cause of those that came after them. The first are these offspring of the Word, and those that come after them are the irrational things.

After the primary substances come the others, those that follow their causes. But these primary and firstborn beings are intelligent souls, for whose sake even the stock of bodies subject to suffering had been prepared.
For was it not for the inhabitants that a home sufficient for them was to be prepared? For this reason the heavens appeared first, as a place fitting for those citizens above it and within it.
And the vaults within heaven were set apart for inhabitants of its own kind. But as for the citizens on earth, never call them,
O soul, brute animals, or the race of creeping creatures that discharge their venom, or any of those things that share the nature and name of irrational beings.
For these are your servants, subjected to you by the law of nature, and they are compelled to render to rational beings, as their masters, the service that is due.
For the ox works for human beings, willingly placing its neck under the yoke for labor. The donkey, when carrying a load, acknowledges its nature.
And the [?] rejoices when its master rides it. The dog hunts and wags its tail for the one who feeds it.

45. Sheep and flocks, too, give human beings everything they possess, and wild animals provide an outlet for courage. We kill and subdue even these, and by the resourcefulness of reason we catch the birds that fly on high.
And we bring up the creatures below, in the depths of the sea and within it. Nature plainly teaches that all these things were established for the sake of humanity.
But the human being is the offspring of the divine Word, made not for anything else, but to behold his Father, the Word, and through knowledge of him to discern all his Father's wisdom.

that throughout the whole created order, both what is visible and [?], while still a child [?], he should become like his Father and emulate him in everything—in law, speech, knowledge, and wisdom—and should learn to live as an image

of virtue, and that, together with those assemblies in heaven, he should learn, like a prophet and priest [?], to offer up from earth the praises that are fitting for the King of all and for God, the cause of everything.
46. In these images, then, the Word, the teacher of all nature,
marveling at the distinctive excellence of human beings, cries out in divine songs of praise and says: “What is a human being, that you remember him,
or a son of man, that you care for him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you clothed him with honor and glory.

You gave him authority over the work of your hands, and you placed everything under his feet: all sheep and cattle, also the wild animals, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea that dwell in the paths of the seas.”
47. This alone, among the kinds of creatures on earth, is rational and loves God.

Speaking about this creature, another prophet spoke of God and taught in a mystery that the human being came into existence in his own substance in the image of God. He says plainly: “And God said, ‘Let us make humanity in our image, according to our likeness, and let them rule over the fish in the sea and over the birds of heaven,

and over the livestock and over the whole earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.’” He also joined the deed to the word: “And God made the human being,” and he said that he made him in the image of God.

Furthermore, he established the image of the divine likeness still more fully through the divine breathing, when he said: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul.”

He teaches that God gave him preeminent leadership and kingship by saying that they should rule over everything on earth: livestock, birds, creeping things, and wild animals. Nature itself bears witness to all these statements: everything works under his hand, and everything is subject to this creature,

which is rational. Even if you have not heard the divine words, I do not think your mind is so completely dark that you would fail to consider within yourself whether it is bodies and flesh [?], or something else, something divine that moves the body,

that is capable of this excellence. I mean the ability to know, to employ discerning reason concerning the substance of something that exists, to preserve learning through memory, and to reach out toward the contemplation of everything

that exists. Turn to yourself and ask whether the nature of the body is capable of knowing the constitution of the world, the activity of the elements, the beginning, end, and middle, number, the succession of seasons, and the changes

of times, the cycle of years, the arrangement of the stars, and the many other things that human beings have discovered through practical experience in measurement, calculation, and arithmetic. For these things are incorporeal
and are objects of rational contemplation. To attach them to bones, flesh, and blood is immense and boundless folly.

It is right to ask those who think this way about them: since these five senses encompass all the powers of the body, which of them is capable of teaching a human being the understanding that comes through learning?
Is it perhaps the sight of the eyes? But this only distinguishes colors and shapes. And if you say hearing, you are speaking of an instrument,
you say, that receives high and low sounds, not rational understanding. Taste, likewise, is a perception of sweetness [?] and of food of that kind; and smell
tests odors, not branches of learning. Again, this sense that extends throughout the whole body encounters hot and cold things, hard and soft things,
but not virtue or wisdom, which is far more excellent.

And what about those animals that lack reason? Do they not have eyes, ears, nostrils, taste, and touch? Yet none of these has attained the excellence of rationality, because it does not belong to the body or to irrational sensation.
Rationality alone receives these philosophical disciplines, and it dwells only within the human race. Now, if someone should wish to argue shamelessly
and say that we have nothing beyond these irrational animals, since we are born and perish just as they do,
because we all have the same food from the earth, the same bodily nature subject to suffering, sensation that is no better in any respect, and likewise the same fatigue and rest, which are alike—

to all of us, and the decay of the body and its dissolution into its elements. But you still do not say that any of them, like this rational living creature, has approached visions of things without bodies.
Nor has it received rational instruction, or stored education in its memory, or considered discussions of virtue and evil. Philosophy has never even entered its mind.
But leave all these things aside, since not all human beings possess them. These are the questions I put to your argument:
Has a city ever been built by irrational animals? Do they have any conception of carpentry, building, weaving, or farming? Has a ship ever been constructed by them?
And has the wonderful art of navigation ever even entered their minds?
Yet in bodily qualities their superiority is much greater than ours, for the human body is inferior to all the animals.
As the poets sing, the human race is weak. In bodily size, it is impossible to say how far it falls short of the elephant. In strength and superiority,
it cannot even be reckoned alongside the race of camels. In vigor and swiftness of foot, it concedes victory to countless animals.
As for tracking dogs, which learn to follow a scent with their noses,

what creatures have a keener sense of smell than they do? Gazelles are said to see better than all others; because of their sight, they received their Greek name, meaning “those that see.” From this we must go on to say how much weaker by nature
the human body is than bears, lions, leopards, and countless other creatures. It is quickly overcome by animals that attack it and is easy to take by trickery. Yet this small creature

subjects all these creatures just mentioned whenever it wishes—not through bodily or physical strength, for it is very small and would not suffice to fill even one bear’s belly. Rather, it has within it a nature superior to the body:

the power of the mind and of the understanding soul. Through the excellence of wisdom, it devises these wonderful things. Through these you have been honored by God like a beloved son. Why do you dishonor

your own greatness, imagining that you are entirely this flesh and this body, and likening the divine and rational understanding within you to creatures that lack reason and are wholly subject to decay?
Does not even the nature of irrational animals convince you, or their common designation as irrational, or this evident service
they provide for your use, carrying burdens and working—tasks they have never refused? For God has given you authority and dominion over all these creatures.
48. Thus the human being alone among earthly creatures was made in the image of God. He leads and brings them wherever he wishes, sometimes driving those animals suited for running,
sometimes tending [?] suited to this, sometimes employing tame animals in his service. He soothes and calms a savage nature, sometimes overcoming it so as to bring it to gentleness, and sometimes

gathering them by the many devices of reason and confining them inside a house. Not only this, but he even takes harmful creeping creatures in his hand and plays with them. Those that breathe death and spit venom he makes his playthings.
49. The human being alone among earthly creatures was not content to live in the wilderness, in caves and on the heights, but built cities with walls,
and adorned them with streets, fortresses, dwellings, and other buildings.
50 [?]. The human being alone among earthly creatures does not obtain his food in the same manner as irrational animals. For they, lacking knowledge, rely solely on nature’s assistance

and feed on the stalk itself, without its being cultivated or cleared of weeds. But through his knowledge he cleans it, then grinds it finely and prepares it thoroughly, and carefully subjects it to fire,
making wheat into bread whenever he wishes. He takes care to prepare food so that it will provide healthy nourishment. All the produce of the vineyard and the olive tree,
and of fruit trees yielding every kind of delight, he tends; and he alone applies these things to the healing of the body.

51. He alone among earthly creatures discovered through law and reason a way of life marked by orderly conduct. He became a general, trained athletes, and developed the intermediate arts and these higher ones,
which instruction imparts through rational excellence. 52. He alone among earthly creatures, while preserving the likeness of virtue—the scales of justice, weights, measures, and kinds

he devised and distinguished, directing by reason what should be done and what should not. He knows how to give each person what he deserves. For, it is said, fish, birds, and animals eat one another,
because there is no law among them. But to human beings he gave justice, which is far better. What one of the poets said seems very fine to me.

53. He alone among earthly creatures, displaying in himself the image of the Word of God, established a tribunal on high. Acting in the likeness of God, the righteous judge, he distinguishes between life and death, assigning life to some
and giving death to others. 54. He alone among earthly creatures entrusts to a small piece of wood
his life, and discovered the [?] of navigation. He guides God [?] over the surface of the sea, lets himself down into the depths of the watery substance, and pushes away death standing beside him,
by looking upward into heaven and fastening the lifeline of those who sail to the Ruler of all.

55. The human being alone among earthly creatures discovered the science of the movements of the stars. Though he walks below in the body and is clothed in the weight of mortality, in his mind he ascends above,

and traces the circuit of the heavens [the sun], the moon, and the stars. He announces beforehand what is to come and the eclipse of the moon, and predicts the changing seasons and the alterations of the times.

56. The human being alone among earthly creatures has proved to be nature’s helper. He discovered the methods of medicine and grasped in his mind the properties of roots and drugs, and their blending and mixing in sweetness and balance,
and devised healing for sick bodies and help for human lives.

57. He alone among earthly creatures has proved to be nature’s helper. He discovered the methods of medicine and grasped in his mind the properties of roots and drugs, and their blending and mixing by weight and in balance,
and devised healing for sick bodies and help for human lives.

57. He alone among earthly creatures did not adopt the way of life of grass-eating animals, but followed nature well. In winter he casts seed into the earth, and at the time of blossoming he puts in his sweaty labor, and in summer he receives the fruits of his toil.
58. He alone among earthly creatures,
through rational understanding, gathered knowledge of everything, education, musical composition, and skill in speech. He advanced to the life and name of philosophy
and hastened toward the love of virtue in the soul. He made use not of bodily sensation, but of the power of knowledge and the vigorous exercise of reason.
59. The human being alone among earthly creatures has taken into his memory accounts of things that happened long ago, in ancient times, and converses with those who are no longer here as
with those who are nearby. He examines the thoughts of the wise who lived long ago and receives more help from them than from those who are with him. And through the power
of reason, through kinship of thought, he is with those who passed away before him.

60. He alone among earthly creatures has finely fashioned this articulate voice through the parts of the joints. Through the art of grammar he distinguished the primary letters, discovered the parts and power of speech, and devised the combination of verbs

and nouns, and the teaching of rhetoric and grammar. He gathers all these things and keeps them in his memory, bringing them together as into a storehouse filled with everything. He holds ancient events and histories in a single mind.
Whenever he wishes, he pours these things out like a river from a spring that never runs dry, flooding the hearing of those nearby.
61. The human being alone among earthly creatures imitates in his works God, who is over all. He fashions whatever animals he wishes and transforms this lifeless matter into likenesses and forms.

And he bears the forms of all animals in this [?] nature, through the rational power implanted by the Maker of all. A human being makes another human being, sometimes in stone, sometimes in wood, and sometimes

with pigments of various colors and in likenesses that do not differ from their originals. By these techniques he reproduces every kind of animal and plant, and through his works fully displays the power of the image of God.
62. He alone among those on earth has reproduced the vault of heaven on the earth on which he walks. He has fashioned a likeness of heaven in bronze, and the arrangement
of the wandering and fixed stars he sets within it. With the craftsman's art he arranges the sequence of seasons and times, and places the figures of animals around the outside.
Through his abundant knowledge he reproduces the heavenly sphere by a technique of visual representations.

Like God, he sets it in motion, so that the heaven on earth revolves in its course along with the universe. This revolves in a boundless wonder, and the things on earth revolve along with those in heaven—an earthly likeness made of matter. And the messenger of the hour cries out in a loud voice.
All of them move together with a single impulse. Those doors open by themselves when the hours arrive, and the lifeless figures of birds placed around it speak in chirps. And the moon on earth, from
the one in heaven, runs its course [?]. The bronze itself changes its shapes in the likeness of the moon, displaying its light when it is half, when it is diminished, and when it is full.
The representations of the hours follow the hours of nature, and in making a world, the human being rivals the creative work of the Word of God.

63. The human being alone among those on earth can drive far away the hidden, invisible nature of demons, through unutterable words, through prayers pleasing to God, and through the power of reverence for God in speech and conduct.
But even when he has turned aside from the straight path, he has been able, through the power of God, to subject this entire race that flies through the air by chants and incantations. And again,
by coercive devices and the enticing bonds of nature, he captures those bodiless powers that fly near the earth as though they were flying birds.
He draws them, binds them wherever he wishes, and seats them upon statues that he has made into gods. More than his fabricated divinity, he displays his own power through these works of his.
64. The human being alone shows how great is the excellence of his incorporeal, intelligent substance, and demonstrates that his power is neither enslaved nor diminished by sufferings.
He prepares his body for fire, iron, wild beasts, and the depths of the sea.
He approaches every kind of torture, knowing what his nature is. He hastens toward destruction; he is beaten and torn apart, yet he does not surrender what is within.
He demonstrates that he is someone other than the one receiving the blows, crying out, “Strike, strike the sack [the empty sack]; for it is not me that you are striking.”
And another cries out with freedom of speech, “Burn and roast my body, and satisfy yourself with me as you drink black blood.
For before the stars descend to earth and the earth rises to heaven, no wavering word from me will reach you.”

And one of God's friends, while enduring sufferings, uttered these words: “Who will separate me from the love of God? Distress, or affliction, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?”
Indeed, I myself have now seen some of them having their eyes gouged out, others deprived of their feet by cauterization, and others being crucified.
Their whole body is beaten, and their mortal nature is torn apart, but the understanding that loves God, which
dwells within them, remains unshaken and unsubdued. Nor does it surrender to those harsh torments.
Through the power of their virtue, they plainly demonstrate to those whose understanding has not perished that their mind is something other than that which is being destroyed.
65. He alone among the living creatures on earth has shared in the divine breath and has been deemed worthy of the revelation of God. And he speaks with the angel of God.

And he gained foreknowledge of what was to come, sometimes through dreams in sleep and sometimes when, clothed with the Spirit by divine power, he could even prophesy about the future and confirm his fellowship with the divine through the disclosure of those events.
66. He alone recognized that great reality, superior to everything visible throughout the universe—the one who cannot be seen with the eyes or perceived by touch or by the power
of any bodily sense, but is visible only to the mind and understanding. Through his own learning and the instruction of his nature, he acknowledged him and called him God.
He praised him and, through this knowledge, showed his kinship with the divine. 67. He alone stood as a spectator of the great works

of the Word of God, and was deemed worthy to praise his Father, who is above heaven, with praises fitting for God, and to resemble the assembly of angels in heaven. For he alone among the living creatures on earth received this distinction.
Through it, by the understanding belonging to his nature, he recognized the one who is the cause of all good things.
And he is commanded to offer praises of thanksgiving and fitting blessings as the repayment owed to a father.
68. The teaching of divine instruction itself confirms the testimony to all these things: that this one alone among those on earth has an immortal nature and is akin to the citizens of heaven—

this knowing and rational substance within human beings—and that he is the beloved offspring of the divine Word, the universal Savior of all, who is by nature perfect in the image and likeness of his own Father.
69. If, then, this rational living being, who has shared in all this
excellence, who alone among those on earth is in the likeness of God, this brother of the divine powers and the angels in heaven,
had conducted his life according to his nature and followed the divine law, he would already have been freed from this earthly and perishable dwelling. And while occupied with the affairs

of earth as though on a journey, if he had first trained himself in divine things, he would already have made his departure from here to the things that are his own and been enrolled among mature people, leaving behind his deficiency and the condition
of his childhood. Thus, then, by his Father's mercy, the human being necessarily put on a perishable body subject to dissolution, so that he would not struggle forever or remain bound without end
to what is perishable, but would soon shed the [?] and receive fellowship with those who are imperishable. For just as one conceived in the womb is wrapped in the covering belonging to that place,
and when the time comes for the months to be completed, the one being born strips off that very covering, then comes out into the light and draws in [?] air,

and from then on is counted among human beings, so also the race considered mature among human beings is, in comparison with the higher race, an unborn child, still being carried in the womb of the earth.

It is wrapped in this perishable skin. Through the mercy of God's great gift, it must necessarily strip this off, so that it will not be worn down forever amid those deficiencies, but will in due time come out
into the light and pass to an imperishable dwelling. For this reason, groups of wise people who loved God rightly felt distressed at sharing in these perishable bodies and longed
for their transformation into a better state. They pursued their kin and fellow citizens above, as did the one who said with a sighing voice, “Wretched human being that I am!
Who will rescue me from this body of death?” And again, “Although we live in the body, we do not serve according to the flesh.” And [?] he adds and says,
“For our citizenship is in heaven,” and, “We have drawn near to the city of the living God in heaven, and to the assembly of myriads of angels,
and to the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.” These are the utterances of knowledgeable people who love God.
70. But if there are many who [?] [love] the desirable things here, who are still children in their understanding,
what does this have to do with the true account? For the one conceived in the womb rejoices in the place to which he is accustomed and fears leaving it and emerging from the darkness within.
When he comes out into the light, he cries. Yet they too, if these natural processes of childbirth happen to them [?], come out of darkness into the light.
They are born sound and well formed, and are born at the proper time and season. He receives breath and the completion of his nature, and takes on human life. [?]
He enjoys the nourishment of the breasts and of infancy. Then he comes under the care of a nurse and is entrusted to guardians, instructors, and teachers.

Until he reaches full manhood. Then he passes through an excellent and distinguished life, with great wealth, abundant possessions, authority, leadership, and other ranks, with these advantages of upbringing that come from his good birth,
And those with which he was enriched through education [the enrichments], and other great advantages that he added to a pleasant life.
71. But if the one conceived in the womb undergoes an unnatural reversal, with the consequences that accompany his emergence in childbirth, why need I say that the infant turns inward,
And refuses to come out into the light, and suffers an unnatural reversal, while the iron instruments prepared for childbirth are applied to him forcibly and under pressure?

He is not found worthy of even a single birth, nor of human life, nor of the things that accompany it. Instead, he comes out of darkness into darkness and is deprived not only of human life but even of the name.
72. So, in the same way as these things, [?] the person who passes through human life on earth
Is no different from an infant without speech or knowledge, or from one still carried in the womb, and cannot be compared with those bodies outside, belonging to angels and divine spirits.

He too is a newborn without knowledge, and because of his great childishness he delights in the covering of flesh around him and loves his own womb. He does not know the place surrounding him, where killing
And darkness and other kinds of destruction graze as though in meadows of evil and darkness, as one of the ancients said when describing this air above

The earth, which is moist and murky, containing many mixtures from the multitude of vapors rising from the earth. Let us suppose, however, that there is someone, although he is still very much an infant.
But if he passes through this present life as befits his nature, and renders to the law of his nature a corresponding way of life, so that he does not think beyond the measure
Of his stature, and does not kick against nature, which carries him like a mother, and does not, moreover, forget his Father, but knows his Father in heaven, the common Savior of all,
And offers him praise and thanksgiving because he has given him a share in good things, and grows up under the discipline of righteousness,
And in his earthly conduct practices beforehand the heavenly way of life, then, when this person departs from this mortal life and puts off the body,
God’s angels assist at his birth when he is born into another life. The good powers receive him like a nurse, and the divine assemblies attend to him.

And to bring him to the fullness of good things, the Word of God himself, the teacher of heavenly conduct, leads him like a beloved son and trains him in the teaching of the kingdom of heaven. And when
He has made him mature and wise, he gives him to his Father, the King of all. They will clothe him, in body and soul, in an incorruptible garment of indescribable light,
So that from then on he too may be a help to everyone. Such, then, is this person’s end.

But the person who kicks against the course of his nature, joins in an evil reversal, dishonors the earth, his mother who carries him, acts wickedly besides, and does not acknowledge the Word of God, the common Savior of all,
And records countless fathers who do not exist in place of the one who does exist, and names as gods those who have never existed, in place of the one alone who truly exists,
And then, after these things, immerses himself entirely in the foul, lawless desires of this moist and corruptible substance,
Does these things not involuntarily, like that infant, but willingly and by the decision of his own free will.
He chose these evils for himself and committed them. The likeness offered by the illustration clearly shows what his end will be. For it is not cheerful faces and the laughter of

good angels that appear to him. Nor, when he comes out into the light, do the nurturing powers of God welcome him. Instead, at his end he flees from the exit and hides within the contemptible body, in its very limbs. When the body's dissolution approaches, and the change

contrary to nature takes place, those appointed to this task forcibly drag his soul away and seize it. Then, after his departure from here, while his miserable soul groans and sighs, it is not light or a life of good things,
but darkness and a place of destruction that will receive him.

And God's judgment will consign him, polluted and unclean, foul and loathsome, to purification through fire and punishment, because he was not admonished by the word and did not follow the divine law while he was able.

73. For the unborn infant in the illustration is deficient in every respect and entirely lacking in power: the soul does not yet make use of its understanding or of the body's senses. But the person whose mind is still

childlike among human beings, when compared and examined alongside the incorporeal and divine rational beings in heaven, is rightly called a newborn [?], even if he is wiser than all other human beings.

Even the most perfect of those on earth is no more than an infant when he himself, with all his perfection, is compared with them. But it is easy to consider in this way what he will become in excellence when he reaches manhood.
For if, while he is still a newborn and confined within this hard wall of earthly and perishable substance, he possesses such a power of excellence that he can not only know the things on earth
and work skillfully, but can even anticipate the way of life in heaven, becoming like God, and can make, whenever he wishes, likenesses of the things in heaven and of those on earth—all such things

as we have now listed—he can accomplish these while immersed in all this sediment of flesh and blood. How, then, should we not expect him to act when he reaches the full measure of a man's stature and is released
from these painful and perishable bonds and from these flowing, moist constituents of the body, and shares in a weightless existence and an immortal body? For if the mere seed of rational power
is so strong and capable on earth, although it has not yet attained its fully developed growth, and is even cast into the moist place of the perishable body's sediment, it is possible from this

to know how great the fully developed, fruit-bearing growth of the seed within souls will be, once it receives the cultivation it needs, is transplanted from here, and is planted in a better place, in good and fruitful soil.
There the heavenly Word himself, the sower of everything and the planter of all good things, will receive his own seed, and in the meadows of souls without bodies and without
physical substance, as in a paradise of those who love God, he himself will water his own planting, bring it to maturity, and lead it to an abundance of great blessings.

74. You can recognize the greatness of the excellent perfection of the human being from his changes and growth here, if you consider that a newborn infant is no better than a worm: it does not even use its bodily senses as irrational animals do.
Yet this deficient, helpless, weak, and unthinking creature, as it grows in stature, undergoes all this transformation and change over the course of time, and receives excellence, strength,
and beauty of both body and soul, so that even those who begot him, if they saw him, would not recognize whether this was the one who was sown in secret and conceived in darkness,
and whether this was the one who came out of darkness and was raised on milk and roots—whether this is the very same human being who now surveys the whole world with wisdom and knowledge,

who subjects to himself everything on earth. But if someone [?], in comparing the divine power and that of the angels with that of the newborn infant, were to place the fully grown man between them, he would not find an exact correspondence between the newborn's relation

to the fully grown man and the fully grown man's relation to the superior power. For the infant's condition falls far shorter of the fully grown man's than the latter's falls short of the power of the angels. For the newborn
human infant does not even resemble newborn irrational animals in its condition. But the one who has developed into a fully grown man and has shown himself to be a friend of God.
From here he enters into fellowship with the divine Spirit and speaks with angels, and he comes to love and delight in heavenly communion. And through a chaste way of life

and the fear of God, let him prepare himself beforehand. It is not across a great mountainous distance that he comes to share in equality with the angels, their life, and their excellence. The [?] word also shows this when it says, “What is man that you remember him, and the son of man that you care for him?
You made him a little lower than the angels. You clothed him with honor and glory.”
75. If, then, that newborn child, when he has grown to his natural stature and attained the understanding and discipline appropriate to him,
undergoes all this change and transformation, and no one can disbelieve his transformation because experience makes it plain,
why should we be amazed if the mind that brings a human being to maturity, being as it is,
and still a child compared with the full maturity of the higher beings, becomes equal to the angels when it reaches the completion of its own growth in stature?
But we see that human nature is dissolved at death. What of that? Is it not precisely from this that we affirm all the more strongly concerning the soul
that it does not die? For if, while immersed in a corruptible and mortal body, it displays all this power of excellence,

which our preceding discussion has shown, then, when it has been separated from fellowship with what is corruptible and has laid aside what is mortal like a fetter, how will it not then act, more than now, with its power
unhindered? Have you not seen that even here it acts badly when it has an attachment to the body? But if it renounces fellowship with the body, it comes to be by itself.
From this it is also clearly known that its substance is not corporeal. For how can that which opposes the body belong to the same nature as the body?
For the soul’s thoughts are healthy when the body’s passions are weak, whereas the soul is dark and gloomy when the body is stirred by its desires.
