For this reason, when the soul becomes foolish, it is wholly devoted to the body; and when it loves the body, it is deprived of its own excellence.
But when it gains strength against the body and flees from the passion of desires, it becomes wise. And when it becomes wise, it turns its face away from fellowship with what is mortal.
Immediately it devotes itself to chaste knowledge and withdraws a little from the onrush of the body’s nature. It becomes more fully illuminated, ordered, and alert,
when it holds firmly to its own wealth. Then it shares in knowledge, wisdom, and every excellence, when it turns its face away from the stirring of the body’s passions. Indeed,

it does not even consider it fitting to approach through the body’s eyes or to act through its other senses when it is contemplating excellence. And when it firmly closes its eyes and gathers itself inward,
it goes far away from those things that lie close to the senses and are visible. It remains near the body alone, but turns the soul’s eye in another direction.
When it is alone by itself, it then makes use of a clear mind and a pure memory. Speech goes forth without [?] and gives it drink, and all its rational powers act without hindrance.
But if something that strikes the body suddenly rushes in, just as a wave deprives the eyes of sight,
it immediately disturbs the soul’s vision. But if the soul relaxes and gives itself over to the body, and then shares in drunkenness, food, desires, and the rest of the pleasures
of the body, it strengthens the evil within it. Like a vicious and savage animal, that corruptible body rises against it, while the soul sinks down into the depths
and is filled with error, ignorance, and every kind of folly. Why, then, should we fear death, which is the separation of the soul [?] from the body? And why
should we not accept the laying aside of what is inferior as a help to what is superior, and acknowledge that then the lives of those who love God truly become pure and blessed?
when nothing disturbs them. For, conversely, if that rational nature, while it is in this place and in this vessel, dwelling on earth and clothed in a dense body
of earth, like an earthenware vessel, is so constrained in this garment, yet strives to leap upward in its thought and put to death its bodily members, the instruments of desires,
through endurance and restraint of desires, and eagerly hastens toward the dwelling of those who have no bodies,

and through a wise way of life continually separates and frees itself from its association with what is inferior, continually anticipating with delight its approaching death, when it will at last be released from its bonds and grow wings through its exercises and efforts here, and then fly away at its departure
and leave its earthly place and encounter what it has loved—do not ask how this will happen.
For when it receives fellowship equal to that of the angels in heaven, in its very body, whose nature is changed from corruption to incorruption, it becomes like light and like radiance, in that
form in which the race of divine angels also lives, according to the accepted teaching. Likewise, it shares both in their excellence and in their immortality.

76. For just as this form belonging to the seed that falls upon the earth is hidden from many, there is a hidden principle by which the little seed grows, which [?] is confined within the seed, quietly enclosed like a butterfly within its dense body.
And when this seed falls into the earth and its dense garment, wrapped around it on the outside, is dissolved through decay, it then shows itself to be alive.

The power within it stirs and takes hold of the matter beneath it. Then it begins to act, and its nature receives strength. It takes off its old, dense outer garment and puts on a new one, far superior to the old.
77. So it is also with the nature of the rational power within a human being,
which is now bound in a corruptible body and exercises only a little of its own power. But if it is freed from the corruptible thing surrounding it and receives a place in heaven,
and is sown and planted from here into the fellowship there, and is found worthy of a heavenly and angelic garment—

how it will be when it shares in pure life and is freed from its association with what is mortal is not for me to say. Yet this is readily understandable to anyone who considers the illustration. For the whole grain of wheat does not decay.
Rather, its outer part decays when it falls upon the earth, while the hidden principle within, and the power within it, lives and endures and becomes something better than it was,
so that it even produces living ears of grain. The same principle applies to plants and likewise to all seeds.

Is it only in the case of a human being that everything decays completely when it is dissolved in death, and that, together with the outer garment, the principle dwelling within it also decays? And is the incorporeal understanding that shares in all these powers, which because of its excellence was likened to God,

not even like these seeds that fall upon the earth—or is it not far superior? For it produces neither [?] nor grass, but these full and abundant ears of its own excellence, when it escapes from earthly corruption.

Thus, as though released from bonds, it exchanges earthly fellowship for heavenly fellowship, not without understanding. And when it is beside God, it will truly, like the angels, bring forth fruits pleasing to God, whose seed and power had previously been confined
in a mortal body and constrained as though in a furnace.

78. Now that all these things have been said to demonstrate the knowing and rational substance within a human being, let us proceed in our discourse to what follows. If, then, that human being who was brought up in earthly fellowship
had known his own greatness and had devoted himself to learning about God, there would have been no obstacle preventing him, once he departed from here,
from enjoying fellowship like that of the angels and sharing in the dwelling of his Father's kingdom
in [?]. But since it was not one human being, or two, or merely a few, but the entire rational race upon the earth that received the power of self-government,
because its nature is free, having received the seed of kingship from the divine Word, the King, it did not make good use of its own power.

But he worked with great pride at all the other things necessary for bodily use and helpful to life through the practical arts, and devised ways of cultivating the land, building ships, trading, and purchasing property.
And not only this, but also a great increase of wealth, with an unrestrained appetite for desirable things of every kind.
He lived abundantly from every source. But all those things that contribute to the salvation of the soul and to the righteous way of life that God loves—
these he destroyed at their root in his mind, and forgot his own excellence and that of his race.

He made those in heaven his brothers, yet by his own free choice he honored these foul bodily desires above his own greatness. He neglected the righteousness of his Father in heaven and his glory, and chose the irrational abasements of childishness and lust.
These are the things that the foolish among them habitually do,
like children who run away from the teaching, discipline, and care of those who cultivate their minds, and who fear these things at the time.

They honor beyond all measure the things that destroy souls and bodies alike. Through error and foolish training, they ensnare their souls in empty, senseless amusement. And while they were in this condition, an increase of evil came upon all humanity.
That envious one, who hates good things and plots against beautiful things, lay in ambush for them. In his evil envy, he prepared traps, snares, and a great abundance of devices of every kind
against the salvation of everyone, in partnership with evil demons. From above he drove them into the depths of evil, so that all these people might not see [?] upon
the earth, and might transgress the law of their nature. He made the growth of evil spring up within them instead of the seed of virtue. And the one who had been the most peaceful and wise of all,
and the most rational of all earthly creatures, fell into the utmost brutishness and irrationality.

Thus one of those who love God would weep over the reversal involved in their downfall, crying out and saying, “A human being in his honor did not understand, but was handed over to the beast and became like it.”
79. For these reasons, then, they fittingly needed a great Savior, greater than human beings. And this was he:
the very Word of God, who bears the burden and cares for everything. Like a good and loving father, he demonstrated in deeds his care for the rational souls upon the earth.
In his mission he hastened to seek and heal those who had wandered and were lost. The first discourse of Caesarea is finished.
The second discourse, against the philosophers. 1. A saving God, my beloved,
was needed by the human race: a God who brings abundant relief to those in perplexity, and who alone can give life to those cast down to death.
And the coming of God and the divine revelation of the universal Savior of all, which we say shone upon humanity, were necessary, because in the raging
of evils, in the depths of godless error, in the madness of many gods, and through the envious activity of demons, everything upon the earth had been corrupted.
2. But so that the reason for the divine revelation among humanity of the universal Savior of all may become still better known,
let us now begin, before anything else, to speak about the great downfall of the human race and their lawless wickedness,
and about their wrongdoing. Then we shall turn again to the hidden things of the mystery of the teaching concerning the divine revelation.
3. For the disease was not one affecting a single person; it had grown great against everyone.
That evil demon led them beyond every evil and disgrace, and, like destruction clothed in death, he shepherded the whole human race.

Thus he would drive the most peaceable of all to the utmost savagery, and the rational being would become the most irrational of all. And henceforth, God who is above all, the cause and maker of everything, the worshipful name of the unique nature without beginning,
and him who exists before everything, the Word of God, the father of intelligent and rational being, him who rules in heaven and on earth,
him who is always near this world and exists within it, and who is the cause of every good thing for everyone, the providence, the savior, the burden-bearer, the
giver of rain, the provider of light, and the ruler of life, the Creator of all—human beings, in the blindness of their souls, did not know him. And to the sun [?] and the moon
and to heaven itself and the stars they gave the title of objects of worship. Nor did they stop at these things.
4. But also the substances that are hot and [?], moist and dry—water itself, earth, air, and fire, whose nature is without soul and without
reason, as we see with our own eyes—and the remaining parts of the world they named Poseidon, Hephaestus, Zeus, Hera, and other such names, and honored them with the title of God.
Nor did they stop at these things. 5. They also made earthly nature, the fruits of the earth, and bodily nourishment of every kind
into gods: Demeter, Kore, and Dionysus. And others akin to these they made into idols. Nor did they stop at these things.
6. But they did not hesitate to call even the thought of their own minds, and speech itself, the interpreter of these things, gods. They called their mind Athena and named their speech Hermes.
And these available powers of learning they called Mnemosyne and the Muses. Nor did they stop at these things.
7. As they advanced in an abundance of [?] and in the enormity of their transgression, their own passions—which they ought to have driven away and healed through self-controlled reasoning—they made
into gods: their own lust, their shameful disease, the passions of their souls, the honored organs associated with filthy acts, and the parts of the body.
And again, their licentious pursuit of wanton desires they named Eros, Priapus, Aphrodite, and others akin to these. Nor did they stop at these things.
8. But they also sank to bodily reproduction and to the mortal dwelling here below. They made mortal human beings into gods, and after the death common to all,
they proclaimed them demigods and gods. For they supposed that the immortal divine being wandered beside tombs and among corpses. Nor did they stop at these things.
9. But they also honored every kind of irrational animal and venomous creeping creature with a worshipful name. Nor did they stop at these things.
10. But they also cut down trees and carved stones, and deposits in the earth—of copper, iron, and other material—
they searched out. They fashioned female figures, the forms of male human beings, and likenesses of animals and creeping creatures. And again, they gave these very things the name of gods.
Nor did they stop at these things. 11. But even those who lurk within the images and are immersed in the depths of darkness—the evil demons—
they fatten with libations and the reek of sacrifices, and they gave them the very name of gods. Nor did they stop at these things.

12. But also, through the bonds of abominable sorcery, through songs and whispered spells of unlawful compulsion, they drew the invisible powers that fly through the air to dwell with them. And in turn, as helpers in their delusion about the gods they had made,
they employed them. Thus they made other mortal human beings into gods for others.
For the Greeks honored Dionysus, Heracles, Asclepius, Apollo, and other human beings with the names of demigods and gods.

The Egyptians, in turn, regarded Horus, Isis, Osiris, and other human beings like them as gods. And those who boast of the excellence of their wisdom in discovering foreknowledge, Chaldean astrology, and numerical divination,

They did not know or understand. Those wise men should have weighed and considered within themselves the difference between the measure of God's power and [?] mortal, irrational nature. Because of this, they did not hesitate to call even irrational animals gods.
The Phoenicians called Mocuthroron and Usorus gods, along with other mortal human beings even more contemptible than these.
The Arabs likewise honored Dusares and Obodas, the Getae Zalmoxis, the Cilicians Mopsus, and the Thebans Amphiaraus; and among other peoples
there were still others who differed in their nature in no way from mortals. Although they were truly only human beings, they honored them with the name of gods.
13. Thus all the Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Greeks—the entire
mortal race, wherever the sun's rising illuminates the regions of the world—the elements themselves, the fruits that spring from the earth, and their own passions,
and even the madness of demons and lust, and, above all these, mortal human beings who were subject to human adversities
and established no teaching of virtue during their lifetimes,
and devised no instruction in chaste living for humanity, demonstrated no systems of philosophy, discovered no useful works, and left no disciples of their virtue
behind, and handed down neither words nor writings of peace for a good life, but were preoccupied with women and foul desires—and, as it happened,

I do not know through what error arising from association with demonic activities, they called them gods and demigods, honoring them with sacrifices and acts of worship, together with the deception of sorcerers.
They built shrines and temples in cities and villages. But him who alone is beyond the world, truly the Word of God, the King of all and Maker of all, they regarded as nothing.
These people advanced so far in madness and corruption of mind that, on the one hand, they called the human beings whom they accepted gods, while, on the other,
they attributed to these very beings the sufferings of mortals, assigning to them unlawful adulteries, foul deeds, perverted lives, and deaths. And these things
are not accusations brought against them by others, as they claim. Rather, they themselves bear witness to these things and acknowledge misguided mourning rites and deaths and, above all, adulteries
and the sexual abuse of males and the abduction of women. They have filled absolutely every city, village, and place with shrines, images, and temples.

14. And not only this: from the stories they made up about their gods, they also took provisions for a foul and lawless life. Through every form of obscenity, they proceeded to corrupt both their bodies and their souls. What sort of things they were doing

in imitation of their gods can be examined at close quarters among our neighbors, the Phoenicians. We see the things still being done at Baalbek, where remnants of ancient harm and traces of destructive evils
are still zealously maintained. The women there are not first joined in lawful marriage
unless they have first been dishonored through unlawful sexual violation and have participated in the lawless service of the mystery of Aphrodite. But now, as a demonstration of ancient evils,
this city alone is sick with this madness. Formerly, countless others suffered in this way, when the disease of demons held a stronger grip.

15. And not only this: those people who were consecrated to the gods already mentioned learn about that father and ruler of all the gods, who was overcome by bodily desire and fell in love with Ganymede,

through praises, songs, sacrifices, mysteries, writings, and votive images. Following the example of their gods' lust, they crossed the boundary of nature and became entangled in transgressions beyond description.
Without fear, they dishonored one another with things that are not lawful even to hear about, males committing shameful acts with males.
And they received in themselves the repayment due for their error, as the divine words say.

16. And not only this: they also perverted their inner understanding. They made irrational fate and natural compulsion the substance and foundation of everything, and lived the lives of animals, leading a life unworthy of being called life.
They neither investigated the nature of the soul nor believed in God's righteous judgment.
They did not bring to mind either the reward for virtue or, again, the punishment for an unjust life. 17. And not only this:

but in the middle of the theater they also rushed along like a herd—old men and young men together, and mothers with their sons and daughters, accompanied by slaves. They clothed themselves in every kind of depravity and licentiousness.
They filled themselves with drunkenness and obscenity as men gathered together with women. And what good, indeed, were they doing?
For they were not filling their ears with the sound of modest and God-fearing words,
nor using their eyes for the benefit of their souls, but to learn depraved words and to watch representations of every kind of obscenity.
For such were the spectacles they took pains to provide for all the crowds to see: the frenzied rivalry of horse racing, the wicked entertainment involving those devoured by wild beasts, and [?]

[?] the inhuman treatment of those killed in gladiatorial combat; and, again, obscene laughter over indecent acts, foolish excitement aroused by music, the shameful spectacle of men impersonating women, and loud shouting over songs.
For these things and others like them, countless multitudes of foolish crowds would gather, together with their rulers, generals, and governors, and they were given soul-defiling corruption to drink.
18. And not only this: they also built schools for godless teachings among the nations and in the cities.

Instead of teachings of righteousness that benefit the world, and instead of instruction in modesty and love for God, they used the inventions of wicked poets, containing depraved stories and tales about gods,

both male and female, and sufferings full of every kind of shame, and bitter mourning, in which they differed in no respect from mortal beings. Through instruction and practice in the false writings of dramas,
comedies, and tragedies, they first absorbed into their own memories these things that corrupt and ruin life, and afterward sowed them in the souls of the young.
But the first and last of all their wrongdoing was this: all people together, without exception—rulers and subjects, kings of nations, lawmakers, armies, and crowds in villages and cities,

among Greeks and among barbarians—turned in the opposite direction the praise that is owed and rightly belongs to the King of all alone. They called the demons who had corrupted them gods, and sang songs

to earthly and evil spirits, to lifeless elements, and to the perceptible parts of the world. And the congregations of rational living beings on earth offered no priestly praise [?], nor did their brothers
in heaven—the holy angels and divine spirits who praise the King of all—receive from them praise, praise in harmony with their own. Instead, contrary to their duty, they sang what was discordant
at celebrations and festivals to those deceptive spirits
who lead the world astray. They bestowed on them the honor of worship, so that by then the whole earthly order, together with all the nations throughout creation,
was no better than a ship caught in a storm, whose disastrous wreck was soon threatened by a final wave that would destroy it completely.

19. Therefore, because of all these things, the human race rightly needed God as its savior and helper. If only the crowds had been led into this error, the evil might perhaps have been small. But now, without exception,

the heads of cities, the leaders of nations, the kings of various places, the rulers of territories, and the satraps of nations—all of them together—were afflicted with this same demonic error of many gods.
Moreover, even those among the Greeks who prided themselves on philosophy and claimed to possess greater knowledge than most people
appeared in the marketplaces with an air of scrupulous purity, behaving arrogantly and wrapping their robes broadly around themselves; and over a vast and lengthy stretch of land they wandered [?].
And they appropriated this excellence in the study of discourse from other nations: surveying from here, and arithmetic from another quarter.
And again, from another place, music and medicine and those other arts that involve reasoned experience.
They gathered these things and others like them from everywhere, but fell into a mortal and godless way of thinking.

By devising persuasive arguments, some of them established indivisible bodies, without sides or with slanting sides, and unlimited in number, as the beginning of everything—though they had never actually experienced their existence. These same people also defined pleasure as the ultimate goal of happiness.
This is more destructive than all evils, and similarly [?]. For what could be more precious than pleasure to those who acknowledged neither providence, nor God, nor an immortal soul, nor a substance
capable of knowing, nor the Word of God who is above everything, nor any beginning or end in this existing universe, but only these irrational and soulless bodies that cannot be
divided? These are minute bodies, which, because of their extreme smallness, do not even fall within the reach of the senses. These very things, which are soulless, irrational, and without beginning,

they asserted to be ungenerated and unlimited in number, scattered about from ages beyond reckoning as they happened to encounter one another. Yet, although they are like this, they said that they are the cause

of the ordering of everything, and that there is neither God, nor providence, nor a Word that sees or rules over everything. Rather, even if he exists, he is to have no concerns himself, nor impose any on others.
And, as I suppose, it is pleasure that they love.

They attributed it even to God himself. Such were the views of the followers of Epicurus and Democritus, who were philosophers with their hair standing on end; and their entire tradition flourished among the Greeks.
Although they were like this, they approached assemblies as virtuous men. At times they went to the temples with the crowds.
At times they presented themselves as worshippers of the gods, out of fear of the punishment prescribed by law. Such, then, were those who fought on behalf of pleasure.
40. Others, however, fixed the boundary of providence at the moon.
The company of Aristotle’s followers excluded it from the remaining parts of the universe. These same people also defined the ultimate goal of happiness as neither virtue nor philosophy,
unless it is accompanied by abundant possessions and an abundance of gold and silver,
together with noble birth and fame among the multitude. And what prevented these men themselves from boasting of these things—men who, as though with bars and a gate, confined
the providence that governs everything to the moon? They said that the knowing and rational soul in a human being is mortal, and that it is nothing except something like the body, like

its appearance and its form. They are also accustomed to call it an entelechy. They did not regard the philosophical life, or even the virtue gained through training, as fully attaining the highest good.
Instead, they inclined toward the things of fortune: wealth, greatness, and noble birth. For, they say, virtue worthy of reason exists only with these things, and without them it is nothing.
The wise man has no advantage unless he is also rich. Nor does any good come near the man who concerns himself with self-control,
unless he is of noble birth. Not even justice itself and its perfect equity of virtue, if present in a human soul, are sufficient
for a life of happiness, unless a fine arrangement of the body’s limbs accompanies it. These people supposed that the Deity was somewhere outside human affairs, above the moon,
and said that God’s providence does not see what happens on earth. Nor did they recognize the universal Savior of all, the Word of God, the guardian of everything.
Nevertheless, they also came forward to worship the gods of the various places and cities. In their thoughts they philosophized about one set of things, but in their deeds they practiced another.

And they swore oaths by the gods in their writings and their public statements, but in their own thinking this was not really so. Rather, they considered doing this a way to win favor with the multitude.
For these are therefore demons and not human beings, [?] since they reject all sound philosophy.
21. Others besides these, who boast that they are philosophers, excellent in words, dared without hesitation to say that God is a body and that his nature is in no way different
from fire. This is another error of the Stoics, who said that this perceptible world is itself God and established a wicked and utterly corrupting doctrine.
For they said that the active cause and the passive capacity of matter come from one and the same substance, and that both are bodies, acting and being acted upon.

And the King of all, God who is over all, is in no way distinct [?] from perceptible fire, but is also mingled together with everything; he is in no way distinct from perceptible fire, but is also mingled together

with everything, like fire, in a cycle at appointed times. And the great evil is that, they say, God changes and then bursts into flame again. This, then, is the teaching of the Stoic philosophers: that the whole

substance and the whole world are, they say, mingled at a certain time with God in fire, and everything changes into something like a seed. Then, from this, the ordered arrangement of everything is brought to completion again, just as it was before.

And all these gods are like all the parts of the world, because the whole that is constituted from its parts is itself God—the entire world in its entirety. These same men also spoke of this intelligent and rational soul in a human being,
saying that it is perishable, since it is bodily. For what could restrain those who, against God,
the King of all, dared to say such things? They also defined souls themselves as consisting of matter and bodies,
and as being nothing other than mixtures of bodies and vapors. Yet after the end of life they remain for the periods appointed for them—
not the souls of everyone, but only the souls of philosophers. Finally, however, when everything burns, they too burn together with God and with the entire
world. Together these souls of the wicked and the righteous dissolve, those of the just along with those of the godless, as though melted down in one and the same fire.
And once again worlds are born from this fire that consumes everything, differing in nothing but corresponding in every respect to the former worlds, so that once more the very same people

will be born in them as before, and the very same completion will come about. Their lives will again be alike in every respect, without variation, and their appearances, customs, conduct, and experiences will be exactly
the same. Likewise, the same griefs, honors, comforts, and afflictions will again be received by those very same people, so that once again Helen and the calamities of Ilium

will be witnessed; and again Anytus and Meletus, and Socrates’ deadly poison; and again the very same disputes and divisions among the philosophers. Finally, everything will once more be consumed by fire.
After it has burned, it is restored again from the beginning and once more follows these same cycles. But these men, too, clung obstinately to their error.
22. The earliest philosophers, who are called natural philosophers and came before all the others, placed the origin of everything in a lifeless element.
They recognized neither God nor providence, neither the Creator nor the Maker of everything.

Idly and vainly they falsely claimed for themselves the name and appearance of philosophers. Some of them said that earth, a dry substance, was the origin of everything. Others said that Oceanus was the begetter of everything, thus giving this name to moist substance and water.
Some proposed fire, others air, and others mixtures of these, along with many male gods,
just as they also introduced female gods, marriage feasts, and the births of children. Through naturalistic [?], the invented stories of the poets

they recast in fine words as an adornment for their boasting. Thus these men too, as though by a reversal, fell back down from the heights onto the material elements and the perceptible parts of this world.
23. Others, however, apart from these, devised things contrary to all that has been said.

They maintained that there is nothing divine in this [?]—neither the God who is over all nor those who exist in particular places—and that this name is superfluous and applied to a substance that does not exist. They went to extremes of great wickedness.
24. Plato alone, out of all the Greeks, seems to me to have pursued philosophy nobly and to have held a correct understanding of the Good, who is first and the cause of everything.
He also understood correctly the second, who is the creator of everything.
25. He also established well and rightly that the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars, and, in short, the entire universe are created things that came into being from the God of all.
26. He also said that the substance of the soul is incorporeal and is not subject to decay.
He also knew about intellectual substances and about the Mind that is over all, whom we call the Word of God.
He acknowledged that he is the king of all. He also showed that he has authority over everything and, like a helmsman, cares for and governs everything well and properly.
He alone, out of all the Greeks, acknowledged the Word of God, the creator of the universe, as we ourselves do. We can readily hear this from him when he speaks about God as follows:
27. “Let us pay honor neither to the one belonging to the year nor to the one belonging to the month, and let us assign no share to them.

Nor should we honor the time in which the visible universe runs its course and completes it—the universe that the Word of God ordered from everything within it. The blessed person first marvels at it and afterward comes to love contemplating it, as far as mortal nature can.”
28. He also named the Father, the Lord of all, and the ruler of everything—
the one whom he has just called the divine Word—using the same words as we do, and he speaks as follows:
29. “All three of you are to read this letter, and not in a larger gathering.

Otherwise, read it privately between two, as circumstances allow. As far as you can, consider [variant: make use of] the greater part [?], through an agreement [?], through law, and through the lord who is
justice. Swear by care, together with wisdom, and by discipline, the sister of care, and by the ruler of all things that exist and that are to come.
And swear by the Father of the ruler and of the cause, the Lord whom, if we become true philosophers, we shall all know clearly, to the extent of our ability, as blessed people among humankind.”

30. He also taught that there is a just judgment of God, who repays each person as he deserves. He showed, in a most godly way, that the ultimate good is to become like the divine, to follow it, and to be united with it through virtue.
Yet he too, more than all the others, justly fell under the same accusation. Why? Because he knew the God who exists but did not glorify him as God.

Instead, he concealed the truth and supplied falsehood to the multitude. To those whom he loved, he properly revealed, as a philosopher, the Father and creator of this whole universe. But with the inhabitants
of Athens he behaved unlike a philosopher: in his account he brought Socrates down to Piraeus to pray to the goddess and to celebrate the festival of Bendis together with the whole population.
He also said of his teacher that, when the end of his life was near, he gave instructions

that they should sacrifice a rooster. This most distinguished of philosophers neither hesitated nor felt ashamed that, for the father of his own philosophy, through created, earthly matter, a little blood,
and the body of a dead bird, he had commanded them to appease the god.

He also called those honored in the cities demons, and he did well in this. But he also acknowledged that they have greater foreknowledge than mortal human beings. He said that this is what they are, and he spoke the truth.
But since he advised people to worship these beings as gods, and descended with the crowds into their error, it is fitting that we should also write about them, because under the guise
of philosophy he concealed the true account and brought himself down to falsehood. Now hear what Timaeus said [in the Timaeus].
31. To speak about the other divine beings and to know their power is beyond us.
But let us believe those who spoke before us, who are children of gods, as he said, and clearly know their own fathers. It is therefore impossible not to accept the children of gods,

even though they speak without comparisons and without reliable demonstrations. But since they claim to be recounting matters concerning their own family, let us follow the law and believe them. Thus,
then, as they say, let the birth of those gods be set out and recounted: Oceanus and Tethys were children of Earth and Heaven, and their children were Phorcys and Cronus
and Rhea; and from Cronus and Rhea came Zeus and Hera and the others whom we know, all those who are called their siblings, and also others who were their children.
32. Do you see how the philosopher, from the heights, from the patterns above the world, and from incorporeal, intelligible substances, came down to earth and to
Oceanus and sank into the depths of error, introducing a birth of gods—he who alone, beyond other human beings, was able to speak with such lofty-sounding thought?
33. What is that which always exists and has no coming into being? It is that which is grasped by understanding together with reason and always remains the same.
But that which is apprehended by sensation without reason comes into being and passes away, yet never exists fully.
34. This very thing, then—what comes into being and passes away and never exists fully—this clever fellow

now honors with the name of gods because of its coming into being and its course. Yet this same man, when rebuking those who proclaimed this account of the gods, said of them that they had not spread this error about those gods on the basis of comparisons and reliable demonstration.
After accusing them in this way, he next said that we should believe them and accept their claims, even though they say nothing truthfully. But even when he calls

them children of gods, it is clearly evident that he introduces their fathers as mortals, like everyone else. Again, he mentioned mortal gods and mortal children who resemble everyone else. And again, he mentioned

mortal gods and mortal children who resemble their fathers. They say that they clearly know their own fathers, and he makes no attempt to conceal it when he says that it is therefore impossible not to believe the children of gods.
Yet immediately he accused these very people of having spoken without comparisons and without reliable demonstrations.

He adds that we should accept them as people who claim to be recounting matters concerning their own family. It is not at all without purpose that he says, not that they recount these things, but that they claim to recount them, and that we should believe them. It is for us, he says, to believe that they are children of gods. He explains where he got this by saying, “As they said.”
For they said this, not I. That is, although they say these things about themselves and cannot establish them either from comparisons or through demonstrations
concerning themselves, nevertheless let us believe them. He then said, “Thus, then, as they say, let the birth of the gods be set out.” He necessarily said, “As they say.”
For these things are to be recounted, he says, not as my own views, but as their opinion.
35. You see, then, that he advised that one ought to follow error. And what reason does he give? Nothing else but the law—that is, the death penalty imposed by the law.
He openly admitted this very thing when he said, “Let us follow the law and believe.”
Indeed, fear of human beings and of the law removed from the philosophers that reverence and law of truth.
And where are those excellent and wise expressions of this elegant tongue, by means of which he used to speak so grandly in such utterly marvelous language?
36. For neither law nor any order is superior to education, nor is it right for the mind to obey anything or be enslaved to it. Rather, it is the ruler of everything, if it is truly
free by nature. And this is the same man who said, “Wherever someone stations himself, believing it best, there, as I think, he ought to remain amid danger,
taking no account of anything, neither death nor anything else, in comparison with disgraceful conduct.” And afterward he said, “For fearing death, gentlemen, is nothing
other than imagining [?] that one is wise when one is not wise.”

37. Why, then, wise man, after these statements, were you frightened of death, and why are you compelled by the law to honor mortal gods? And why have you judged those sons of gods worthy of belief and assent?

In your discourse you disparage and ridicule them because they have said nothing sound and offered no proofs about their fathers. How, then, while accusing them of these things, do you advise people to believe them? Let us examine who their fathers are.
38. “Earth and Heaven,” he says, “had children: Oceanus and Tethys, and also Phorcys, Cronus, and Rhea.”
And then, after all these, Zeus and Hera! Zeus after Earth and Heaven! Zeus after Cronus and Rhea! After all these! What are you saying, clever man?
Where is that great Zeus who drove a flying chariot in heaven? Or was that not your statement, which everyone applauds and admires, when you speak as follows?
39. “So the great Zeus himself drives a flying chariot in heaven and leads the way,
and hosts of gods and demons follow him.” 40. But I do not understand these things.

How did Zeus appear after Earth, after the sea, after Oceanus, and after the mortals Rhea and Cronus? And how does this statement of yours agree with that one? “Let us believe those who spoke before us,
who are sons of gods, as they say, and clearly know their own fathers. It is therefore impossible not to believe the sons of gods, even though they speak without analogies or reliable proofs.”

And he adds, “So let the account of the birth of these gods stand and be told as they relate it.” And look at what follows: a long discourse and the story of the birth of the gods that the poets tell.
He confirms it for us and says, “From [?] Cronus and Rhea came Zeus and Hera, and all those [?] whom we know and who are all called their siblings, and also others, their children.”
41. Do you notice, then, how this man tells his stories? What he relates is by no means inoffensive—[?] and contrary to his own philosophy.
For it was this very man who, in the Republic, rigorously drove away those whom he here calls sons of gods—all those ancient men who related stories about their divinity: Homer,
Hesiod, and, before them, Orpheus—far from his republic. Yet now the philosopher advises us to believe these very men, calling them sons of gods.
He sought gods through birth and conception, after Earth and Heaven and after that watery substance which he called Oceanus—even that father of all human beings and gods,
and Hera and those others after them whom he said are called their siblings and children. He acknowledges that these come from Earth and Oceanus, and afterward advises people to worship them as gods.
And where is that greatness of the intellectual essences? Where is the bodiless form beyond the universe, or that divine account of the nature that has neither color nor form?
And if every soul is immortal, why do you subject to mortals

those who are immortal, and to the bodies of demons that which is bodiless, and the intellectual and rational essence to things that are perceptible and perishable? So I think it right to criticize this man more than the others, although

affection draws me toward him because of the kinship of his teachings. For he alone, among all the Greeks, seems to me to have approached the outer gates of truth, and in many statements he showed his kinship with us.

But this man must not be honored above the truth for that reason. I think I should criticize him more than all the others. For he was a friend of the light and of the things that follow from the teaching,

He acted [?]; let him be accused and condemned to death. Although he supposed that there were no gods, nevertheless let him be judged, because, like the other living creatures, he knew only the things close at hand.

42. The Peripatetics, in turn, likewise support an opinion resembling this one. They followed this philosophy and supposed that the soul in human beings is mortal. They said that its form and its body were an entelechy [?]. In exchange for this life here, which they

alone knew, they will fall under many [?]. Those who supposed that the gods had never existed, in accordance with the law of the state, will be judged because of their fear of death and of the punishment imposed by law.
43. Again, the Stoics taught that everything is a body, that this perceptible world alone is God, and that the gods are
parts of it. They persuaded themselves to do whatever followed from these teachings of theirs, even if such things were shameful. Because they called the parts of the world gods
and worshiped earthly substance, will they really be beyond reproach? And those who defined the elements as the beginning of everything should, consistently, worship the elements.
44. But the man who, as though through divine revelation, defined what always exists and cannot come into being, and what is grasped through knowledge together with reason and at all times
remains the same and just as it is [?]—he spoke plainly, in clear terms, beautifully and wisely, giving a true account of the divine nature in these words:
“God, then, as our ancient saying also has it, holds the beginning, the end, and the middle of everything that exists, and brings things to their proper completion as he proceeds according to nature.
Justice always follows him, imposing punishment on those who depart from the divine law.” How, then, did he depart from the divine law and think so little of the justice
that governs everything, and provide us with these laws for mortals? And did this philosopher fear this death—this man who sends the soul above the vault of heaven? But I do not think
that this man firmly maintained that this human soul is immortal, because he made his teaching apply universally.
For it is not only the souls of human beings, but also those of dogs, monkeys, ants, horses, donkeys, and the rest of the irrational animals that are immortal.

And he said, in Egyptian fashion, that in its substance it differs in no way from the soul of philosophers. He supposed that these very souls pass through every kind of body and into the nature of these animals
the souls of human beings are poured. Because of these things, let him be rejected on this point as well:

how he affirmed the truth in one respect but spoke falsely in another. For although this man is indeed remarkable in having been able to apprehend the maker and creator of this universe, nevertheless, because he did not extend the principle of justice to everyone, let him be blamed all the more. For he knew God but did not glorify him as God.

Instead, he worshiped and served creation rather than its creator. He calls gods, and worships, those things fixed in visible bodies—the sun, the moon, and the stars—while at the very same time acknowledging
that they are made and perishable, composed by nature of fire [?], earth, and the rest of the elements. Yet he worships and honors these very things and calls them gods.
Then again, afterward, he acknowledges that these very things can be dissolved and are perishable. It is easy to hear him saying this in the Timaeus:
45. “God of gods, I am your creator. Everything, then, that has been bound together can be dissolved. Thus, because you have come into being, you are not immortal,
nor are you entirely indissoluble.” Again, concerning their coming into being—how it occurred and how it is defined—he says: “As fire is to air, so air is to water,

and water to earth. From these he bound together and established the visible and perceptible heavens. Through these elements and from them, being of this kind and four in number, the body of the world came into being.”

And afterward he says: “For the coming into being of time, so that time might exist, the sun, the moon, and five other stars, which bear the name ‘wanderers,’ came into being to define and preserve the numbering of time.
God made bodies for each one of them and set them in motion.”
Again he said about heaven: “Whether it always existed, having no beginning of its coming into being—not even one—or whether it came into being at some initial beginning.”
And then he answers himself, saying, “It came into being, for it is visible and perceptible to the senses.”
And it has a body. And all things of this kind are perceptible to the senses, and things perceptible to the senses are grasped by opinion and have been shown to be things that come into being.

46. Did the man who spoke so well and correctly about these things not stray far from sound reasoning when he called them gods and acknowledged that they were made from the perishable matter of bodies, of fire and water

and acknowledged that they were made from the perishable matter of bodies, of fire, water, air, and earth, which are dissoluble by nature? He says that they are perishable, and yet he calls these same things honored gods.
What, then, do perceptible and dissoluble bodies have in common with the name and honor of the one who is the cause of everything?

Or what shared meaning of the word permits the one who always exists and cannot come into being to be associated with that which is always coming into being and never exists, so that these may be called gods?
For if the one who always exists and does not come into being is truly God, anything that is not like this is not God. But if that which is always coming into being and never exists is God,
whatever is otherwise is not God. And what statement could be more impious than this?

For these two are opposite in their natures: that which is grasped by reason and understanding, and that which is apprehended through unreasoning sensation; that which can act, and that which can be acted upon. How can these opposites be entitled to a single name?
For it is as though someone admired the skill of a master carpenter but attached the honor to the work produced by him and reversed their rank.
Or as though someone called a ship its pilot, or a horse-drawn chariot its charioteer. Thus the man who dared to call God's creation gods acted very foolishly, although he was not unaware of this.
Indeed, he openly acknowledged that they are bound by the bond of God, the creator of all, and were constituted from the lifeless elements: fire, water, air, and earth.
But let this too stand as it is. 47. Why must I now bring to light how the philosophers assembled as though in battle formation,

and split into opposing sides and separated, and armed themselves vigorously against one another as though arrayed for war and combat, and how they clashed with shields and spears and the strength of men? One of the
poets might say, “A great cloud of turmoil was rising, of destroyers and those being destroyed.” For Plato called their war against one another a battle of giants, saying as follows:
48. “And indeed, there seemed to be something like a battle of giants among them because of their dispute with one another about being.”

49. But Plato himself said these things about the philosophers who preceded him or were his contemporaries. As for those who afterward cried out against him in turn and took up arms against him, the testimony is plain.

For Aristotle departed from discipleship to his teachings, along with his entire company, which he arrayed against Plato. Later still, after a time, other young men arose and censured those clever doctrines of Aristotle.
And on the other side they inclined toward the Stoics. But others, the Skeptics, set about tearing them apart and overturning them, and laughed at everyone alike.
For they all wholeheartedly undertook a great war of souls against one another. With words, almost as though with spears and shields, they armed themselves and fought.
And they struck one another down. They disagreed where they should not have done so, and where they ought to have fought with all their strength, I do not know how they came to agree.
Above all, they agreed in the error of many gods, which they knew before anyone else, and better than all other people, to be nothing.

That is, the Epicureans with the Stoics, the Aristotelians with the Platonists, and the natural philosophers with the Skeptics went to the temples together with their wives and daughters and the crowd of ordinary people.
And they approached lifeless idols in human form to worship them with vows as though they were gods, and with libations and incense and blood and sacrifices
of irrational animals they showed themselves honoring these things. In this one thing alone they laid aside their hostility toward one another.
In this they were all vainly acknowledging their error: where the truth had been revealed to them, they acted against it.
For wherever their knowledge was true, they ought also to have shown that their conduct was true:
to struggle and fight for it, and, if necessary, even to die for the truth.
They should readily and lovingly have accepted this, as people who boast that they are philosophers. But these men were friends with one another in this respect: they joined together

in falsehood. On matters over which they ought not to have fought, because of the obscurity of these unknown things, they disputed as though on behalf of the truth, and readily fought over trivialities,
hurling countless verbal blows at one another and striking one another. And why must I recount the wise men's fighting with one another, their opposing statements, and the civil war they stirred up,
into which they fell? For they employed human wisdom and the reasoning of a mortal mind, and did not accept God as their teacher.
[?] What then? Did those who fought over these things perhaps have no god?
Yet their multitude of gods was great: the one at Delphi, and the one at Miletus, gave oracles, and another, from another quarter,
cried out. Yet not one of these could become a teacher to those wise men, so that they might grasp the truth. They all worshiped these gods, just as their fathers had,
and all the Greeks acknowledged that they were gods. Yet they received no further help in discovering divine teachings, although nothing prevented them from immediately
being guided in truth and employing as teachers the gods who were near them on earth. They should not have fought or quarreled with one another, but should have ceased their disputes
and asked the gods about the matters they disputed, learning the truth from them as from physicians and receiving help. First, the followers of Epicurus ought to have learned not to be without gods
or enslaved to pleasure, nor to be deceived by those ridiculous notions that attribute the power to create the world to tiny, indivisible bodies. Instead, they should have been persuaded
by the gods themselves, receiving instruction about these matters. As for the followers of Aristotle, with their own eyes they saw temples, shrines, and images on earth,

not of one god, but of countless gods, in every city and every place. They ought to have investigated their power, and from the facts themselves no longer restricted their statements about providence to what is above heaven, or even above the moon. Rather, they should have been persuaded that also on

earth there are gods, and that they care for the human beings among whom they live. They could have learned about these matters from the gods themselves, and no longer fought with those arrayed against them over whether the soul is mortal or immortal.
Instead, they should have asked the god who was nearby and accepted a true statement as coming from gods. The same applies to the Stoics, and likewise to the Platonists,
and likewise to the Skeptics called Pyrrhonists, and likewise again to those of old who were called natural philosophers: they should not have failed to attain the truth, nor
like someone playing dice—natural philosophers: they should not have failed to attain the truth, nor, like someone playing dice, supposed that whatever came into their minds was the truth.
Instead, they should have asked the gods who lived among them about everything unknown. But not one of the wise men did these things; it did not even enter his mind.
Or were they perhaps without a god, and did they, with an impious disposition, grow weary of the gods and reject this? But in this way they are all alike without a god,
and the philosophers especially are shown to be so, and to be far worse than ignorant people,
who, concerning marriage, a journey, blindness, or bodily illness,
did not grow weary of asking the gods. And the gods readily listened and gave oracles without grudging to those who asked them.
Yet surely the wise ought to have questioned those gods among them, whom they worshiped and honored, not about their bodies but about the healing of their souls.
But the fact that not one of those remarkable philosophers did this establishes one of two things for us to recognize:
either these men are not wise, or those beings are not gods. For if, while they truly were gods,

these men despised them, then they are not wise but foolish and ignorant. But if they truly devoted themselves to the love of wisdom and excelled in knowledge beyond the multitude, it is clear that, with sober judgment, they laughed at the foolishness of the multitude. And likewise,
51. But if those who are called gods really existed, why indeed did they come to dwell amid earthly affairs?
Or was it entirely for the common benefit of all humanity? If that was the case, why did they not abandon these
empty tales and proclaim to everyone the things that help people acquire virtue?
And why did they not devote themselves to establishing laws for humanity, setting common conduct right and prescribing for everyone actions conducive to a virtuous life?
And why were they not more concerned with healing the passions of souls than those of bodies, and with freeing from foolishness and ignorance, rather than from a lack of possessions, those

who sought refuge with them? And when they saw people who loved wisdom suffering day and night in their search for truth, laboring and disputing as they sought an account of the worship of these gods,
and also entering the shrines of divination, sacrificing as their ancestors had done and honoring them with the customary honors, why did they not welcome them with loving words and, for their labor,

praise them, then release them from their disputes with one another, and give them help in their toil so that they might become truly wise concerning God and become philosophers? Why did they not teach them the wisdom of true philosophy, which does not deceive?

But because they did not do this, they made it clear to everyone that they are not gods, and that those who boast of being philosophers are not worthy of this name either. For if they had truly been wise,
they would never have thought them gods, since they gave them nothing worthy of gods and were unable to teach divine matters to those who were intent on knowing them.
52. But those men, who were not really like this,
instead conformed to the multitude and called gods those whom they knew more certainly than anyone else were not gods. What name do they deserve? I have no need
to say more, except that those men, with their flowing locks, went to the temples together with shopkeepers, contemptible men, and prostitutes.
And what, indeed, did these wise men ask of the gods? No one can say that they asked for things that help philosophers. Thus, indeed, no god presented himself to them as a teacher of instruction

that would benefit them. Rather, as the diviners say, they were supposedly useful helpers in the lives of ordinary people: for finding a slave if he should [?] and run away, or an article that had been lost, or for buying a village, or for trade, or for taking

a wife, or for other similar matters. Over these things, with a little rooster's blood, or the sacrifice of a ram or a bull, and with [?] and bowls, or a little flour, or wreaths that they bought, they regarded their gods
with wonder and amazement. But they had no god who was a true teacher concerning the things that lead to virtue, or concerning the healing of the soul.
Not one. For this reason, it seems to me, these wise men labored so strenuously in their battles with one another.
They greatly intensified their divisions with one another and fell short of the true knowledge of God. Thus, in their speech, there were gods, sons of gods, demigods, and good spirits
to be heard from them, but in their deeds everything was the opposite, and they boasted of setting one contrary thing against another.
It is as though someone wished to show the sun and the heavenly lights to a person who was unwilling to lift his eyes upward.
And he would lower his hands to the ground and throw himself onto the earth, seeking these heavenly powers in clay and mud.
Likewise, then, the whole human race, together with philosophers and kings, through madness of mind and the deception of evil demons, believed that the essence
that is intelligent and divine, beyond heaven and beyond the world, existed down here in a particular place, in bodily forms and in the passions of mortals and immortals.
And since all this madness of mind was afflicting the whole human race, how could we not rightly say that our way of life needed God as Savior, a divine revelation, and a helper [?] common to all?
53. Furthermore, they were all led into great madness, so that they even sacrificed their loved ones to those who were thought to be gods.
They showed no compassion for their own flesh, but even killed their only children and their beloved sons in forgetfulness and dullness
of mind. For what madness is greater than this: to sacrifice human

beings and defile all their cities and all their homes with the blood of their own people? Indeed, do not the Greeks testify to these things? Their entire historical literature is full of accounts of them.

54. For every year the Phoenicians used to sacrifice their loved ones and their only sons to Cronus. At Rhodes too, a human being was sacrificed to this same god on the sixth day of the month of Kanun.
This custom prevailed for a long time and was then changed. They would keep one of those publicly condemned to death until the festival of Cronus.
When the festival arrived, they brought the man outside the gate, opposite the statue of Aristobule, gave him wine to drink, and killed him.
55. In the city now called Salamis, formerly called Coronia, a human being used to be sacrificed in the month called Aphrodisius among the Cypriots,

to Agraulos, the daughter of Cecrops and daughter-in-law of Agraulides. This custom continued until the time of Diomedes, and was then changed so that they sacrificed a human being to Diomedes himself. The temple of Athena, Agraulos, and Diomedes stood within a single enclosure. As for the person who was sacrificed,
when those of his own age led him along, he would go around the altar three times.
Then the priest struck him in the stomach with a spear, and afterward burned his whole body on the fire that had been prepared.
Diphilus, king of Cyprus, abolished this practice in the time of Seleucus, who discoursed about God. He changed this custom to the sacrifice of an ox.
56. Amasis also abolished this practice of sacrificing human beings at Heliopolis in Egypt, as Manetho testifies in his writings On Ancient Matters and On Justice.
57. Human beings were also sacrificed to Hera. They were selected in the same way that unblemished calves are sought out, and were slaughtered.
Three were sacrificed each day. Amasis ordered wax images resembling them to be set up instead.
58. At Chios too, they used to sacrifice a human being to Dionysus Marios [?], while
tearing him apart; and also at Tenedos, as Euelpis of Carystus says.
59. The Lacedaemonians too, as Apollodorus says, used to sacrifice a human being to Ares. And the Phoenicians, during their great calamities, whether wars, plagues, or famines, used to sacrifice
one of their loved ones, chosen for Cronus. This history of Phoenicia is full of accounts of those who were sacrificed. It was written in the Phoenician language by [?] [Sanchuniathon].
Philo of Byblos translated it into Greek in eight books.
60. Istrus says that in ancient times the Cretans used to sacrifice selected boys at their sacrificial assemblies.
Human sacrifices were completely abolished everywhere, according to Pallas, who compiled an extensive account of the mysteries of Mithras in the days of the emperor Hadrian.
61. In Laodicea in Syria, a virgin used to be sacrificed to Athena every year, but nowadays a doe is sacrificed.
62. The Carthaginians in Libya also used to perform this sacrifice, which Iphicrates put an end to. The people of Dumatha in Arabia used to sacrifice a boy every year,
whom they buried beneath the altar and used as an idol.
63. Phylarchus wrote that all the Greeks together used to sacrifice human beings before going out to war.
64. I pass over the Thracians and the Scythians, and the fact that the Athenians too killed the daughter of Erechtheus and Praxithea.
But who is unaware that even now a human being is sacrificed in the great city at the festival of Zeus Latiaris?
Even now, it is not only in Arcadia, to Lougkos [Lycaeus], nor only in Carthage, to Cronus, that they all sacrifice human beings.
Rather, to commemorate the custom, every year they regularly sprinkle their own blood on the altars. Distinguished philosophers also testify that these things are so. Diodorus,

who abridged the Library of History, said that the Libyans publicly sacrificed two hundred boys from their leading families to Cronus. In addition to these, they themselves added to the sacrifices no fewer than
three hundred others. The man named Dionysius who wrote the history [?] of the Romans said that Zeus and Apollo once demanded human sacrifices in Italy from those

called Aborigines. Those who received this demand sacrificed to the gods a selection of all their fruits and flowers. But because they did not sacrifice human beings, they fell into every kind of calamity.

They had no relief from these evils until they gave a tenth of themselves. Thus, when tithes of human beings were selected and sacrificed to Zeus and Apollo, they became a cause of the land's devastation.
All this destruction of lives was wiping out human habitation.
They could find no other hope of deliverance to record except that which came from God the Savior, who alone, and no other, was needed by the mortal race.
65. Such, then, was the condition of all people everywhere in matters concerning the soul.
Yet it was not enough for them to act wickedly in these matters. They were also being crushed by countless other outward troubles, by incurable calamities everywhere and in every country.
For all the nations throughout the inhabited world, barbarians and Greeks alike, as though driven by the activity of demonic madness, were afflicted with a severe and terrible disease.
They were thrown into turmoil, so that the human race had neither fellowship nor agreement within itself. The great body of our common nature was torn apart in every direction.
People lived in every corner of the earth, fighting one another over their customs and laws.

Not only that, but they also became savage in the persistent hostility with which they opposed one another, so that at all times and throughout their lives they were occupied with fighting one another
and with war. Thus anyone who wished to travel somewhere for trade could not do so,
unless he armed himself as for battle. In villages and fields, farmers had to wear swords
and acquire a greater stock of weapons than of the tools needed to cultivate the land. Raiding and abducting people from their neighbors was regarded as a virtue
among them. The entire historical literature of the Greeks and barbarians bears witness to our account. For the books preserved among the Jews teach that, before the time of Augustus,
and of Tiberius, in whose days this Savior of ours appeared among the people. Previously, kings and regional rulers were everywhere, in every city and every village.
66. Then, immediately after the exodus from Egypt under Moses, when the Jews came to the land of Palestine, they drove thirty kings in all from their cities. But there remained, without being
uprooted, those who lived in Gaza, Ashkelon, and Joppa, retaining their inhabitants, settlements, and kings. Azotus too rebelled independently.
Scythopolis and the cities around it likewise had their own kingdoms, as may be understood from these things,
so that they spent their entire lives in struggles and wars with their neighbors. And when the magnificent temple in Jerusalem had also been built,
which Solomon built, what need is there to tell how many wars afterward brought punishment upon the Jewish people themselves,
because of their neglect of the worship of their God? Because of this, they themselves also separated from one another
and rose up against themselves, having separate kings who were enemies. Some of them held what was formerly called Samaria,
and is now called Sebaste, as their royal city. Others lived in Jerusalem, and they were continually at war with their fellow countrymen,
and those with them. 67. Those who lived in the land of Arabia also suffered things like these.
For there were many local rulers among them too, and among the Syrians as well. They guarded their own territories so that no one could mingle with them or pass through them,
while continually ravaging the land of their neighbors and constantly engaging in the siege of cities and taking one another captive.

And not only this: all Libya and Egypt were also subject to all these rulers and kings as though they were gods. They had tens of thousands of gods in the villages and the different cities, and kings likewise,

who also established conflicting laws for them and were the inventors of every likeness of the gods. Because of this, to this day places among the Egyptians are named, and laws belonging to those who ruled in those places [?],
and both gods and laws together are made known to those under their authority. They made them enemies and haters of their neighbors. As a result, these too spent the whole of their lives in struggles
and were thrown into turmoil against one another, since they had so many rulers who were evil demons.
From here the error of many gods also began, like some evil disease that destroys souls, and spread to the other territories of the nations.
The Egyptians surpassed all other people in the worship of the gods, and were more ingenious than anyone else in devising ways to honor them. But as for what fruits they received in return
for their worship, do not ask! For in former times they did not have these fruits of peace and harmony with one another that are now plainly visible, but everything contrary to them.

Because of this, they wore themselves out throughout their lives in wars and struggles against one another, and filled their own lands with their own blood and slaughter, while the gods themselves provided them with these and similar deeds as the reward for their worship.
68. Even if these things are not known to everyone, who among those who love reading Greek writings is unaware of
the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, which Thucydides recorded, in which Greeks fought against Greeks? How they besieged the Potidaeans,
and how they overtook the Thebans and Plataeans; how the Thracians and Macedonians sometimes helped the Athenians and at other times became their enemies;
how the Athenians besieged Corinth; how they ravaged the land of [?] and of the Troezenians; how they devastated the Lacedaemonians, and in turn suffered the same things from the Lacedaemonians,
when they came to Attica and ravaged the land of the Athenians; and how, at another time, the Olynthians fought against the Athenians.
And they in turn fought with others, and these with their neighbors. Every kind of warfare flourished among them: fighting in ships and fighting on land,

and fighting on horseback. All these things happened when the gods, so to speak, numbered in the tens of thousands among the Greeks. Not only that, but they also associated with human beings and were honored and served.
It was not as it is now. Rather, as they say, those people of old worshiped them as their fathers,
and sought their favor so that they would be friendly toward them and speak with them, since the gods were there with them and lived with them on earth.
They helped them in many ways through divination and revelations. Yet these were the fruits of honoring the gods: wars, battles, devastation, and captivity.
69. But if you wish to examine things older than these, turn your mind to the one who sat at Delphi before the Greeks—to Pythius.
I mean the one proclaimed among all the Greeks.

This was the one who cried out to that Lydian and exerted himself, saying, “I know the number of the grains of sand and the measure of the sea; I listen to the mute and hear those who do not speak.” And the Lydian sent him, as payment for this song, gold ingots weighing two talents,
and golden bowls and basins as well. Yet for Croesus himself this god proved utterly powerless with his oracles.
Nor did this great god help the members of his own household at all to live peacefully and temperately. Instead, Pisistratus treated the Athenians harshly while Pythius looked on.

Among the Greeks, the other gods also held authority over them and were even partners in [?]. The people of Argos fought against the Corinthians, the Lacedaemonians against the Troezenians, and the Locrians in turn waged war against other Greeks.
And the Corcyraeans fought against others, and Messene was captured
four times by the Lacedaemonians. The Arcadians were confined, and the possessions of the Orchomenians and their walls were uprooted.
The Athenians defeated the Aeginetans, and in turn the Megarians defeated the Corinthians, the Lacedaemonians the Athenians, the Athenians the Boeotians, and the Locrians the Phocians.
All these were Greeks attacking Greeks, while the gods sat beside Zeus as all these things were happening:
Pythius himself, the Clarian, the Dodonaean, and the one at [?]. These sacrifices from demons,
and these sacrifices of a hundred bulls from the herds, and human sacrifices of their loved ones—perhaps because they were demons and were full of filth,
they took great pleasure in them and accepted them. Yet when people were [?] in this evil madness and love of war, and were behaving recklessly toward one another,
they did not restrain them, although the Greek gods were right there with them—those friends and caretakers, those lovers of the Greeks, those guardians. But indeed, if we ought to speak truthfully,
they were lovers of war, haters of humanity, and fighters against God.
For they themselves were the cause of all these things, because they loved the slaughter of human beings.
And whenever they were not allowed to obtain this through wars, they were immediately satisfied through the human sacrifices offered in every city, for they delighted in libations of human blood.

70. It must therefore be one of two things: either they were nothing, and an evil delusion gripped the people of that time, so that they honored lifeless images as gods and, vainly and pointlessly, sacrificed their loved ones in madness;
or, if there was a power [?] in them, it was certainly either a doer of good or a doer of evil. If, then, they were gods who were good
by nature, and were present on earth and occupied the center of the city, they would not have acted ineffectively.

this, but for the help and deliverance of those who lived with them. But if they were evil demons, they would have done everything contrary to what is good. What, then, is the sure test of these things?
Nothing but the fruits of their governance, for a tree is known by its fruits.

71. It is time, then, to examine the wars and battles—not those of enemies or of barbarians who rose against the Greeks, but those of the Greeks themselves, which they attributed to their ancestral gods, while they raged
against one another. What were the fruits? And the gods were close by, inside the gates,
and were honored all day long by the people of their city. What did they give their worshipers that was worthy of this worship? Or, first of all, peace, so that in a quiet and restful way of life
they might live, and then sound laws and the preservation of the good things they possessed. If, then, these things happened as stated above, there is no need
to doubt the nature of these good governors. But if the worst of evils had taken hold of the whole Greek world,
and the gods were more numerous than the human inhabitants, and were honored not only in every city but also in the houses, and while they were being honored,
they gave those who honored them nothing more than slaughter in wars, the devastation of villages, the destruction of cities, captivity, and exile,
while Greeks [?] against Greeks in these things, what remains for us to recognize and say except one of two possibilities? Either they could do nothing—
the gods, because they were nothing, and thus they were also far removed from being the cause of these evils—or they possessed some power
and were themselves the cause of the evils, either by allowing these things to happen in this way or by doing them themselves.
If, then, they themselves were the agents of the evils being committed, [?] they were negligent, they are again betrayers of their friends, not helpers but deceivers, and therefore evil.
72. For if they were not gods,
and did not even possess a nature superior to ours, but were simply human beings clothed in decency because of their virtue and wisdom, would they not have stepped in as mediators
and freed their friends from conflict, either persuading them with words or rescuing them by force and moving them far away from one another? And they would have advised them to do what was right,
acting as good people do, freeing them from their hostility and bringing them together for [?], since, after all, they were their friends.

73. What, then? Even good human beings would have done this if they had been welcomed. But the gods, though they were near and present with them, moving among the Greeks and receiving honor from them all,

neglected their friends, handing them over to bloodshed, the sword, and the slaughter of their lives. And why? Because they could not help them, or because, although they could, they were unwilling? For if, although
they could, they were unwilling, they were treating those who honored them not as helpers would, but as enemies and deceivers. For those who could have delivered them from evils
and did not do this very thing were no better than enemies.
But if they were willing yet unable, they deserve forgiveness because of their weakness. If, then, this was their condition, the claim that they are gods is unwarranted.
And this title of helpers was not truthfully attributed to them, since they did not even help human beings toward deliverance, because of the weakness of their nature.
74. But if they bring Fate against us, saying that it holds sway over everything, even over the gods themselves, and that it is the cause of war and of everything that happens
among human beings, our whole way of life is overturned when what lies within our power is abolished, and evil teaching and desire [and falsehood] come upon us in its place.
And so their belief in the gods is also nullified, since the gods can do nothing beyond what is fated.
These things must necessarily happen as they do, even when the gods do not wish it. And so, again, the devotion of those who fear the gods.
And so, again, the devotion of those who fear the gods becomes empty and futile, because they honor beings who can do nothing.
75. But in this those marvelous beings were caught out: they have no power to remedy human misfortunes, and they delight in the foul and contemptible stories about their divinity

and in the wicked and unlawful sacrifices offered by human beings. They were openly exposed. From these things, therefore, we should conclude concerning these gods, who used to do these things among human
beings, that they were such because their nature loved evil and loved war. Their own deeds exposed them.
