He managed the matter well and excellently, as was fitting. He relinquished the body for a short time and handed over what was mortal to death, to the poverty of its nature. Then, before long, he raised that very body from death
as a demonstration of divine power. He showed that the eternal life he proclaimed, which was in his hands, was stronger than every kind of death.
58. This, then, is the first reason. The second is this demonstration that divine power dwelt in the body. For in former times, those
mortal human beings who had been conquered by death, and in whom the common end had truly been seen, were made into gods by other people.
They called those who were held by death heroes and gods. In this he clearly revealed himself.
For this reason, the merciful Word of God showed human beings a nature stronger than death.

After its dissolution, he brought that mortal body itself to a second life. He presented to everyone, for them to see, the trophy of immortal life’s victory over death, and taught them to acknowledge that in him alone was the true God,
teaching this through death—he who bound upon his head the crown of victory over death.

59. The third reason for the saving death is this, which is expressed in hidden words. And what are these? The sacrifice that was slain on behalf of the [?] of all human beings, a sacrifice turning them away from the error of demons. Thus, one sacrifice

and a great offering, greater than every sacrifice—the body of our Savior, which was sacrificed like a lamb on behalf of the entire human race and all the nations, who were held in the wickedness of their ancestors’ demonic error—
was offered up on behalf of their souls. From then on, the whole unclean and unholy power of the demons was overthrown, and all error was dissolved and destroyed from its place by a superior power.
Empty and earthly. Thus the saving sacrifice taken from among humankind—the bodily vessel belonging to God the Word—was being sacrificed in place of the [?] of all humankind.
And this was the one who, through the slander of human beings, was handed over to death as a sacrifice. About him the voices of the divine words sometimes cry out, saying:
“Look, the Lamb of God! Look, the one who takes away the sin of the world!” And at other times they proclaim beforehand: “Like a lamb
he was led to slaughter, and like a ewe before its shearer he was silent.”
And Scripture itself teaches the reason, saying: “Truly, he endured our sufferings and bore our pains, but we considered him afflicted, struck by God, and humbled.

He is killed because of our sins and humbled because of our wrongdoing. The punishment that brings us peace was upon him, and by his wounds we shall be healed. We have all gone astray like sheep, and each of us has turned his own way.
And the Lord laid upon him the sins of us all.” For these reasons, then, that bodily [?] vessel of the Word of God is sacrificed. But he himself is the high priest.
The one who serves as priest to God, the King of all and Lord of all, is distinct from the sacrifice: the Word of God, the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God.
And before long he raised that mortal vessel from death, establishing it as the firstfruits of salvation for us all and of participation in the undying life with God.

And he set it up as a trophy clothed in victory over death, over the deeds of demons, and over those involving human sacrifice. For this reason he was also given the name “Christ,” which among the Hebrews, in this form

of the high priesthood, came into use. Thus he received both names: the name “Jesus” signifies the saving sacrifice, while the Hebrew custom concerning “Christ” indicates the high priest, the Word of God, who serves as priest on behalf of us all.
60. Besides what has been said, there is also another important reason for the saving death, namely the following.

For his disciples needed to see clearly with their own eyes the life after death, the second birth, on which he had taught them to set their hope and for whose sake he had also encouraged them to persevere under the yoke of righteousness.

He therefore rightly granted them the opportunity to see this with their own eyes. For it was not [?] those who were to enter a life of righteousness who needed first of all to receive this teaching through a clear vision,
but far more those who were soon to proclaim it throughout the whole world and to make the knowledge of God, given by him to all nations, shine among all human beings. These very people

needed to receive strong assurance of life after death, so that, without fear or dread of death, they might undertake this struggle against the error of the many gods in their delusion. For if they had not been trained

to despise death, they would never have prepared themselves to face afflictions. For this reason he especially armed them against the power of death. He did not impart this teaching to them through words and utterances,
nor did he, like human beings, set out persuasive arguments and analogies concerning the immortal soul.
Instead, through the deed itself, he showed them the trophy of victory over death.

61. For in former times death was terrible to all human beings, the destroyer of our mortal race. It was regarded as the dissolution of the whole human nature, soul and body together. Such was its dominion.
And no one had ever been able to remove this terror from humankind. Everyone mourned in fear, small and great, rulers and subjects, kings and common people alike, and all the multitudes of nations

and families, because of death. There was no consolation for human beings against this evil: neither speech nor outward practice, neither a way of life nor the thinking of the wise, neither the writings of the ancients nor the prophecy of prophets nor the revelation of angels.
It surpassed everything and stood above everything. That bloody, boastful, arrogant death held victory over all.
The whole mortal race was subject to it and engaged in every kind of injustice, in the defilement of bloodshed, in unlawful deeds,
and in the deception of every scheme of evil, godless wickedness. For death was the cause of all these things.
For, as though they no longer existed after death, many used to do things worthy of death in their conduct; and as though they were not
subject to punishment, they therefore lived a life of dissolution brought on by death—a life without life. They took no thought of God or of God's just judgment.
Nor did they keep alive the memory of the intelligent substance of their souls. Instead, they dealt with one cruel ruler, death. And the destruction that came from it, which was the dissolution
of everything, was what they convinced themselves of. For this reason they called death Pluto, a wealthy god.
And death was not their only god, but also those things held in honor before it, which brought their life of desire
to fulfillment. Thus they had gods: bodily desire was a god; food was a god; the seed that falls into the earth was a god; its blossom was a god;

the flowers of [?] were a god; the pleasure of drunkenness was a god; bodily love was a god; desire for these things was a god. From this came the mysteries of Demeter and Persephone, and the abduction of Kore to the underworld,

and her subsequent return. From this came the festivals of Dionysus, and Heracles, who was overcome by drunkenness as though by a great god. From this came the mysteries of the sexual immorality of Eros and Aphrodite.
From this came Zeus, who went mad after women and loved Ganymede—the fabrication of stories about gods who loved desire and filthy passions. And death was the cause of all these things.

For they thought that death was the end and conclusion of everything, the dissolution and destruction of souls and bodies alike, and that there was no other life besides this bodily, physical life. They lived a life worse than that of every kind of irrational animal.
The King of all, the Word of God, had compassion on these people at the prompting of his Father's mercy, and hastened to help them, like a king who is very
merciful. He devised a way to rebuke death through human nature, although he himself is life, the Word of God, and the power of God.
But he arranged for that fearsome one who was at work among human beings to be rebuked, not apart from the one being helped. For this reason he used a human weapon and a mortal body.
He who is without a body conquered death through what was mortal. This was how his first mystery involving the body was accomplished.
From this came the sign of victory, the cross. And from this came the remembrance of immortal life forever, his commemoration [?].
For he used a mortal weapon and showed everyone a great wonder: the sign of the victory of immortal life, which he raised against death.
For he gave up what was mortal as food for the beast, and he was immediately nailed to the wood
of the cross, so that his mortal nature might be known to everyone, and what had happened might not be hidden from anyone—not from
human beings, nor from demons, nor from the higher powers. For it was fitting that they should all clearly see what was mortal, as in a great theater,
as it bore witness to its own nature, and that afterward death should come like an evil beast and devour what was its portion.
Then the power of life would come after death and once again establish for everyone a victory over death,
showing what was mortal to be immortal. So the power that had held the body—the Word of God—left it for a short time.
And it hung on the wood for a little while and was dead. But the Word that gives life to all was not dead.
Rather, what was mortal bore witness to its own nature. Afterward, that dead body, which had been seized by death, was now being taken down by human beings.
It received the customary care and was handed over for burial according to human custom.
The tomb was a cave newly cut out, a cave that had just been hollowed out in the rock and had never held another body.
For it was to be reserved for that dead man alone [?], who alone was wondrous. It is indeed wonderful to see.
The rock itself stands upright, alone on level ground, and contains only one cave within it, lest, if there were many caves in it, they should obscure the marvel of the one who conquered death.
So the dead body, the vessel of the living Word, lay there, and a large stone closed the cave. Death boasted greatly of this, as though declaring that, look,

it had also seized this one under its power, along with those it had held from ages past. But before a period of three days had yet passed, life itself appeared again, after a sufficient rebuke had been administered to death.
For if he had risen immediately, ahead of time, he would not even have been thought to have died. But he was truly lifted up, and he truly died,
and for a time he truly endured death. Then the Word of God itself, which gives life to all, revealed the hope held in store for all humanity
through the second birth of that mortal body. 62. What, then, happened after these things?
From now on I will not be your teacher about what happened. Instead, let those who saw these things be witnesses,
excellent witnesses worthy of the truth, who with their blood and their lives confirmed the truth of the events they had seen for themselves.
And through the power of the one about whom they testified, they filled the whole creation with the righteousness they proclaimed.
Those, then, who were eyewitnesses of what happened at that time, and who saw with their own eyes the second birth
that had reached them, handed these things down in their testimonies. For the events were not merely heard by them in words and spoken reports; they were also seen in actual fact
and carefully examined by touch by those who testified about them. For this reason, they themselves, having plainly grasped these things by sight and in reality,

and having seen the trophy of victory over death, learned well to despise death. They taught this very thing to their disciples: that they had received from their Savior the certainty of life that does not
die. Thus afterward the whole mortal race also found relief from the terror of death, because the one who had formerly been feared
was rebuked before everyone, and they gained firm confidence in life after death.
This was not through the skillful words of sophists, nor through the invention of persuasive speeches, but through the actual deeds that had come to light.
They no longer feared death as they had before, but laughed heartily and abundantly at the hour of that terrifying one,
so that they even pursued death out of love for the undying life that follows it.
63. From this time onward, people became concerned with a holy and chaste way of life, with zeal for every virtue, with remembrance of God, and with much discussion of
true righteousness and turning away from evil and godlessness. Not only this, but firm convictions about life after death also began to stir in everyone,

along with a sound and true understanding of the righteous judgment before God, the King of all. Because of this, from that time onward the entire human race was transformed toward virtue in ways beyond words.
It spits in the faces of idols, tramples on the unlawful ordinances of demons, and laughs at the ancient error handed down by its ancestors.
64. From this time onward, people are instructed in heavenly teaching and in words imparting knowledge of God, so that henceforth, in this creation visible to the eyes
they should not marvel at the body, nor, when they look upward and see the sun, moon, and stars, should they limit their wonder to these things, but rather to the one who is beyond
these things, the hidden one who cannot be seen, the Creator of all, who is the maker of everything. They have learned to acknowledge him and to fear him alone.
65. And again, unlike before, this bodily nature—miserable and perishable, without soul or reason—and even its primary elements, earth and water
and air and fire, are not considered gods by the person trained in the new teaching. For he has learned that the excellence of his own soul is far greater than theirs.
65. And again, unlike before, this bodily nature—miserable and perishable, without soul or reason—and even its primary elements, earth and water
and air and fire, are not considered gods by the person trained in the new teaching. For he has learned that the excellence of his own soul is [?] greater than theirs.
66. And again, unlike before, he is no longer a slave to his own passions, nor is he overcome by filthy desires.
Back then, however, he was overcome and did not overcome them. He even made gods for himself.
For he was commanded to root out evil itself from his mind and soul, along with every evil desire and foolishness, so that he would not even dare to look at a woman with
shameful lust. 67. And again, unlike before, he does not marvel at the [?] of his soul and dare to call it a god. Nor does he call his own mind Athena.
Nor does he use other similar names from fables. Instead, he knows and blesses the Word of God, who is beyond everything, the maker of all, the Wisdom of the God of all, who alone is his Savior.
68. And again, unlike before, mortal people who departed from the world in a shameful death and surrendered control of their lives to death are no longer named heroes
and called gods by him. For he acknowledges as his Savior only the one who is above death, the victor who holds the trophy of victory over the might of death.
69. And again, unlike before, he does not marvel at lifeless idols, nor does he unnaturally honor the irrational nature of animals through the worship of demons. Instead, he laughs
at the error of his ancestors and turns his face away from their manner of life, which lacks knowledge and sight of God.
70. And again, unlike before, he does not marvel at the appearance of evil demons or at the deceptive mirage of earthly spirits.
For, bound [?] by the mighty power of a single word of the King of all, he has the power to undo that race of humanity’s accusers
and has learned to put an end to those harmful beings and drive them out of bodies and souls.
71. And again, unlike before, he is not defiled by libations and incense, or by blood and sacrifices, not even by sacrifices of irrational animals.
Much less does he take pleasure in killing human beings and in human sacrifices. For he has learned that God needs nothing and takes no pleasure in bodily matter or in the smoke of earthly sacrifice,
but only in an enlightened mind, purity of soul, holiness of life, and sacrifices without smoke or blood,
which the Savior of all himself ordained should be offered through the words of the mysteries, throughout the whole human world, in remembrance of him.

72. And again, unlike before, he does not dare to call bodily nourishment, drunkenness, desire itself, or his passions gods. For he has learned from the sayings of his Savior to put to death his members that are on earth.
73. And again, he is not shaken when he hears about death, nor does he fear the separation of his soul from his body, nor does he call death a god. For he acknowledges only the one who is above all,
the life-giving Word of God, who is his Savior and the conqueror of death.
74. Equipped, then, with all these teachings of righteousness, the person trained in the new teaching does not surrender the truth even to those eager to fight against God.
Instead, he stands with firm resolve before fire and iron, and endures before savage beasts and the depths of the sea,
and before all the other terrors of death. They make sport of death, which formerly was harsh and, even to hear of,
was terrifying. Children and women by nature, and men, both barbarians and Greeks, have received from our Savior’s resurrection great assurance concerning immortal life,
and pursue a life of excellent wisdom and reverence for God. They credit their Savior with the trophy of their victory over death and of the eternal life that follows.
75. Consequently, the rational human race, whose lot it is to live on earth for this purpose,
acts in accordance with its nature and is taught to live in remembrance of God, who is full of every good thing. This agrees with the prophecy of the prophets,
who long ago, tens of thousands of years beforehand, proclaimed this in advance: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord their God,
and all the families of the nations will worship before him. For the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and he rules over the nations.”
76. Consequently, places of instruction have been established throughout the whole human world,
and the words of God and instruction in a chaste and God-fearing life are proclaimed for all the nations to hear.
77. Consequently, in every city and every place, assemblies drawn from everywhere honor the Word of God, who gives life to all, with songs of victory.
78. Consequently, songs in harmony with those of the assemblies of angels in [?], addressed to God, the King of all,
are also offered in harmony by the human race. Henceforth, together with those who dwell near God, who is above all—
the spirits and intelligent, bodiless powers—those whose lot it is to dwell below, in the earthly element,

the rational souls of the righteous, also send up fitting songs and blessings that are owed to their one Savior and the source of all their good things, using the bodies they wear as musical instruments. And what had never happened before,

now takes place throughout the whole human world: all humanity, as if with a single utterance, offers the fruit owed to God, the King of all, throughout each day, at the same hours and at corresponding times.
79. Now those genealogies of demons and stories about gods have grown old,
decayed with time, and been forgotten. But the word of Christ is renewed among everyone and remains forever. Now divine laws and readings are proclaimed throughout the earth,
and teach all people self-restraint. Instruction in true reverence for God has filled every region of barbarians and Greeks.
Now the [?] voices and the many voices of languages, with one way of life and one utterance,
offer harmonious blessings to the Creator of all; and one word, the same law, and one mystery worthy of God,
and the same way of life are what they follow. Now a single harmony of souls and agreement in teaching have been established throughout the inhabited world.
And from their own places, together with those who live in the east, those whose lot it is to live where the sun sets praise the one God who is beyond all, the Lord of the whole world,
at the same moment, with the same teachings. They credit no one else, but only the Christ of God, as the source of their help.
And those who occupy the northern region call him Savior, together with those in the south.
And they honor him as God in the same words, so that a barbarian can no longer readily be distinguished.
And even if a Greek seems [?] in speech, it is not that a Greek is otherwise different from a barbarian. For with God there is neither barbarian nor Greek, because everyone who fears God is wise.
And now Egyptians, Syrians, Scythians, Italians, Moors, Persians, and Indians have all alike become wise through Christ’s teaching, and through these things they are becoming wise.
And they all alike train themselves to face death boldly and to despise this life, while holding out one good hope founded on the promise of the Word, our Savior.

But they have also learned that they will receive the immortal life of the soul in the dwelling of the blessed in heaven, and the kingdom of God promised to those here, as a trust pledged to them. For he confirmed the promise by his deeds,
their Savior himself, through his struggle with death. Through this he showed his disciples that death, which had been fearful to everyone, was nothing.
And he himself set the promised life before their eyes in a visible manifestation for them to see, and the firstfruits of our hope and of the life of our body
without corruption, and of the soul without death, and of our exaltation to be like angels, he made his own image through his resurrection.
80. These, then, are the saving deeds, beneficial to the world, of the manifestation of the Word of God among human beings. But if anyone should further desire
to be enriched by countless other proofs concerning his divine power, he needs leisure to examine what has been written about him.
From these, a few predictions concerning the deeds that he was to perform,

as proofs of his divinity proclaimed beforehand, I will select from the writings of his disciples and set at the beginning of my next discourse for those who do not know them. The third book is finished. Of Caesarea.
The fourth book. Of Caesarea. 1. It is now fitting that we hear from him himself, the common Savior of all, who speaks with human beings and, like a good father with his sons, acted as their parent.
And he gives his answer in a way that mortal nature can hear, through the instrument that he assumed,
as through an interpreter. For when he was making his divine manifestation among human beings,
he displayed many other clear proofs of the power of his divinity through his deeds. Anyone who wishes can gather these from the writings about him.
And this evidence established from his own utterances is also no small demonstration of his truth. These very utterances must be presented to those who do not readily agree to believe his deeds,

which are wondrous and divine, so that they may also believe the other things proclaimed about him. Through the power of his words, these utterances also provide no small proof to those who have understanding.
For just as we often do not see people with our eyes, but only hear their voices,
we know and distinguish the speaker from hearing alone—whether we should take him to be a Greek,
or a Roman, or even an Egyptian; whether he is old or young in age; and whether the sound is a woman’s or a man’s,
and whether the voice belongs to someone wise and eloquent or, on the contrary, to someone foolish and uneducated—so also in these matters,
even if it was not possible for us to perceive and see with our own eyes the divine deeds that the Word of God performed while living on earth, nevertheless, also from the teaching
of his own words, whose voice [?] and penetrates the inner mind, and from his foreknowledge of the future things that he foretold, and from the things that he promised.
that he would also act in later times. And from the outcome of those things spoken of earlier, and from the fulfillment of these things which, down to the present, before our eyes, by his power

are being accomplished, there has been no small demonstration concerning the things that testify to his divinity. For the miracles performed by him are divided between periods: the past, in which his activities on earth

that he carried out are remembered, and the later period, which extends to our own time. For those great deeds he performed long ago, while he was among human beings, were accessible to those who were present
at that time to see plainly. But those things are hidden from us and remain unseen. Likewise, these things too, which in our own time, in accordance with his earlier words,

have been fulfilled in their proper order and are visible to us in the actual events down to the present—the outcome of these matters was not yet known to those who lived then, at the time when they were being foretold.
And perhaps those who did not believe thought it impossible for them to happen. But it seems that even then those whose outlook was thoughtful, although they did not see the outcome of the
earlier words, nevertheless had reason to believe them because of his other deeds. For those who saw with their own eyes God's manifest mighty works and miracles and marvelous deeds and works

that put all mortal nature to shame—was it not reasonable for them to believe not only in the things visible then, but, on their evidence, also in the things concerning later times that his foreknowledge confirmed,
with ready confidence? Likewise, we too ought, on the evidence of these miracles that we perceive with our own eyes, to accept those things to which his disciples testified at that time.

For the things conveyed to the people of old through hearing alone are visible to us with our own eyes, and for those whose understanding is not corrupt they are sufficient demonstrations to confirm what was written.
And what are these things, which did not exist then, had not yet been established, and had not entered people's minds,
but were spoken of by him through divine foreknowledge, were fulfilled in later times, and are visible even now in our own time?

It is easy to learn from the following.

2. A certain distinguished man [?] held a position in the service of the Roman leadership and high command.
Because his beloved servant's limbs were paralyzed and he lay at home, when he saw our Savior displaying mighty works in others,
healing the sick, and curing every pain and every illness,

he recognized in his mind that this miracle was not the work of a human being. He approached him as God, without focusing on the visible vessel of the body, the mortal instrument through which he was revealing these extraordinary powers of his.
He fell down and worshiped before him, pleading and persisting so that he too might receive help from God through his servant.
And when our Savior said to him, “I will come and heal him,” the commander of a thousand answered him—for he had been deemed worthy of this office among the Romans—
and said to him, “Lord, I am not worthy for you to enter under my roof. But only speak a word, and the servant will be healed. For I too am a man in authority,
and I have soldiers under my command. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes.
And I say to my servant, ‘Do such and such,’ and he does it.” What, then, did our Savior do in response to this request? Listen, not to me, but to the writer himself,
who teaches as follows in these very words: “When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who were following him,
‘Not even in Israel have I found faith like this. But I tell you that many will come from the east and from the west and recline at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.
But the children of the kingdom will go out into the outer darkness.’” Then, after these words, he said to the commander,
“Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” And his servant was healed from that hour. When the commander returned home, he found his servant well at that very hour.
3. With how much authority, then, our Savior’s voice went out! How much excellence it displayed, how much power it held, and how much compassion!
And also the ease with which he so readily promised to bring welcome help! And what of the very wonder that accompanied the deed,
which we cannot understand as it deserves? For he said nothing more to the commander of a thousand than, “Let it be for you as you have believed,” and together with
the word he also granted healing to his son. How does this not show that it was truly God speaking through a mortal voice?
But if someone finds this hard to believe because of the extraordinary nature of the miracle itself,

he nevertheless has no right to object to his prediction. In it the great convincing force of the deed itself is displayed, if one considers that at that time there was just one Roman who approached our Savior—the commander of a thousand—who displayed great

and outstanding faith in him, far beyond that of the Jewish people. Our Savior himself prophesied that, instead of one, there would be many who, like him, would come to him from among those who live where the day rises, in the eastern region, and where the sun

sets. Through knowing him and confessing faith in him, they would be counted worthy of equal honor before God with the ancestors of the Hebrews. Now the father of their ancestors is the celebrated Abraham,
who left his idol-bearing ancestors and changed his dwelling, and turned from the error of many gods
to acknowledge the one God who is above all. And he foretold that people resembling this man and his sons, Isaac and Jacob,

would number in the tens of thousands among humanity throughout the whole inhabited world. These are, above all, the nations who live in the east and where the sun sets. And he adds to this the greatness of his
prediction itself: those Jews, he says, who are descendants of those friends of God and boast of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, because they opposed him and did not believe in him,
having deprived themselves of the light of knowledge, will go out, he says, into the outer darkness—to their ignorance, their utter lack of understanding, and their deprivation of the saving light.

This is what he foretold. Here we should turn our attention to the outcomes and take in with our own eyes how the Jews, who boast that they descend from those men called friends of God, have been rejected,

not only from the kingdom of God, but also from that very mother of their cities, the outstanding royal city, in which alone the law prescribed that they should carry out their splendid worship. They became slaves instead of free people,
though formerly they had been children of distinguished ancestors.

And, mingling with foreign nations, they submit to something over which they have no authority in a land not their own [?]. They are not even permitted to see from a distance that land where they worshiped.
They were left without rulers and without kings who exercised authority among them by hereditary succession; and to those who uprooted their temple from its foundations
and seized all the fruits of their labor, they are subject. They have no prophet among them as they formerly did, nor anyone who reveals things as in former times,

nor any help or intervention from God. All these things came upon them in their fullness, not formerly, but after our Savior turned his face away from them, in accordance with his predictions. Such, then, are the things concerning the Jews.
3. But in place of that one commander of a thousand who approached our Savior at that time, an untold number of people from all the nations—not only commanders of a thousand, but also the great mass
of the Roman armies, as well as tens of thousands of rulers and governors who exercise authority over nations and regions, and others who stand far above
these in the honor of high office, those who take pride in royal courts—approach God’s Christ just as that commander of a thousand did. Through his teaching they have come to know the God of those
God-loving men who arose among the Hebrews, and have been counted worthy of an equal reward with them from God, the King of all. But if someone considers

how great a multitude of Christians is said to exist, and churches with congregations numbering in the tens of thousands, in the land of the Persians and of the Indians who live where the sun rises, and how, through our Savior’s own words

Among them, women love virginity, and men advance to perfect chastity and to perseverance in a life of philosophy and self-control, and to the great deeds of those who confess God while they are still alive.
5. And how these same people acknowledge that the one who arose from Abraham’s offspring is God’s Messiah, and through a new birth in him become children of Abraham.
And they confirm that earlier saying of our Savior. Likewise also in the regions
of the western world—all the lands of Spain and Gaul,

and the lands of the Moors and Africans, and in the Ocean itself and in Britain—they enroll themselves as followers of Christ. They have also come to know the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and invoke him in their prayers.

They have shown themselves to be partners with these men in the worship of God. If anyone, then, takes these very things to heart, he will understand the power of that saying which proclaimed beforehand and said, “Many will come from the east and from

the west and recline in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” He spoke these words to the military commander, and at other times, when speaking with the teachers of the Jews, he prophesied similar things.

He said it in this form: “When you see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves are cast outside. And they will come from the east and from the north and from the south, and recline in the kingdom of God.”

The truth of these things is plainly demonstrated by the turning of all the nations to God who is over all. These things, then, he told them about the turning of all the nations to God who is over all.

6. And through which people he was soon to bring about the calling of the nations, you learn from the account written by his disciples, which reads as follows: “As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee,

he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting nets into the sea, for they were fishermen. He said to them, ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers of people.’ Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
Going on from there, he saw two brothers, James the son of Zebedee
and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father. He called them, and immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him.”
Another writer recorded that he spoke to Simon twice in terms like this earlier saying. For when a large crowd was pressing upon Jesus,
he says that he got into one of the boats, the one belonging to Simon, and sat in it and taught the crowd. But after
sufficient teaching, since it was fitting that he should add a divine deed to his words to stir those who were watching, he commanded Simon to cast his net for a catch.
He said to him, “We have worked hard all night and caught nothing.

But at your word I will cast the net.” He did what he was commanded. When he enclosed a very large number of fish, their nets began to tear, weighed down by the great number, and they called to those in the boat beside them to help them.
Then, when they brought up the fish, they filled both boats so full that they were on the point of sinking. Simon was astonished and amazed at these things, and confessed that he was not worthy for

our Savior to approach him. But he, having shown him an image of what was to come, also revealed its meaning. Jesus said to him, “Do not be afraid. From now on you will catch people alive.” To Galileans who knew nothing

beyond the Syriac language and the humble, limited trade of fishing by which they made their living, our Savior rightly promised that he would make them fishers of people and heralds of his teaching. And he made them so,

and did not prove false to his promise. He showed the power of God accomplishing something beyond all human ability. For if he had drawn to himself eloquent and wise men, and those men among the Jews who were distinguished and wealthy,
and had used them as teachers of his words, it might perhaps have seemed reasonable to suppose that the matter had been arranged by human means. For most people are accustomed
to submit, or to be humbled by gifts from the wealthy, or to be led astray by excellence of speech and the glitter of wisdom, or to be overawed by the greatness of distinguished people. But he
He did not make use of disciples like these, but, on the contrary, of poor and despised men, uneducated in their speech, Syrians in their accent, humble and lowly in their appearance.
His work clearly revealed that he used divine power alone. He demonstrated this by first calling them with a single utterance and making them follow him, and then promising to make them fishers
and heralds of humanity, so that, instead of the nets they had, they would receive from him this net, woven from all the words of the Law and the Prophets and from those of the divine teaching,

and cast it into the human sea of the world, and reckon [?] that they could, with their rational nets full of every kind of rational fish. But at that time, when these things were heard in his utterance, they were words and sounds, and nothing more.
But the work of his divine power confirmed them before long. Those very things that had previously been spoken about them in words, he fulfilled in deeds.

Thus, in a short time, through those poor and uneducated men, he would gain tens of thousands of great crowds from the whole human race at once, and his churches would be filled in every land of Greeks and barbarians.
This was because of that single beginning [promise] of the divine utterance, in which he promised not to teach his disciples, but himself to make them fishers of people.

Consequently, he was shown not merely to know beforehand, nor merely to foretell something that was to come, but also to bring about everything he knew. He spoke in words and acted in deeds; he established what was to come through a demonstration and a likeness, and fulfilled it through actual action.

For those who, from ancient times in the old order, had toiled at night in darkness, away from the light of truth and the knowledge of God, and had been unable to catch anything that brought salvation—
he dawned upon them with his radiance. And he commanded those who were now in daylight and in the light, not through their own skill,
but [?] to trust his word and cast their nets into the deep. And they gathered this whole abundance of fish,
so that the equipment of their nets was torn, and the boats were forced by the weight to sink into the depths.
And because these events, as they happened in this way, brought Simon to amazement and no small fear, our Savior said these words to him:
“Do not let these things amaze you, for they are still only temporary and a likeness of what is to come. These are fish without voice or reason, and those boats and nets were made from matter
without life. But the counterparts of these things are not like them. So, a little later,
as for those [?], now, at once and on the spot, you will catch people alive. You will cease the fruitless toil of this fishing and become a fisher of rational creatures instead of these that have no
reason. And you will no longer draw them from the depths of the sea, but from the bitterness of an ugly
way of life, from the dark chambers of godlessness and from evil. You will draw those whom you catch into the light of understanding and the clear open air.
That is, you will catch them alive, because you provide them with life, not death. For those fish from the sea,
which previously lived in darkness in the deep, perish the moment they receive light and open air.

But those people who are caught by your hands are changed from the darkness of ignorance and caught for divine life.” For this reason he said, “From now on you will catch people alive.” Our Savior foretold these things through divine power.

And our Savior himself showed through the deeds themselves that these things were trustworthy and true. He himself, then, is the fisher who cast the net woven from hidden words through divine power, which cannot
be numbered. What is visible is a manifestation of something hidden. For the long course of the world before the divine appearing of our Savior had never experienced these things [?],
nor had Moses, who gave the Law to the Hebrews, nor the prophets of God
who came after Moses, nor tens of thousands of other fishers who had long ago taken up the teaching of God for humanity.
And they toiled hard throughout the night, but before his appearing they could not accomplish it.
Those things were done by that mighty Galilean, that poor man whose speech was barbarous—Simon himself. But the proofs of those things which at that time
were handed down by Simon are the churches that shine to this day, filled with rational fish far more abundantly than those boats, such as
the one in Caesarea in Palestine, the one in Antioch in Syria, and the one in the city of the Romans.

For we remember those churches and all the neighboring ones as having been established by Simon himself. Those in Egypt and in Alexandria itself he likewise established, not with his own hands, but through Mark, who had become his disciple.
For he himself remained in Italy and among the neighboring nations,
and he made his disciple Mark a teacher and fisher of those in Egypt. Turn your attention also to the rest of our Savior’s disciples, those whom he promised to make
fishers of people. And he demonstrated his word in action.
Even to this day he continues to do this, and throughout nearly the whole earth he fills his rational net with the whole human creation, and draws fish of every kind—
rational fish, both barbarians and Greeks—from the depths of wickedness and the darkness of godlessness, turning human souls back every day and every hour

toward the light of the knowledge of God that was handed down from him. Since these things are thus visible to our eyes, it seems to me that they establish unquestionable testimony to our Savior’s divine appearing.
7. Do you also wish to hear a third saying of the divine voice, which foretold
that his disciples would shine throughout the world? Listen to this as well. It runs as follows: “You are the light of the world. A city built on a mountain cannot be hidden.
Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a lampstand, and it gives light to everyone in the house.

In the same way, let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.” Here again he spoke to those fishermen, those who came from the land of Galilee. This is a district of Judea, as it is called, situated beside the sea.
Concerning it, Isaiah also, one of the prophets, both made known the obscurity of the land

and at the same time proclaimed our Savior’s appearing there, crying out: “Galilee of the nations! The people who sit in darkness have seen a great light.” So it was to those who came from there, insignificant and lowly men, uneducated in their speech and poor in their way of life—
to those very fishermen—that he said they would be the light of the world, and he confirmed this promise by his action.

That Simon himself, who was called Peter, should go out from Capernaum, a village in Galilee, and illuminate tens of thousands of human souls with the light of the knowledge of God, and become known throughout the inhabited world as far as the regions of the west,
and that his memory should remain among the Romans to this day, surpassing that of those who lived long ago,

so that he should even be deemed worthy of a splendid tomb outside the city, and tens of thousands of people from the Roman Empire should flock to it as to a great sanctuary and temple of God—how does this not bear true witness to the one who said to his disciples, “You are
the light of the world”? So too with John the son of Zebedee, whom he saw fishing with his father and brothers, mending the net,
and whom he deemed worthy of the calling and the promise: his name has shone throughout the inhabited world, and his words illuminate human souls through the written Gospel handed down from him,

which has been translated into all the languages of Greeks and barbarians and is proclaimed every day in the hearing of all nations. Moreover, his burial place in Ephesus in Asia is also held in splendid honor, and displays the memory of the light of his virtue, so that it may never be forgotten.
Likewise, the writings of Paul the apostle are proclaimed throughout the inhabited world and illuminate human souls. The witness of his death also, and the tomb over him, most splendidly

And to this day it is greatly celebrated in the city of Rome. What need is there to say that this way of life was also established throughout the whole world by the hands of our Savior’s own disciples?
Like a visible memorial monument in a celebrated city, where nothing is hidden, it stands continually in the midst of all the cities, in accordance with our Savior’s declaration.
It resembles a city set on a mountain. This is the message they proclaimed about their Lord.

It was not hidden under a measuring basket and consigned to oblivion and darkness. Rather, like something placed high on a lampstand, it was raised to a lofty height and shone upon everyone in the house—that is, throughout the whole world.
This is foreknowledge and prophecy, not merely a command but also a declaration of what was to come: “Let your light shine before people.” He called them all collectively “light,”
when he said, “You are the light of the world”—not many lights, but all of them together one light,
so that through their common unity there would be a dawning of light for the whole world. For it belonged to him alone to say, “I am the light of the world.”
And it was truly said of him that he was the light that came into the world and enlightens everyone. But when these things had thus been spoken
and fulfilled, see how he also spoke these further words to his disciples and explained: “What I tell you in darkness, you must speak
in the light; and what you hear in your ears, proclaim on the rooftops. Do not fear those who kill the body
but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” Through these words too, at the beginning of his disciples’ work, when they did not know

these things and were, as it were, in darkness, he promised knowledge of the light. And he foretold that those who were hearing his commands secretly and in darkness, while he was unseen, would proclaim him openly to everyone.

He exhorted them not to be ashamed, but to endure [?] affliction with their whole soul and proclaim him for everyone to hear, and not to be intimidated by those who kill the mortal body. For the soul cannot be killed by human beings,
because it is incorporeal and does not die. For God alone can kill both body and soul together and inflict punishment.
Notice that through these words he taught that the soul is incorporeal, and established a system of philosophy in a few words.
At the beginning he told his disciples that he would make them fishers of people. And at the end, openly and from his own place,
he foretold, with his own power, that they would make disciples of all nations. From the Gospel of Matthew.
8. After his resurrection from among the dead, they all went together, as they had been commanded, to Galilee, where he had told them.
When they saw him, some of them worshiped him, while others doubted. But he approached them and spoke with them, saying, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me by my Father.
Go and make disciples of all nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
Teach them to observe everything I have commanded you. And look, I am with you every day until the end of the world.”
Notice in these very things the disciples’ disposition and their careful judgment: not all of them worshiped him when they saw him, but some did so with faith and love,
while others held back for the time being, so that they would not assent to this marvel lightly or hastily. Rather, with much examination and with all
care, they too were finally convinced and went out to all humanity.
They became heralds of his resurrection. Now, because it had been said in the writings of the prophets in his own person,
In the prophecy: “Ask me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.”
Since the testimony of the prophecy had now been fulfilled in deed, he said to his disciples, “All authority has been given to me, in heaven as well as on earth.”
For he had held dominion over the things in heaven from eternity. But he went on to say that dominion over those on earth had now been given to him by his Father.
As in the saying, “Ask me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” For formerly, as Moses testifies,
“When the Most High divided the nations, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels.” These were the angels of God who formerly ruled over everything on earth.
But when humanity turned to the error of many gods, those ruling angels could do nothing to help with this.
Therefore the common Savior of all, through his divine manifestation, teaches after his victory over death that authority over the nations was no longer given to angels, but to him by his Father,
over those on earth. For this reason he commanded his disciples, not formerly, but

now, to travel about and make disciples of all the nations. He also necessarily added the mystery of purification, for it was fitting that those turning from the nations should be cleansed through his power from all impurity and defilement,

because they had been defiled by the deception of demons and held captive by idol worship and defilement of every kind. Now, first of all, they were changed from their shameful and lawless way of life. He instructed them to teach these same people,
after the purification through the mystery of his teaching, not the commandments of the Jews or the law of Moses, but to observe everything that he himself had commanded them. And these
are the things with which all his disciples alike traveled among all the nations, and which he handed on to all the churches throughout creation. He necessarily encouraged them
and gave them confidence to travel readily among all the nations and make disciples of every race of humanity, through the promise he made to them when he said, “Look, I
am with you.” For he added action to this word of promise: in divine power he was with each one of them, and he was close to all of them together.
He acted and worked with them and secured the victory of the teachers of all the nations, whom he had made teachers of the reverence for God handed down by him.
They therefore relied on this promise and immediately fulfilled his words in deed, without hesitating at all.

With complete readiness they went out to make disciples of all the nations, for they had received actual proof and had seen with their own eyes that the one who had died a short time before was alive.
The very one whom they had denied under oath because of what had happened to them, they now saw clearly, in person and close at hand.
He spoke with them as usual and made them the promises we mentioned earlier. They could not disbelieve his promises because of the sight of him that they were beholding.

For they had an excuse concerning this command: their rusticity and lack of education in speech, of which they themselves were aware. For this reason they might have hesitated, and they would rightly have thought
that it was impossible for them, whose language was Syriac and who knew nothing beyond fishing, to become teachers alike of Greeks, Romans, Egyptians,
Persians, and the rest of the barbarian nations, and to establish laws in opposition to all the lawmakers and kings throughout creation, contrary
to the traditions about their ancestral gods that had been handed down to them from [?]. But they were not permitted to entertain these thoughts, since they heard the voice of God saying
to them, “Look, I am with you every day.”

And they clearly saw that the divinity of the one speaking with them had been shown to be stronger than death. For this reason fear had also come upon them lest they fail to obey; so from then on they endured affliction with all their soul.
They received from their Master himself the assurance of life after death, and confidently went out to travel among all the nations, confirming their Master's own promises in practice. He,
however, added a further statement to his promises to them, and even now shows this to be more astonishing than anything else: what he said to them, “Look, I am with you every day.”
And he added, “Until the end of the world.” This applies not only to
those men, but also to all those who came after them and received his teaching from them. From that time until now, he is near to all those who become his disciples.

For this reason his church, which is protected by him and gathered by his power, increases every day, grows to great numbers, and continues to expand until the end of the world. On the conversion of all the nations to God.
From the Gospel of Luke. 9. Again, on another occasion after his resurrection from the dead, he appeared to others of his disciples.
While they were still doubtful and did not believe him, he addressed these words to them, saying, “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: everything must be fulfilled

that is written about me in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets, and in the Psalms.” Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. And he said to them, “Thus it was necessary for the Messiah to suffer

and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be proclaimed in his name among all the nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.”
And once he said that repentance would be proclaimed in his name to all the nations, if the deed did not follow the word,
not even his resurrection from the dead would be believed. But if, even until now, the things foretold by his word continue in practice,
and his word itself is alive and active throughout creation and is visible to our eyes, then we must no longer disbelieve the one who spoke this word.
For when someone's power is alive and active and visible to the eyes, it is above all necessary to acknowledge that he is alive and lives the life of God—
the one whose living deeds are seen to agree with his words.
He therefore brought those words of his to the hearing of all the nations, as they were rendered and translated into all the languages of Greeks and barbarians,

so that his teaching might be heard by all the nations, and he might bring to conversion and repentance vast multitudes of those who formerly, in the error of many gods and the worship of idols, had lived wickedly and indecently.
But not forgiveness first and then

repentance; rather, he commanded them to proclaim repentance first and then forgiveness. For to those who showed sincere repentance for their former sins, the grace of our Savior granted forgiveness for their deeds,
since for their sake he even accepted death and gave his own life as a ransom in exchange for the lives of those who would be saved through him. Thus those disciples of his, men
untrained in speaking and entirely without education, poor and wretched in appearance, trusted in the life of the one who had appeared to them after death and had spoken openly with them.
They began from the city of Jerusalem, according to his own commands, and went out to all the nations and did what they had been commanded.
They proclaimed to everyone repentance and forgiveness of the soul's former sins.
And they displayed such excellence that even now, in our own time, the teaching of those poor, uneducated men is active throughout the whole human world.
How his deeds would be heard and proclaimed throughout the whole world. From the Gospel of Matthew and from that of Mark.
10. While our Savior was in Bethany, a village not far from Jerusalem, he was invited to the home of a certain Simon. While he was reclining at table there, a woman took
A flask of balsam worth a great deal of money; she came and poured it over his feet. But his disciples rebuked her and criticized what had happened.
He, however, accepted what had been done as a sign and declared that this very deed would be proclaimed and heard throughout the whole world.
He prophesied in these words: “I tell you, wherever this good news of mine is proclaimed throughout the whole world, what this woman has done will also be told in memory of her.”
He said these things beforehand, when, at that time, the writing of the Gospel had not yet entered anyone’s mind or come to anyone’s hearing.
Apparently, not even those who lived in the neighborhood learned what had happened, but only those who had been entertained there.
Nevertheless, he uttered this entire declaration at once. And that the Gospels written by his disciples would be proclaimed throughout the whole world

he prophesied. He also added the deed to his declaration, saying that, along with those deeds of his recorded in the Gospel, what this woman had done would also be written down and told throughout the whole world in memory of her. This very statement

was shown to be true by what actually happened. For there is no people, country, or place where the memory of that woman is not recounted in the Gospel written about him and proclaimed throughout the whole world along with the teaching about him.
So much, then, concerning this. Now hear what he promised concerning his church: how he mentioned his church by name when it did not yet exist,
and how he said that the gates of death would never overcome it. From the Gospel of Matthew.
11. Once, when he asked his disciples what people were saying about him, and they answered with the opinion held by many, he asked them a second time, “But you, what

do you say?” When Simon said to him, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God,” he answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.
And I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the bars of Sheol will not overpower it.”
He accepted this recognition that he is the Messiah, the Son of the living God. And because it cannot be broken or shaken, he figuratively
called this entire understanding a rock. For this reason, that man himself, that disciple of his who had previously been called Simon,
he called Peter, because of this recognition, about which he subsequently prophesied

and said, “On this rock I will build my church, and the bars of Sheol will not overpower it.” At the same time he prophesied what was to come, promised that he himself would build it, and would bring the work to completion.

By these words he declared that his church [?] would be established and built on this recognition granted concerning him, as on a firm foundation, through his power alone, forever, and that the gates of death would never overcome it.
The fulfillment itself demonstrated this more clearly than any words. For myriads of persecutors and many forms of death surged against his church
and could accomplish nothing against it. Through the actual events, that earlier declaration of his
clearly demonstrated its truth by its fulfillment. And his giving the name “church” to the assembly that was to be established in his name
was no small instance of foreknowledge. For those assemblies of the Jews were called synagogues.
While he was walking among human beings, he stayed in the synagogue of the Jews, and at that time he did not yet have even a single separate synagogue of his own.

Who would not marvel that he knew beforehand of those assemblies that would later, in the distant future, be established in his name, and that he called them not synagogues, according to Jewish custom, but churches?
He added that the bars of Sheol would not overpower them—those churches that we ourselves behold with our own eyes.

We should marvel not only at the prediction but also at its promise. For he says, “I will build my church on the rock, and the gates of Sheol will not overcome it.” Let us recognize that we can also readily see this fulfilled in practice.

For his church was established neither by human power nor by the excellence of speakers. Rather, the one who made the promise and fulfilled his promise in practice continues to this day, throughout the whole inhabited world, to bring about the growth and building of his church by divine power.
On the divisions in households and families that continue to this day because of his teaching. From the Gospel of Matthew.
12. “Do not think that I have come to bring peace on earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.
For I have come to set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.”
As Luke says, however: “Do you think that I have come to bring peace on earth? I tell you, rather, divisions.
For from now on there will be five in one household, divided three against two and two against three. A father will be divided against his son,

and a son against his father; a mother will be divided against her daughter, and a daughter against her mother; a mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”
Who would not marvel that our Savior’s foreknowledge did not overlook even those things that are being fulfilled in individual households, in the distant times afterward, down to the present?
For, like someone close to these events and moving about among the homes of all
humanity, he told his disciples beforehand about the things that continue to happen to this day.
These things had not existed up to that point, nor had they happened at the time when he spoke these words. For the events had not yet taken place then,
when these things were heard only as spoken words. But now that the prediction has been fulfilled through actual events
and is visible to our eyes, how can we fail to acknowledge that these are truly the words of God—all of us who are prepared to think as we ought?
Again, consider also these words: “I have come to divide and to bring a sword and divisions among people.”
In this matter too, we see with our own eyes that no human teaching—neither that of philosophers nor of prophets, neither of Greeks nor of barbarians—has ever displayed power like this:
to take hold of the whole inhabited world, to divide every household, and to sift and separate people among all nations and in every family,

so that some would be counted as his own and others would stand opposed to them. Our Savior alone, who is himself the Word of God, promised to do this, and he confirmed his promise by the events themselves.

He himself taught the reason for the division of people that occurs in households, as we found in a passage in the Gospel circulating among the Jews in the Hebrew language. In it he says, “I will choose for myself the good ones—
the good ones whom my Father in heaven has given me.” From this very statement one can learn that wherever, in all our households, the word of Jesus has prevailed,
the better people have been separated from the worse. Therefore, if someone compares, among brothers,
or among servants, and in all families, the customs, conduct, ways of life, chastity, and humility of those who have chosen our Savior’s teaching,
that is, of those who have been chosen by him, with those who have not yet become worthy of it, he will know what power he exercised: not only that he foretold

what was to come, but also that he brought deeds after his words, along with the other things and with those words he is recorded as saying: “I will choose for myself the good ones—the good ones whom my Father in heaven has given me.”

Nevertheless, here he says, “I have not come to bring peace on earth.” In other passages, however, he explains to his disciples themselves, saying, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you—not as the world gives.”
Peace. And I too give peace in the same way: the knowledge of God and the love that he wished for his disciples.
And tranquility of soul, so that it is not disturbed, and illumination of the mind and steadfastness—he speaks of these in this way.
These things, then, and what concerns them [?], and also what he foreknew and foretold concerning the Jewish people, can readily be examined from the following.
What he prophesied concerning the Jewish people, in parables from the Gospel of Matthew.
13. When the leaders of the Jewish people, the chief priests and the teachers of the law, were gathered together in Jerusalem, he himself was there in the temple.

They were about to act outrageously against him, and he foretold in veiled language, in the following manner, the destruction that would overtake them because of this outrage: “There was a man, a householder.

He planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower in it, handed it over to tenant farmers, and went away. When the fruit season approached, he sent his servants to the farmers to bring him the fruit.
The farmers seized his servants; some they beat, some they stoned, and some they killed.
Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they treated them in the same way.
Finally he sent his son, saying, ‘Perhaps they will respect my son.’ But when those farmers saw his son,
they said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ They seized him, took him outside the vineyard, and killed him.
So when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those farmers?” They said to him, “He will utterly destroy them and hand the vineyard over to other farmers,
who will give him the fruit in its season.” Jesus himself said to them, “Have you never read in Scripture, ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone of the building.
This came from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’? Therefore I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a people who produce fruit.”
This parable is of the same kind as the one in the prophet Isaiah, which takes this very form: “My beloved had a vineyard on a hill in fertile land.
He cultivated it, put a fence around it, planted vine shoots in it, and built a tower within it. He also

made a winepress in it. He waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes.” But this passage in the prophets [the prophet] brought an accusation against the vineyard, for he explained what it was, saying:

“For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are a new and beloved planting. I waited for justice, but there was plunder; for righteousness, but look—an outcry!”

14. Our Savior’s saying was expressed in a way resembling that of the prophet, so that it would be understood and made clear to those standing nearby and listening. But it was not spoken against the vineyard, because the prophet himself had already spoken the earlier saying about it.

What had been left unspoken in the prophets, our speaker himself included in his parable: these things concerning the farmers of the vineyard. These were the elders of the people, the chief priests, the rulers, and the teachers, who were also responsible for the entire

congregation producing bad fruit. Because of them, the vineyard itself was also abandoned to destruction—that is, their entire people—and its fence was uprooted: those who formerly fought on behalf of the people
and protected the people along with their land. The tower in it is the temple, and the winepress is the altar.

All these things, then, were completely removed from their very foundations because those farmers had stained themselves with blood. They openly killed the servants sent to them, the earlier and the later ones—that is, those prophets—at one time after another.
The ancient Scripture bears witness to this statement, as does Elijah among the prophets, who said in his prayer to God:
“Lord, they have killed your prophets [your prophets] and torn down your altar. I alone am left, and they seek to take my life.” These, then, are the words of the prophet.
Through his prayer he accuses the leaders of the Jewish people. Yet the defilement of the prophets’ blood was not enough for them.
Instead, in the end they also killed the Son himself—the Son of God—not without knowing him, but knowing fully and certainly that he was the heir.

Before his suffering, our Savior himself told these things about himself in a parable, foretelling what was to happen through his foreknowledge. While walking in the temple itself, he addressed those vineyard workers—the chief priests and teachers of his time, and the others who stood at the head of the people.

Through the parable he very clearly led them to pronounce judgment against themselves. At the end of the parable, therefore, he asks them, saying, “When the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do

to those workers?” They, not yet understanding that this was said about them, pronounce judgment against themselves and say, “He will utterly destroy those wicked men and hand the vineyard over to other

workers who will give him its fruit at the proper times.” Then Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures, ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone of the building.
This has come from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”
Very fittingly, after his earlier statement about his death, he disclosed his resurrection from the dead through prophetic testimonies.
For he first taught that the son of the vineyard’s owner would be killed by the wicked workers.
He received the verdict from them and then added this: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone of the building,” speaking prophetically in a figure about the resurrection
of himself. For after he was hung up by those workers, who were also builders, he—the precious stone about whom Isaiah spoke,
the prophet, saying, “Look, I am laying in Zion a chosen and precious stone, a cornerstone, a foundation stone, and whoever believes in it will not be put to shame”—
became the cornerstone of another building, about which the passage says, “And this is marvelous in our eyes.” Through these words he pointed to his church.
Then he himself repaid them in keeping with their own verdict, saying, “The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a people who produce fruit.” This
agrees with the statement they themselves had made: “He will give the vineyard to other workers who will give him its fruit at the proper times.” By “the kingdom of God,” he meant the practices
of the worship of God. He said that this would be taken from those workers, expressing and explaining this very clearly, and that it would be given to another people who produce its fruit.
This is the Christian people, who throughout the whole world daily display, in deeds and words, fruits that accord with and are worthy of conduct pleasing to God.
On the rejection of the Jews together, on the calling of the nations, and on those who gather in his church although they are unworthy,
and on their end. From the Gospel of Matthew. 15. After this parable, which was related above, the text of the divine Scripture records
that when the chief priests and Pharisees heard his parables, they knew that he was speaking about them. They wanted to seize him, but they feared the people,
because they regarded him as a prophet. Jesus answered them and spoke to them again in a parable:
“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who held a wedding feast for his son.

He sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding feast, but they were unwilling to come. Again he sent other servants and instructed them, ‘Tell those invited: Look, my meal is prepared, and my fattened oxen have been slaughtered.

Everything is ready for you. Come to the wedding feast.’ But they disregarded it and went away, one to his farm and another to his business. The rest seized his servants, mistreated them, and killed them.
The king became angry, sent his army, killed those murderers, and burned their city.
Then he said to his servants, “My banquet is ready, but those who were invited were not worthy of it.
So go out now to the roads and paths, and invite everyone you find to the banquet.” And those servants went out to the roads.
They gathered everyone they found, good and bad. But in the first parable,
there were a vineyard, a tower, a winepress, and wicked farmers, as well as the earlier and later servants who were sent and killed.

And finally the son of the vineyard’s owner was also killed. Through these were signified the Jewish people, the temple, the altar, the Jewish leaders, the earlier and later prophets, and finally the Son
of God, whom those wicked farmers—the men who stood at the head of the people—killed.
16. But this parable before us plainly introduces a banquet, marriage, the union of bridegroom and bride, and a wedding dinner. Here too there are servants who are beaten and killed,
and those who are invited first and those invited later. Through these things he again indicates in a hidden way what happened after his resurrection from the dead. For the bridegroom
is the Word of God, and the bride is the rational soul that is united with him and receives the divine seed that comes from him,
and the divine and rational communion of his church. After these things comes the spiritual banquet and the wedding dinner of divine and heavenly foods. But the servants here,
who issue the invitations—he was not speaking about those who had previously been sent to the vineyard, but about others. For those were prophets, while these were his apostles,
who were sent to give the first invitation to those of the circumcision. For when he first sent them, he instructed them, saying, “Do not go along the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a town
of the Samaritans. Instead, go especially to the sheep that have strayed from the house of Israel.” So it was these whom the servants first invited. And when
they did not heed the invitation, even though he sent messengers of good news and preachers of the gospel twice in great numbers—those whom he himself chose after the twelve apostles,

another seventy disciples, who also first proclaimed the good news to the Jewish people and invited them to the banquet of the new covenant—they accomplished nothing, because those who were being invited were occupied
with their business affairs. After refusing to heed the servants’ invitation, they mistreated some of them and killed others. From Scripture itself we can discover how many of our Savior’s disciples
they killed in Jerusalem itself and in the rest of Judea in the time that followed. Thus, right at the beginning, Stephen was stoned by them, and after him James, the brother of John,

and again, after them, the man who was the first to [?] the seat of the church there: James, who was called the brother of our Lord. Because of the greatness of his virtues, the people of that time called him “the Just.”
The Jews killed this man too with stones. And how they also mistreated the apostles with flogging
is recounted in the book of Acts. Through divine knowledge he foretold these things before they happened, and prophesied what would befall them at those people’s hands.
Through the parable, before these things happened, he foretold what was to come, in these words: “But the king became angry at the mistreatment and murder
of his servants, and sent an army, killed those murderers, and burned their city.” And what is clearer than this foreknowledge
and the actual fulfillment of these events? For a short time later the Roman army came and [?] the city, and destroyed the temple itself with fire.
And whose army was it but that of the King of all, God who is over all? For this reason it was said, “But the king sent his army, killed those murderers, and burned their city.” So even to this day,
those who go to that region can readily see with their own eyes the traces of burning in the sites of the city, and how those murderers of the apostles were taken captive.
And they paid the just penalty. There is no need [?] to say that it is near at hand; we can find what happened to them in Flavius Josephus’s history of the Romans.
After their killing and the siege of their royal capital, those who remained of the earlier servants heard their master say that those first invited had not been worthy.
“But go to the roads and paths, and invite everyone you find to the banquet.” And they did what they had been commanded.
Thus our Savior himself said to them after his resurrection, “Go and make disciples of all nations in my name.”

It was he who said these things, who had previously commanded, “Do not go along the road of the nations,” and that they should preach only to the Jews. But when they mistreated those who invited them,
then he changes the servants for the second time and says, “Those who were invited were not worthy.
Go to the roads and paths, and invite everyone you find to the banquet.” And as they carried this out in practice,
they went out into all creation and proclaimed the divine and heavenly invitation to all nations, gathering as many as they found, both bad and good.
So let no one be surprised if those who gather in Christ’s church are not all good, but bad people also gather, mixed together with the good. For even this did not escape
our Savior’s foreknowledge. And in keeping with that foreknowledge, this too is seen to have continued in actual practice.
He therefore shows what end awaits those who gather in his church despite being unworthy.
For afterward he teaches these things in the parable, saying, “The banquet hall was filled with guests. But when the king came in
to see those reclining at the meal, he saw there a man who had no wedding clothes. He said to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here when you are not
wearing wedding clothes?’ But he remained silent. Then the king said to the attendants, ‘Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness.
There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there.’ For many are called, but few are chosen.”

In those preceding words he also warned beforehand those who do not conduct themselves rightly in his church.
