Again, concerning the rejection of the Jewish people.

From the Gospel of Matthew. 17.
“Snakes, brood of vipers! How will you escape Gehenna? Therefore, look, I am sending you prophets, wise men, and scribes.
Some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and pursue from city to city,
so that all the blood of the righteous shed on the earth may come upon you, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah,

whom you killed between the sanctuary and the altar. I tell you that all these things will come upon this generation.” There is no need to say that all these things are clear, requiring no explanation at all, since they were fulfilled in actual events in the time that followed.
And through their fulfillment [?] they confirmed our Savior’s foreknowledge.

For afterward the apostles were flogged by the Jews in Jerusalem itself, and they went out from their synagogues rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for his name. Stephen was stoned by them, and James was killed with the sword.
Again, the second James was killed by stoning. As for Simeon, who after James received the episcopal seat
in Jerusalem, the historical account records that he was handed over to be crucified. Many others, too, who were killed by the Jews confirmed our Savior’s foreknowledge.
Because of all these things, divine judgment exacted vengeance on the generation that dared to do all this, and brought back upon it the consequences of all its deeds.
For in that generation their temple and altar were uprooted, and the kingdom that had been preserved through succession from their ancestors down to that time was dissolved.

Their freedom was also taken away from them, and the events themselves showed that all the blood of the righteous was exacted from that generation, in accordance with our Savior’s earlier words. But we must consider
with what great authority and by what power he said, “Look, I am sending you prophets and wise men.” For “Look, I am sending” is an expression of divine authority.
And his calling the Jewish leaders “snakes, offspring of vipers” to their faces was no small demonstration.
And after all this, his prediction of the destruction that was about to overtake them demonstrated the truth of these words through their fulfillment. Enough, then, about these things.

Come, then, let us next consider how, concerning the land that they had always held in honor, and the splendors of the royal capital renowned among them, he foretold that these would be exchanged for the utmost

evils because of its inhabitants’ insolence toward him, bearing witness beforehand through divine foreknowledge. Indeed, in his compassion he even wept over them.
On the Destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem.
18. It has been stated and shown what fulfillment befell the things previously spoken concerning the Jewish people. But since the Word of God himself also prophesied concerning the places themselves,
we should also consider his pronouncements about these things, when they would not tolerate his pure teaching.
Neither his frankness nor his rebuke induced the Jewish leaders to drive him out of their city. But as he was departing from Jerusalem,
he spoke these words concerning their city: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you!
How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling! Look, your house is left desolate.

But I tell you, from now on you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’” The unclean abomination was afterward committed by them, and this was the wickedness they dared to commit against our Savior.
And it was fitting that not only the inhabitants of the city, but also the land in which they took such great pride,
should suffer things commensurate with what its inhabitants had done. These things they did indeed suffer before long, when the Romans came against the city and its inhabitants:
some they killed according to the law of war, some they destroyed by famine, some they led into captivity, and some they drove away. They burned the captive city and the temple

and reduced them to utter ruin. But although these things happened at a later time, our Savior, through foreknowledge of what was to come, as the Word of God, foretold what would happen through the words set before us.
He calls the whole Jewish people the city’s children, and he calls the temple their house. Then he testifies that these things are being inflicted upon them because of their wicked conduct.
For he had often wished to gather their children under the yoke of the worship of God, as one who exists before all things

and had always cared for them. Through each of the prophets, throughout all their generations, he had instructed and called them. But they were unwilling to listen to his call. For this reason he pronounced judgment against them and said,
“Look, your house is left desolate.” Very deliberately, he did not say that the city itself would become desolate, but rather the house within it—that is, the temple.
He no longer wished it to be called his own, or even the house of God, but said that it was theirs, and prophesied that it would become desolate.
This meant nothing other than that it would be deprived of the care formerly bestowed upon it. For this reason he says, “Look, your house is left desolate.”

We should marvel at the fulfillment of this saying, for never at any other time had that place endured such complete destruction—not even when it was uprooted by the Babylonians because of their great wickedness, their worship of idols, and their defilement with the blood of the prophets.

For the entire period of the place’s desolation was seventy years on that occasion. For this reason, it had not been said to them at that time in an absolute sense, “Look, your house is left desolate.”
For the course of events was not allowed to be reversed after a short time, so that it might be granted a better restoration, greater than the former one, as one of the prophets had foretold:
“The glory of this latter house will be much greater than that of the former.” But after the pronouncement of our Savior concerning how you and your house were abandoned by God's judgment,
it came to utter desolation. For those who visit those places, the sight itself most clearly shows the fulfillment of the saying,

and that period has lasted many long years, so that it is not merely twice the seventy years of desolation that occurred in the time of the Babylonians, but exceeds even four times that duration, confirming the judgment pronounced by our Savior.

Again, on another occasion, our Savior himself was walking beside this temple just mentioned. His disciples, marveling at the buildings surrounding it and at the greatness and beauty of the temple itself, were pointing them out to him.
But he answered them, saying, “Do you not see all these things? I tell you that not one stone will be left here upon another that will not be torn down.”
The writings show how worthy of admiration its entire structure and all the later ornamentation of the temple there were. As evidence, a remnant is preserved even now, in which traces are reminders

of those ancient ornaments. But the greater wonder, surpassing everything, is the divine utterance of our Savior's foreknowledge, which pronounced a complete sentence upon those who were marveling at the building:

that in the place they were admiring, not one stone would be left upon another without being uprooted. For because of the insolence of its inhabitants, it was fitting that that place should suffer complete destruction and desolation, since it was a dwelling
place for wicked people. And how the things foretold in that earlier saying remain in actual fact—the whole temple, its wall, and the adorned and beautiful buildings within it, which covered all [?],

have endured desolation from that time until now. The power of that saying grows with time and continues its work of destruction, so that in some places not even traces of the foundations can be seen.

Anyone who wishes is free to see it with his own eyes. And if someone should say that a few places are still standing, he should also expect their destruction, as their desolation increases every day and the prediction that was uttered continually works through a hidden power.
I know, however, that I have heard some people interpret this pronouncement before us incidentally, saying that it was not spoken about all the buildings,

but about the particular place that his disciples pointed out to him while marveling at it. For it was about that place that he made this prediction. Moreover, the writing of his disciples that teaches about him gives the following account concerning the uprooting of the place.
Concerning the siege of the city. From the Gospel of Luke.
19. When he saw the city, he wept over it and said, “If only you had known, even on this day, the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you
when your enemies will surround you, encircle you, and press you on every side. They will uproot you and your children within you.” The things preceding this he prophesied about the temple.
But the words now before us concern the city itself, which the Jews used to call the city of God because of God's temple that had been built within it.
The merciful one wept over the whole city, not so much over its buildings or its land as over the souls of its inhabitants, first and foremost, having compassion on them because of their destruction.
But he also shows the reason for their desolation when he says, “If only you had known, even on this day, the things that make for your peace!”
He is indicating his own coming, which was for the peace of the whole world. For he is the one of whom it was said, “In his days righteousness will dawn,
and abundant peace.” He came for this purpose: to proclaim peace to those who were near and peace to those who were far away. And to those who received him he said,
“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you.” This is the peace that all the nations throughout the whole creation who believed in him received.
But the people of the circumcision, who did not believe in him, did not know the things that made for their peace.
For this reason he went on to say, “But now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you.” These, then, were the things that were about to overtake
them a little later in that siege. Because they had not recognized beforehand the peace that had previously been announced to them, it was hidden from their eyes. Thus they did not foresee
what later happened to them. But he clearly foretold these things through his earlier words, and clearly announced beforehand the siege that the Romans would [?] them.
For he says, “Days will come upon you because you did not recognize the things that would bring you peace.”
For this reason, days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you, bring you to your knees, and press you from every side. They will uproot you and your children within you.
Through these words he describes the form of the war that came
upon them and how it came to an end. These things we can [?] from the history of Josephus, who was a Jew.

He was born of the Jewish people, to parents who were well known and distinguished among that people. He recorded everything that happened to them during the siege and showed that these events fulfilled the earlier words set before us.
Again, concerning the siege of the city, from the Gospel of Luke, [?]. He says, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army,
know that its destruction is near. Then let those in Judea flee to the mountain.
Let those within it escape, and let those in its surrounding countryside not enter it, because these are days of vengeance, so that everything written may be fulfilled.
But woe to pregnant women and nursing mothers in those days!
For there will be great distress upon the land and great wrath against this people. They will fall by the edge of the sword and be taken captive among all the nations.

And Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled.” Earlier he says, “Look, your house is left desolate.” Through the words set before us, he gives signs of the time of the final destruction
of the place, indicating them when he says, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its destruction is near.”
For no one should suppose, he says, that after the siege and destruction of this very place, another restoration will take place for it,

as happened in the time of Cyrus, king of the Persians, and afterward in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, and again in the time of Pompey. For the place endured sieges many times and afterward was granted a greater restoration.
Rather, recognize the final desolation and complete destruction coming upon it when you see it besieged by armies.
By the destruction of Jerusalem he means the destruction of the temple and the abolition of the practices formerly carried out in it according to the law of Moses.
For do not suppose that these words speak of the destruction of the city itself in the sense that no one would ever live in it again.
For afterward he says that the city will be inhabited, not by Jews but by the nations, saying, “And Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations.” Thus he knows that it will be inhabited by
the nations. But he called it its destruction because it would no longer be inhabited by its own children, nor would the worship prescribed in the law be maintained in it.
It does not take many words to show how these things too were fulfilled, because we can see with our own eyes that the Jews are scattered among all the nations,
and that foreign inhabitants and people of another race live in what was formerly Jerusalem. Indeed, it was named Aelia after Aelius Hadrian, who settled it.
The remarkable feature of this prophecy is that he says of the Jews that they will be taken captive among all the nations, and of the nations that Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations.
This outcome for the Jews is astonishing: they fill the whole inhabited world, so that they even remain among the Ethiopians and among
Scythians and at the ends of the earth; only their own city and the place of worship that had been theirs from ancient times are they unable to enter.
If that city had been completely ruined and without inhabitants, someone might perhaps have supposed that this was the reason. But now, by foreign peoples
and people of another race, that place is inhabited, and they alone are not permitted to set foot in it, so that they cannot even see their ancestral land from a distance.
These things were fulfilled in this way, in keeping with the prophecy that said, “They will be taken captive among all the nations,”
and, “Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations.” He also makes known the manner of the captivity,
the war of which he spoke: “For there will be distress upon the earth and great wrath against this people, and they will fall by the edge of the sword.”
How these things happened in their respective places, and how the things foretold by our Savior were fulfilled in fact, can be learned from the history of Flavius Josephus.
He also describes the fulfillment of that earlier saying of our Savior, who said,
“But woe to pregnant women and nursing mothers in those days!” He clearly demonstrated this and related how women roasted their children over a fire and ate them,
because of the severity of the famine that gripped the city. Our Savior therefore foresaw this very famine that occurred in the city,
and advised his disciples that, during the siege that was to come upon the Jews, they should not take refuge in that city as though it were a stronghold protected by God, where many suffered
within it, but should leave there and flee to the mountain; and those within Judea should surrender to the nations.
Those in its countryside should not take refuge in it as though in a fortified place. For this reason he said, “Those in its surrounding districts must not enter it,
for these are days of vengeance, so that everything written may be fulfilled.” Anyone who wishes can therefore learn [?] these things

from the history of Josephus. But if it is appropriate to include even a few passages from him in this book as testimony, nothing prevents us from hearing the historian himself, who writes as follows.

From the sixth book of Josephus’s history. 21. “Why should I speak of the shamelessness of the famine toward lifeless things? For I am about to relate a deed the like of which has never been recorded among either Greeks or barbarians.
It is horrifying to tell and unbelievable to hear. For my part, to avoid appearing to later generations to be telling lies, I would gladly have omitted this suffering, had I not had many witnesses,
who at the time [?]. Otherwise, I would also have done my ancestral land a cold favor by omitting in words what it suffered in fact. A woman, one of those who lived beyond the Jordan,
whose name was Mary, well known for her family and wealth, took refuge in Jerusalem with many others and was besieged with them.
The tyrants seized all the other possessions belonging to this woman that she had brought into the city when she moved from beyond the Jordan. As for what remained of her treasures,
even whatever she managed to obtain for food, the soldiers would rush in every day and seize it. Fierce anger rose within the woman,
and many times, by insulting and cursing the robbers, she provoked them against herself.
But when no one killed her, either in anger or out of pity for her, and she was weary of finding food for others
from every place, and there was doubt whether she could find any at all, hunger clung to her inward parts and her belly.
Her anger burned within her more fiercely than her hunger. Taking fury and necessity as her advisers, she acted against nature and seized her son.
Now she had a nursing infant, and she said, “Wretched child, amid war, famine, and turmoil,
why am I keeping you alive? So that you may become a slave among the Romans?

Even if you survive among them, famine and turmoil come before slavery, and they are terrible. Come, be food for me, vengeance upon the turmoil, and a tale for the world—the one thing still missing from the sufferings of the Jews.” And as she said these things,

she killed her son and then roasted him. She ate half of him, and covered and kept the rest. These sufferings, out of many, suffice in connection with the earlier divine saying of our Savior, which said:
“But woe to pregnant women and those nursing infants in those days!” For this too is added to our Savior’s earlier words: “There will be great distress upon the earth,
and great wrath against this people.” Or, as Matthew said:

“For at that time there will be great distress, such as has not occurred from the beginning of the world until now, and never will occur.” It is good to hear from the historian himself, as he records the outcome of these events as follows:

From Josephus, from the fifth book of his history. 22. “It is impossible to relate each one of their evils individually. But to sum them up, one may say that no other city has suffered all these things,
nor has any generation ever been as productive of evils as this one. For they themselves overthrew the city and compelled the unwilling Romans to be recorded
as winning a bitter victory [?]. In their wickedness they drew fire to the temple without delay. They saw the fire burning in it from the upper city, and they neither grieved nor wept.”
These things concern the saying, “At that time there will be great distress, such as has not occurred from the beginning of the world.” This very prediction, which had been spoken beforehand
by our Savior, was attested by the historian himself as having been fulfilled in its entirety after forty years, in the time of Vespasian, emperor of the Romans.
Our Savior himself adds to his earlier words and sets the limit of the time during which Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations.
For he said, “Until the times of the nations are fulfilled,” and by this he indicated the end of the people.

Again, concerning the laws of the Jews, that they will no longer be fulfilled on the mountains of Gerizim or in Jerusalem; and concerning the worship fitting for God, which was established in his church.
From the Gospel of John. 23. Near this neighboring city of ours, Neapolis in Palestine, which was no small place but a well-known city, a Samaritan woman approached him.
After her other words, she said to him, “Sir, I see that you are a prophet. Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain,
but you say that Jerusalem is the place where people must worship.” In response to these things, our Savior himself gave her this answer:
“Believe me, woman, the hour is coming, and is now here, when true worshipers will worship the Father
in spirit and in truth. For [?] also seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit,
and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth.” Through these words too, he fully displayed foreknowledge of no small importance.

For formerly, in the days of Tiberius, emperor of the Romans, in whose time these things were explicitly spoken, the Jews used to gather in Jerusalem to observe the commandment of their law, and the Samaritans on the mountain called Gerizim,

of Moses, and concerning Jerusalem, the prophet among the Hebrews [?]. But a sentence went forth from the divine voice of our Savior: those who persisted in these places would henceforth worship neither in Jerusalem nor on Mount Gerizim.
This came to pass not long afterward,
in the days of Titus and Vespasian, and in the subsequent siege in the days of Hadrian, when, in accordance with his words, both mountains were laid waste.

For the one beside the city of Neapolis was defiled and desecrated with unlawful images, idols, sacrifices, and the shedding of blood. But the temple in Jerusalem was uprooted from its foundations, and in this final devastation and burning

it remained throughout the whole period mentioned. Indeed, from that time until now, our Savior’s earlier saying has been fulfilled in practice: “The hour is coming when they will worship neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” By “hour” he meant a period of time
that was not yet near, but was to come.
But concerning the rational worship carried out by him and his disciples, he adds: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth.”
Here he necessarily added “and now is.”

For immediately, from the very hour when he spoke those words, the true worshipers—he himself, their head and teacher, and his disciples, who received rational worship from him—were carrying out the worship of God in spirit and in truth.

Through those words the Word who is over all prophesied, declaring that no longer on a mountain, nor in one particular corner of the earth, but throughout all creation, those who are true worshipers would worship God who is over all and offer him bloodless divine worship in spirit and in truth,
performed neither in symbolic form nor in things [?], as were those observances of Moses that the Jews and Samaritans kept through slaughter
and sacrifices, incense, fire, and many other bodily practices. Through the words set before us, the Word of God himself prophesied that these very things would cease.
He said that henceforth true worshipers would offer God fitting worship in truth and in spirit—that is, in a divine manner, with soul and mind.
Concerning the people established from foreign nations through his teaching. From the Gospel of John.
24. “I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and my own know me, just as my Father knows me and I know my Father.
And I lay down my life for my sheep. I also have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them too, and they will hear my voice.
And there will be one flock and one shepherd.” Elsewhere he taught and said, “I have come only for the sheep that have strayed from the house of Israel.”

In this manner he referred to the Jewish people. Through the words set before us, he prophesied that not only those Jews who had become his disciples would be counted among his flock, but that also outside

that fold—this is how the passage customarily refers sometimes to the whole Jewish people, and sometimes to Jerusalem and the worship performed there according to the law of Moses—he would gather other sheep
that were not of that fold. By these words he refers to the nations throughout all creation, and foretells that rational sheep would be gathered to him from among them,
so that all those, both Jews and Gentiles, who believed in him would turn to one and the same worship of God, and there would be one flock and one shepherd:
his church, established from Jews and Gentiles together. This was indeed how it was
at the beginning of the proclamation of the gospel. For many multitudes of Jews together became convinced that he was the Christ of God,
the one proclaimed by the prophets. Together with those from the nations who believed in him, they gathered in one church under the care of one shepherd, the Word of God himself.
For in Jerusalem itself, fifteen bishops of the church there arose in succession from among the Jews, from among the Jews, beginning with James, the first.
There were tens of thousands of Jews and Gentiles there who gathered together until the siege in the days of Hadrian. He revealed to us that he himself was the shepherd,
the one who had often been proclaimed in the words of the prophets, which spoke of the Word of God and taught that he is the shepherd of human souls, as of rational sheep.
Thus, in the prophets it is sometimes said, “The Lord will shepherd me, and I will lack nothing,” and sometimes, “Shepherd of Israel, look upon us, you who lead Joseph like a flock.”
At one point he introduces him and says, “He is the Lord and shepherd of the sheep.” Truly, then, he alone is called the shepherd of rational souls. For just as
in the illustration drawn from human life, the nature of the sheep is one thing and that of the shepherd another, and the rational nature rules and directs the irrational kind,
so too, on a higher level, the shepherd is the Word of God, a nature far superior to human beings.
We, however, are his people, and in comparison with his power we are more irrational than all the sheep.
He is truly the good shepherd and [?], who did not neglect his flock and let it be devoured by wolves—that is, by evil demons that destroy souls. These had to be driven away
by the sound of his voice, which spoke with great authority and power: “I am the good shepherd.” And when he said, “I lay down my life for my sheep,” he spoke in a mystery about his death,
and at the same time taught its purpose: he gave his life to save the souls of the rational sheep. And the statement, “I have other sheep,” reveals that they belong to him.
They are not only the Jews, but also all the nations given to him by his Father, as in the saying, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”
How his death is the cause of salvation for many. From the Gospel of John.
25. He was often among the Jews because they knew the earlier prophecies that the prophets had spoken about him.
But because some Greeks also once approached his disciples and wanted to see him, when they told him this,
it is written that he said, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone.
But if it dies, it produces much fruit.” Clearly, through these words too he spoke in a mystery,

saying that among the Greeks, among foreign nations, and among people of another race, the glories of his divinity would take hold. For his hour to be glorified had not come while he was among the Jews and speaking with them, but when the Greeks approached him.
He then necessarily follows this by indicating his death, his resurrection, and the calling of the nations that came about through him.
For just as a grain of wheat, before it falls into the earth, is alone, yet possesses a life-producing power, and contains within itself the germinal principles

of the ears of grain that will sprout from it, but after it falls into the earth it is like someone who lives after his death, and then multiplies and brings forth many ears of grain through its own power—so he said that similar things would also happen to him.
The outcome of events also demonstrated this plainly.
For after his death, not only the Greeks but a multitude of nations received a share in his power and in the providential care of his divinity.
He, then, is that seed which fell and rose, which died and lived, which multiplied abundantly after its fall in death.
Through his resurrection, he filled the lands of the nations like fields, by an inexpressible divine power. This is why he said, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers
are few.” And again, “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, white for harvest.” With these words he also indicated those who, after his death, would be raised up for him through pure faith in him.

From their great numbers throughout the whole inhabited world of Greeks and barbarians, a church of countless congregations was established, like rational fields [?], where human souls are gathered together in one place,
into the threshing floors of his churches. This is why it was said of him, “He holds the winnowing shovel in his hand,
and clears his threshing floors, and gathers the wheat into storehouses, but burns the chaff with unquenchable fire.” How Simon, the chief of the disciples, [?] his master.
He is handed over [?] to the cross and departs from life. From the Gospel of John. 26. “My children, I am with you for a little while.
You will seek me, and just as I told the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say to you as well.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going, you cannot come now,
but you will come later.” And again, at the end of the book, after his resurrection from the dead:
Jesus said to Peter, “I tell you, when you were young, you used to fasten your belt and walk wherever you wished.

But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and others will fasten your belt and take you where you do not wish to go.” He said these things to indicate by what death he would glorify God.
After saying this, he said to him, “Follow me.” Who would not marvel that, when he said these things to his disciples, they were ready and willing to follow him even to death?
For he was not misleading them, setting down for them a hope of good things and promising them what are considered good things in this life.
And in this way he was persuading them, and promising them what are considered good things in this life.
And in this way he was persuading them to follow him. Rather, openly, with the torments that were going to come upon them because of him left unconcealed [?],
he spoke beforehand. To Simon he even showed beforehand the form of the cross by which he later ended his life when he was in Rome,
by saying, “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and others will fasten your belt.” He also indicated something similar to this in a veiled way,
when he said, “Where I am going, you cannot come now, but you will come later.” For these words were not
spoken to all of them, but to Simon alone, because he alone is recorded as having ended his life in a manner resembling our Savior’s suffering.
How he repeatedly foretold to the rest of his disciples the persecutions that would arise against them. From the Gospel of Matthew.

27. “Beware of people, for they will hand you over to their rulers and flog you in their synagogues. They will bring you before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations.”

And again: “Blessed are you when you are persecuted and insulted, and people say all kinds of evil things against you because of me. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward in heaven is great. For in this way they persecuted the prophets who were before you.”
This added expression, “because of me,” is remarkable. For it was not enough merely to know beforehand and foretell the persecutions that were going
to come upon his disciples; he also showed their cause, saying that they would endure these things because of him, not because of evil deeds or any other accusation.
Rather, he testified beforehand that everything would happen to them because of him. This can readily be recognized in practice. For if anyone in a time of persecution merely denies

that he is a Christian, he is released from every charge and every accusation of the slanderer. Thus he was preparing his disciples to live blamelessly and without sins, so that it would be for no other reason, but because of
their confession of him alone and their testimony, that they would endure every evil. He encouraged them fully and made them ready by comparing them with those ancient prophets who loved God: “Just

as they persecuted the prophets before you,” he says, “so they will persecute you too without cause. As with the prophets, this will be inflicted on you because you worship God who is over all, for this was also why they persecuted the prophets.”
And that he should foretell that both governors and kings would be stirred up against these men, at that time when he was close by
and speaking with his disciples, and that things should happen in this way and his words be confirmed in practice—how is this not a great marvel? For many others who profess wisdom
There were barbarians and also Greeks who spoke at length with their disciples. Page 163 [28*] Some of them held that there was no God, and some rejected the doctrine of providence.

Some of them also [?] those whom many regard as gods, and some arose as leaders of evil sects. Others said that the ultimate goal was tranquility, and others spoke of tranquility without discrimination, according to what they had received.
Yet none of them ever explained such things beforehand to his disciples, nor do we know of persecutions against them like those that arose against the teaching of our Savior.

How, then, can we fail to marvel and acknowledge that these utterances truly come from God? For he not only testified beforehand, through divine foreknowledge, to the persecutions that would come upon his disciples,
but also disclosed their cause beforehand by saying that these things would happen to them because of him.
How even relatives will rise against one another in a time of persecution. From the Gospel of Matthew. 28. A brother will hand over his brother to death, and a father his child.
Children will rise against their parents and put them to death, and you will be hated by everyone because of my name. But whoever endures to the end will be saved.

Why must we say much about how these things continue to be fulfilled in practice even now, when the deeds themselves surpass every report? For with our own eyes we have seen how many such things happened during the persecutions, even in our own time.
But do not understand this statement merely in its ordinary sense: “A brother will hand over his brother to death.” For this too has happened according to its straightforward meaning.
Yet it is also possible to examine it and understand how a brother hands over his brother to death: when he gives his soul over to brotherly affection,

chooses the love of life, and denies God, and especially [?] his brother, who asks him and urges him to worship idols, troubles him, pleads with him, and misuses brotherly love, [?] from the remembrance
of our Savior’s commandment. For then a brother truly hands over his brother to the death of his soul. So too a father has misled his son with words, persuaded him to worship idols, and killed him.
Likewise, children have drawn their parents toward affection for themselves and toward that temporary life.
They chose mortal things rather than those that are with God, and became the cause of their parents’ death and the destruction of their souls.
We have seen many such things with our own eyes during persecution. In them the saying was fulfilled: “You will be hated by everyone
because of my name.” Here too, however, the additional phrase is carefully placed: it teaches that it is not because of some other hateful deed,

but because of his own name that the disciples will be hated.
Concerning those who will gather impurely in his church, and concerning the punishment that will come upon them.
From the Gospel of Matthew. 29. The kingdom of heaven is like a net that was cast into the sea and gathered creatures of every kind.
When it was full, they pulled it up onto the shore, sat down, selected the good ones and put them into containers, but threw the bad ones away.
So it will be at the end of this world. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous,
and throw them into the fiery furnace. There will be weeping and grinding of teeth.
Here, by a figure of speech, he calls his teaching a net, woven from the intermingled thoughts of the old and new Scriptures.
The sea represents the wave-tossed life of human beings, which is harsh in its affairs because of the evils among them. From this life, as from a sea, the net mentioned above draws myriads
upward; beneath it are crowds who differ and are opposed in their conduct, both good and evil in their thinking. Concerning these people, who are caught like fish from the sea, he also,
when first calling his disciples, spoke figuratively: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of people.” Thus, neither did this association of those evil people with the good escape his notice.

They are gathered in his church to this day. He teaches that these same people will be separated at the final time by the angels appointed to this task, and that each of them will receive the punishment he deserves, according to his disposition.
How deceivers and those who lead people astray clothe themselves in his teaching and outwardly make themselves resemble him. From the Gospel of Matthew.
30. Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits, for people do not gather grapes from thorns,
or figs from thistles. In the same way, every good tree produces good fruit,
and a bad tree yields bad fruit.

With foreknowledge he advises us in advance to beware of those godless people of other beliefs who in later times made an outward show of using the expressions of the writings about his divinity and clothed themselves with the name of Christianity. And the signs

and evidence of the wickedness hidden within them, which escapes the notice of many, he reveals when he says, “You will recognize them by their fruits.” Their fruits are the words they utter, which are godless,
and their way of life, which is not upright but perverse.
When these things were being spoken at that time and foretold by our Savior, not a single visible piece of evidence for them had yet plainly
appeared to everyone living then. But the Marcionites, the followers of Valentinus and Basilides, and those other destroyers of souls arose in later times:
Bardaisan, and the man who was filled [?] and was deranged in his mind in our own time, whose name became the designation of the Manichaean sect. They became sources of false, godless teachings.
They did not come out into the open in any other way than by wearing outwardly the skins of our Savior’s lambs. For he plainly called his disciples sheep
and said, “My sheep hear my voice,” and again, “Look, I am sending you like sheep among ravenous wolves.”
How many tens of thousands have those deceivers snatched from our Savior’s flock! They outwardly present themselves as followers of Christ and of Christ’s teaching,

and make a show of speaking the expressions of the teachings about his divinity. But they secretly pass on the godless gall lurking within them to those they ensnare. Thus those who until now had been considered [?]

sheep because of their outward resemblance were revealed after a time to be ravenous wolves. For this reason our Savior teaches us to be on our guard against them beforehand, warning us and saying, “You will recognize them by their fruits.”
How both he himself and his disciples would be thought to have taken hold of people through magicians’ tricks and fellowship with demons. . . . 31. No disciple is greater than his teacher,
nor is a servant greater than his master. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and for the servant to be like his master.
If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they call the members of his household that! So do not be afraid of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed,
and nothing is hidden that will not be known. The Jews believed that Beelzebul was an evil demon and the ruler of demons, and they blasphemed against our Savior,
saying that it was by his power that he drove the other demons out of people.
He gave those who thought these things the appropriate answer, which is also recorded among his sayings. But he told his disciples beforehand that they too would be thought to have overcome human

beings through fellowship with demons and magicians. When this very thing was said by many, it confirmed and established our Savior’s prediction. He also testifies that this suspicion concerning them is refuted by their very life and conduct, and by their pure teaching
and worship of God. For this reason he said, “Do not be afraid of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and nothing is hidden that will not be known.”
Thus the long passage of time itself exposed these things, about which many had previously been mistaken. And this was why these suspicions arose: so that they might be brought to light.

And the teachings about the worship of God would come to light, and his ordinances and commandments would henceforth become known to everyone. And that expectation which formerly [?] many people held concerning those who were to be in his church in complete chastity faded away.

And in a way of life that had not experienced sexual intercourse. From the Gospel of Matthew. 32. When he explained to them that it was not right for a man to divorce his wife except on account of adultery,
his disciples said to him, “If this is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry.” In response to this, it is written that he said,

“Not everyone can accept this saying, but only those to whom it has been given. There are eunuchs who have been so from their mother's womb, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by other people,
and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.
Let anyone who can bear it bear it.” No one had ever uttered this saying openly among human beings, and especially among the Jewish people.
Nor had anyone done anything of this kind, as is clear from the written record of the Scriptures themselves.

And throughout the whole world and among all nations, in cities and villages, myriads—not only of men but also of women—have preserved complete chastity and virginity because of their hope and expectation of the kingdom of heaven, for which

they learned to prepare themselves promptly, beginning here. We see this in actual experience. Yet the fulfillment of the declaration of foreknowledge did not take place in an ordinary way. For we have seen many men known to us [?] who used iron instruments
and made their bodies eunuchs for no other reason than this very hope of the kingdom of heaven. They did not wait and gain strength through our Savior's teaching,
but approached the matter simply and rashly. Concerning these people too, the Word of God truly confirmed our Savior's foreknowledge.
On the differences among those who were to receive the seed of his teaching unequally. From the Gospel of Matthew.
33. When a great crowd of people had come to him, he prophesied through a parable about what those who receive the seed of his teaching would be like, saying:
“Look, a sower went out to sow. As he sowed, some seed fell beside the road, and the birds of the sky came and ate it. Some fell on rock, where there was not much soil.
It sprouted at once [?], but because there was no depth of earth beneath its root, it withered. Some fell among thorns,

and the thorns grew up and choked it. Some fell on good soil and yielded fruit, some a hundredfold, some two hundredfold, and some thirtyfold.” After this he cried out, saying, “Anyone who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
Afterward his disciples asked him what the meaning of the parable was.
He taught them, saying, “You, then, listen to the parable of the seed. Whenever someone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it,
the evil one comes and snatches that seed from his heart. This is the one sown beside the road. And the one
sown on rock is the one who hears the word and receives it hastily, but does not become firmly established in it,
and stumbles at a little affliction. The one that fell among thorns is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deception of wealth choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful.
But the one sown on good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it, and bears fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold.”
And how could human nature have had the ability not only to foretell through foreknowledge what was to happen, but also to distinguish the characteristics of the different kinds of souls,
unless the one who then both prophesied and taught was truly the Word of God, of whom it is said:
“For the Word of God is living and sharp, and cuts more keenly than a two-edged sword, penetrating as far as the divisions of soul and body.”
and joints and marrow, and judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No created thing is hidden from him.
For this reason, the differences among the souls that would receive his teaching in later times
he clearly revealed. He said beforehand that those who receive the seed of his teaching without purity fall into three classes. Likewise, there are three ranks of good people who, like
good soil, bear abundantly and greatly increase the word. He therefore said that there are three causes among those who destroy the seed that has fallen into their souls.
For either, through thoughts about their livelihood, concern for unnecessary things, wealth, and luxuries, they drown the seed within them and resemble those that were choked among the thorns;
or they are those who did not receive it into the depths of their minds and quickly wither when distress overtakes them; or there is the third cause, which brings about the destruction
of the seed within them: they surrender their hearing, allowing those who wish to lead them astray to snatch away the seed that has fallen into their souls. These very people are deprived of

the bearing [?] of fruit in God in no other way than one of the forms already mentioned. But those who are the opposite of these, who with a pure soul and a loving mind have received the seed of salvation,
in turn greatly increase their fruit according to the capacity of their own souls. He also compares the differences among these people to good and beautiful soils: those that yield thirtyfold,
those that yield sixtyfold, and those that yield a hundredfold. For capacities like these are found in human souls in due time. It was therefore about these that he prophesied.
Concerning the great number of those who would bear fruit through the teaching of his words, on another occasion he cries out and says, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.
Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.” Again, concerning these people, he said on another occasion, “Do you not
say, ‘There are still four months, and then the harvest comes’? Lift up your eyes and look at the fields: they are already white for harvest.”
And who would not marvel that he also revealed the shortage of those who would faithfully serve as leaders of his word, saying, “The workers are few”?

And prayer is needed to find them. For this reason he says, “Ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.” But when he says, “The sower went out to sow,” he shows that the sower is one thing
by these words, and the seed is another. From where, then, and to where did he say that he went out? Through the parable that follows this one, he taught that it is in this manner.
On the teaching of other beliefs that would be sown together with his word in human souls. From the Gospel of Matthew.
34. He added another parable and said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed on his farm.
But while the people were asleep, the enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away.

When the wheat came up and produced grain, the weeds also appeared. His servants came and said to him, ‘Our master, did you not sow good seed on your farm? Where, then, did the weeds in it come from?’
He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’
They said to him, ‘Do you want us, then, to go and gather them?’ But he said to them, ‘No, lest while gathering the weeds
you uproot the wheat along with them. Let both grow together until the harvest.
At harvest time I will tell the reapers: Gather the weeds first and tie them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into the storehouses.’”
He also explains this parable to his disciples in the house, when they come to him and say, “Explain to us the account of the weeds on the farm.”
He answered them and said, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is the world. And the seed
that is good—these are the children of the kingdom, and the weeds are the children of the evil one.
The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the world, and the reapers are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and fall into the fire,
so it will be at the end of this world. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom everything that causes people to stumble and those who do evil.
They will throw them into the fiery Gehenna. There will be weeping and grinding of teeth there.

Then the righteous will shine in the kingdom of their Father. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” Our Savior thus explained these things: who the sower was who went out to sow, and what the seed was that he scattered. He showed the meaning of the saying [of the parable],
in which it is said, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man, and the field is the world.” He is accustomed to calling himself the Son of Man
because of his stay among human beings. He therefore went out from inside and came outside. But where was he inside, if not above the world?
For he was there, and at the end of the world he went out and came down to us, who are outside the kingdom of heaven.
He brought with him heavenly seed, which he sowed in human souls as in different plots of land. This passage before us also teaches us about the field in which he scattered the seed.
For he said that the field is the world. And he shows whose this field was: it belonged to no one else, but to him who went out from within his kingdom to those outside,
when he says, “The servants approached and said to him, ‘Our lord, did you not sow good seed in your field?’” He therefore clearly taught that this field too belongs to him.

He interpreted it and showed that it is the world. In that first parable, then, he foretold the differences that would arise among those who received the seed in their souls. But in this one before us, he foretold the perverse teachings of the error of godless heretics,
when not even one of them had yet arisen in this way among human beings.
Yet this thing that was going to happen did not escape his notice. For in the time that followed, throughout the earth,
writings in deceptive books and sayings imitating his teaching, originating from a hostile nature, were sown like weeds alongside the pure and life-giving word
of his teaching. Even now, multitudes boast, some in Mani, some in Marcion, and some in others of those who hold a different, godless belief.
They produce weeds while imitating the teaching of our Savior, using his own name and holding to books of fabricated gospels.
But the father of these things, who first sowed them in the souls of those who received him,

is the devil himself. By divine power, he rightly knew beforehand what was going to happen and testified beforehand to these things, which were fulfilled in actual events in this way. Their fulfillment followed his words. Therefore, just as he truly revealed these things,
and we see in the events themselves the fulfillment of our Savior’s earlier words,
so we ought to expect the rest to happen as well. And what are these things? The harvest, the end, the angels who reap,

the gathering of the weeds and their falling into the fire, and the final blessings for those who preserved and multiplied the living, pure, and life-giving seed. Of them it is said, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”
Concerning those who will falsely call themselves Christians. From the Gospel of Matthew.
35. While he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, his disciples approached him privately and said to him, “Tell us, when will these things happen?”
“And what is the sign of your coming and of the end of the world?” Jesus answered them and said:
“See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name and say, ‘I am the Messiah,’ and they will lead many astray.” And again, a little later, he said:
“At that time, if anyone says to you, ‘The Messiah is here,’ or ‘Over there,’ do not believe it. For false messiahs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders,
so as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen. Look, I have told you beforehand.

“So if they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; or, ‘Look, he is in the inner room,’ do not believe it. For just as lightning flashes from the east and is visible as far as the west,
so it will be at the coming of the Son of Man.” And on another occasion, while speaking with the Jews, he added these words:
“I came in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.” He foretold these things about that false Antichrist whom they await,

while warning his disciples. But he indicated in the letter to the Thessalonians that there would be one other at the end. Our Savior himself foretold that, even before that one, others would arise in various places.
For he said, “Many will come in my name and say, ‘I am the Messiah,’ and they will lead many astray.” And after he spoke, there were indeed many.

Thus, immediately afterward, Dositheus, who appeared after the time of our Savior, persuaded the Samaritans that he was the prophet about whom Moses had prophesied, and led them astray into saying that he was the Messiah. And again, another:

in the time of the apostles, they called Simon the magician “the Great Power of God,” and thought that he was the Messiah. Others in Phrygia thought this of Montanus, and still others elsewhere thought this of other people. And the deceivers do not stop.
For we should not think [?] that many more like these will arise. From these very people, too, testimony is obtained to the truth of our Savior’s foreknowledge.
Our Savior himself teaches that his glorious second coming will not again take place in one location, like his first.

And someone might suppose that it would be seen in a corner of the earth. So that no one should think this, he teaches and says, “If anyone says to you, ‘Look, the Messiah is here,’ or ‘Over there,’ do not believe it.” For expectations of this kind do not apply to him,
but to false messiahs and false prophets. He himself, however, once appeared in human form in a single corner of the earth.
He teaches what his glorious second coming from heaven will be like, saying, “For just as lightning comes from the east and is visible as far as the west,

so will the coming of the Son of Man be.”
Concerning the things that happen at the end of all things, from the Gospel of Matthew.
36. “You are [?] to hear of wars and reports of wars.
See that you are not alarmed, for these things must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.
There will be famines, plagues, and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginning of the birth pains. Then they will hand you over to suffering
and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name.” He continues immediately afterward, saying, “Then many will fall away, betray one another, and hate one another.
Many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. Because wickedness increases, the love of many will fade. But whoever endures to the end will be saved.
The good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.” Clearly,
through these words too, he prophesied that his good news must first be proclaimed throughout all creation as a testimony to all nations. And then the end will come.

For the foretold end of the world will not take place beforehand, but only when his word has taken hold among all nations. So, as long as there remain nations among whom his good news has not been proclaimed,

Likewise, the time until the end is short, and he teaches and says, “You are going to hear of wars and reports of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for these things must happen, but the end has not yet come.”
But he indicates when this will happen and says:

“The good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come,” when there are also famines, plagues, and earthquakes in various places,
and nation rises against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there are fierce persecutions and great afflictions. After these things he says:
“You will be hated by all nations”—not because of other hateful deeds, but because of his own name.
37. These are the proofs of our Savior’s divine manifestation, which are visible to the eyes even now, demonstrating both his words and his divine deeds. For formerly his utterances were heard

simply as words, but now, in our own times, the fulfillment of those words is plainly seen in action, along with powers that encompass the whole of mortal nature. But if some people are not persuaded by them,
we should not be surprised, because human beings are accustomed to opposing even what is obvious.
Thus a person even dares to speak against the providence that governs everything with arguments opposing it, and in this way also denies God himself.
In the same way, he also fights shamelessly against many other things to which the truth bears witness. But just as the stubborn opposition of such people does no harm to the true account of nature
at all, so too the wicked unbelief of some people does no harm at all to the manifest excellence of our Savior’s divinity.

But if it is right to set a limit to these matters too, proportionate to our intellectual labor, it is time to present the proofs of the good news to them appropriately here as well, and to recount those things that were previously examined elsewhere,
now also, for those who were not [?] persuaded by what was said. The fourth book of the author from Caesarea is finished.
The fifth book of the author from Caesarea. 1. Such are the proofs of the divine manifestation of Jesus Christ, the common Savior of all,
which are visible to the eyes even now, demonstrating both his words and his divine deeds. For formerly his utterances were heard
simply as words foretelling things that were going to happen—things that he prophesied before his disciples while he was present with them.
But now, in our own times, the fulfillment of those words is plainly seen in deeds, along with powers that encompass the whole of mortal nature.
But if some people are not persuaded by these things, we should not be surprised, because human beings are accustomed to opposing even what is obvious.
Thus a person even dares to speak against the providence that governs everything with arguments opposing it, and in this way also denies God himself.
In the same way, he also fights shamelessly against many other things to which the truth bears witness. But just as the stubborn opposition of such people does no harm to the true account
of nature at all, so too the wicked unbelief of some people does no harm at all to the manifest excellence of our Savior’s divinity.
Therefore these people do not even deserve to have us engage them in discussion.

For those whom God’s deeds do not persuade are unlikely to be persuaded by a human being’s words. Nevertheless, as an additional measure, let us again take up against them those same matters that we ourselves previously examined through questions in the demonstrations of the Gospel.
If, then, after this and all this truth, someone acts shamelessly and without

restraint dares to say that the Christ of God is not as we believe him to be, but is a sorcerer, a deceiver, and one who leads people astray, let us present to him, as to someone childish in his thinking, these very matters that we have already examined.
Against those who thought that God’s Messiah was a magician and a deceiver.
2. Now let us [?] whether anyone, anywhere in the world, has ever heard of a deceiver and magician who became a teacher of humility, gentleness, and chastity,
and every other virtue; and whether it is right to call by these names someone who does not even allow people to look at women with shameful desire;
and whether someone is a magician who imparted the highest philosophy by instructing his disciples to follow him stripped of their possessions,
and to abound greatly in compassion and generosity; and whether someone is a magician who forbids participation in gatherings of crowds and the savagery of disturbances,
and taught them to love only this leisure devoted to divine words. And someone who drives away every kind of falsehood and urges them to honor truth above everything, so that even concerning
a truthful oath they should hesitate, how much more a false one—how can he rightly be called a magician? And why must I now say so much, when it is possible, from his own sayings,

which are proclaimed throughout the earth to this very day, to learn what kind of conduct he planted in the world? From this, everyone who loves the truth acknowledges not only that he was not a magician and deceiver, but that he truly is the Word of God and a teacher of divine philosophy and righteousness,
and not of this ordinary worldly philosophy.
3. Such, then, was the character of his teaching. But come, let us examine whether his deception lay in those great teachings of his.
Is it not written of him that it was God, the King of all, who alone is the cause of every good thing,

whom he taught and presented to his disciples? To this day, the words of his teaching raise the thoughts of all Greeks and non-Greeks upward to God who is above all, to the Maker of heaven and earth and the whole
world, and carry them beyond all visible and tangible nature. Was this, then, his deception? Or was it because he would not allow them to worship many gods,
those who clearly and unmistakably fell headlong from the worship of God alone into this genuine error? But this was nothing new, nor was it a teaching peculiar to him.
Rather, it belonged to those God-loving Hebrews who appeared long ago, from whom even the later philosophers received help in these great matters and agreed with their teaching.

Even the wise Greeks boast of the oracles of their gods, which mention the Hebrews in these words: “Wisdom has come only to the Chaldeans, and the Hebrews worship purely the self-existent God, the King of all.”
4. If, then, even in ancient times those who loved God,
to whom the oracles themselves bore particular witness, offered worship to God who is above all, why should we acknowledge this man as a deceiver

and not as a wonderful teacher of the worship of God, since he extended to all humanity those things formerly known only to the descendants of the Hebrew patriarchs? Thus, no longer, as in ancient times, would just a few people,

few in number, have a correct understanding of God, but countless crowds of non-Greeks, including those who had formerly been savage, together with wise people and Greeks, who, like the ancient prophets and righteous people,
were instructed in the worship of God through his power alone and through his teaching.

5. But let us also examine this third point. Was this why they called him a deceiver: because he [?] that they should no longer, through the slaughter of bulls, sacrifices of irrational animals, blood and fire, or incense from the earth,
honor God, because these things are inferior and earthly?

He showed that they are never appropriate to that immortal, bodiless nature. He explained that, of all our sacrifices, this is acceptable and fitting for God: that they should keep the divine commandments
and be purified in their hands, their very bodies, and their souls, and, with an enlightened mind and instruction in the worship of God, toward likeness to God
He taught them to stop imitating them. But if any of the Greeks criticizes these things, let him know that he is not considering what is accepted concerning his own teachers.
They laid down many rules about this: that people should not suppose they can honor God through the blood and sacrifices of irrational animals, or through fire, smoke, and soot.
6. After these things, we know that we learned from him that the world was made, and that heaven itself, the sun, the moon, and the stars are works of God.
And that it is right for us to worship not these things, but their Maker and the Creator of them all. It is therefore good to examine whether he perhaps deceived us by teaching us in this way.

Let us consider that this was not something new, but belonged to the Hebrews. Those renowned men agreed with them: they said that heaven itself, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the whole world were made by that Creator of all.
And further, that the soul we possess does not die.

He taught us to believe that it is not at all like the irrational animals, but that it contains likenesses of the powers of God. And he instructed all the barbarians and uneducated people to acquire this understanding, to live this way, and to know these things.
Has he not, indeed, made us wiser than those wise men among the Egyptians and those Greeks who raise their eyebrows, who said
that the human soul is in no way superior in its essence to [?], fleas, worms, and flies, nor even to the soul of a snake,
and that the souls of a viper, flies, a leopard, and a pig do not differ at all in their essence?

7. After these things, he repeatedly spoke of God's judgment and set down in writing the punishments and retribution awaiting the wicked, which they cannot escape, and the promise to the righteous of life

everlasting, the kingdom of heaven, and a blessed dwelling with God. Whom, then, was he deceiving? Was he not rather encouraging people to hasten toward virtue because of the rewards reserved for the righteous,
and to flee from all evil and drive it away from themselves because of the punishments appointed for the wicked? For such were the instructions contained in the words of the teachings
of our Savior. What room, then, remains for suspicion that he was a deceiver and a sorcerer? But let us examine these things as well.
8. When a sorcerer makes his companions partners in his wickedness, what kind of people does he make them? Surely sorcerers, deceivers, and makers of potions, who resemble him in everything.
Has anyone, then, ever been found among the whole Christian people who, as a result of our Savior's teaching,
practices sorcery or makes potions? No one can say so. On the contrary, they are seen turning to the teachings of divine philosophy.

What, then, should he rightly be called, who became the source of a pure and chaste life and of the knowledge of the worship of the Creator of all for every nation throughout the inhabited human world? Surely this: that he truly is the common Savior of all,
and the teacher of a life devoted to the worship of God.
9. Those who followed him from the beginning, and those afterward who received the tradition of their way of life, were all so far removed from evil and bitter suspicion
that they would not even permit the sick to perform those practices that are so widespread among so many people, or to write on a metal plate, or to use incantations, or to turn their attention

to those who profess to whisper charms, or to seek relief for themselves through the fumes of roots and stones and other similar remedies for pains. All these things are therefore excluded from the teaching
of our Savior, and no Christian can ever be found using incantations, whispered charms, the device of written [?], or any other practices like these,
which many people indiscriminately regard as useful. What argument, then, can be made for supposing that those trained in these things were disciples of a master sorcerer, when
the fellowship of the disciples is a great test of anyone who professes any teaching? Thus, people skilled and thoroughly knowledgeable about the one who became the source of their instruction [?].
They say that he is superior to them. For just as healings also bear witness to the soundness of their teaching, which is their master's, [?] what other title do they give them except [?]
and [?] to [?], and things like these, including those of a magician.
His disciples would be excellent witnesses to these things, since they fully resembled their teacher and did these things themselves as well. But throughout all these years, no one has ever
been found who was both a magician and a disciple of our Savior, although in every age kings and governors have diligently investigated these matters through cruel tortures.
10. Thus, then, not a single magician was his disciple, since freedom and exemption from all prosecution were granted

to anyone whom they were compelling merely to sacrifice.
11. But so that our discussion does not stray outside the Scriptures, receive the evidence for these things
also from the record of those first acquaintances and disciples of our Savior, in the book of their Acts. They so influenced those from the nations who approached their teaching
that many of them, who had previously been accused of sorcery, completely changed their way of life, so that they dared to bring into the midst of the assemblies
those contemptible books that they had previously kept hidden, and to hand them over to the fire in everyone's presence. Now hear where the account of these things is found:
12. Many of those who had practiced sorcery brought in their books and burned them in everyone's presence. They calculated their prices and found that they were worth fifty thousand.
13. Such, then, were the disciples of our Savior, and such was the power of the message that they brought forth

in speaking to their hearers, so that their words would be fixed deep within their souls and would strike and [?] each person's mind, so that they would no longer consent to conceal those things in which they had previously gone far astray,
but would bring those hidden things into the open and themselves become witnesses against themselves and their former wickedness. Such also were
those who became their disciples: pure and radiant in their souls and outstanding in their love, so that they would not leave anything blameworthy concealed within themselves, but
would glory and take pride in their transformation from wickedness to virtue. Since the disciples of our Savior were thus shown to have been such people,
how could their teacher himself not have been far more excellent before them? But if you wish to learn what their teacher was like from the disciples themselves,
you have, even now, tens of thousands of disciples of our Savior's words. Among them are numerous communities of men who have armed themselves against the natural desires of the body
and are training themselves to keep their minds unharmed by all shameful passions. They have grown old in purity throughout their lives

and, through their steadfast adherence to his words, have displayed glorious deaths.
14. And it was not only men who, under him,
became philosophers in this way, but also tens of thousands of women throughout the world. Like priestesses of the God who is over all, they have loved the service that is above
and have been possessed by a love of heavenly wisdom, looking down on bearing children of the flesh.
They devote all their care to their souls and keep them pure from every filth and stain. They have loved complete holiness and virginity. Yet about one shepherd who abandoned
his place for the sake of philosophy, the Greeks sing and circulate the story far and wide—this was Democritus. They also marvel at a certain Crates, who gave his property to his fellow citizens
and restrained himself, taking pride in his freely chosen endurance. But those who emulate the words of our Savior
number in the tens of thousands. It was not just one or two who sold their property and gave it to the unfortunate and needy.

For we too are witnesses of these things, since we have lived among the people of this time, and in their deeds we have seen the fulfillment of our Savior’s teaching. And why need we speak of the many tens of thousands, including those among the barbarians, and not

only them, but also the Greeks, who through instruction in our Savior’s words have risen above the whole error of many gods and have come to know and acknowledge the one God alone, the Father and Creator of this entire world?
Long ago, Plato alone knew him, and admitted that he did not dare speak of him before everyone, because he did not have anything like this great power of devotion to God. But those
disciples of our Savior, who through their Master’s help were able easily to know and find the Father and Creator of all, throughout the whole human race
revealed him and proclaimed the knowledge of him to everyone throughout creation. Thus, through their teaching, even now, among all nations, tens of thousands of people in gatherings—not
only men, but also women, children, slaves, and villagers—are in all this no less than that philosopher, so that the Maker and Creator of this entire world
they not only know, but also serve as his messengers everywhere. Such, then, are the victories of the Savior common to all!
Such are the deceptions of the one who was considered a deceiver! And these are merely his disciples and acquaintances, from whom it was right to learn what their Master was like.
15. Come, then, let us examine the matter again in this way too. You there—you say that he was a sorcerer, and indeed that he practiced sorcery.
You call him cunning and a deceiver. But was he alone the first to arise as the discoverer of this practice? Or is it like customary practices, whose origin should be traced back to teachers?
If, then, without anyone teaching him, he alone was the first to discover this practice, having never learned anything from others or even associated with earlier practitioners,

how should we not acknowledge that his nature was divine, since without a book, without instruction, and without teachers, he taught himself and showed himself independently knowledgeable and able to accomplish these things?
For it is impossible to receive instruction in the craft of metalworking, or in rational knowledge, or even in the first elements, without someone to guide and teach
unless one is beyond nature. No one, then, has ever emerged self-taught as a teacher of grammar, or as an orator without studying,
nor as a physician, nor as a carpenter, nor as a practitioner of any other craft, although these are small matters and belong to human beings.
But for someone to say of the teacher of the whole inhabited world that the one who performed those wonders recorded in the book was merely human—the one
whose disciples [?] that he became like this on his own, neither receiving it from earlier people nor being helped by contemporary teachers who had done similar things before him—
what else is there for them to do but testify and acknowledge that this is truly a divine matter, and that he surpasses the whole of human nature?
16. But you say of him that he had deceptive teachers, and that the Egyptians’ wisdom did not escape him,

nor those secret things that had long been proclaimed among them; that he gathered these things from them and appeared as the sort of man the account describes. Why, then, if others appeared who were superior to him
and preceded him in time and were his teachers, whether in Egypt or anywhere else,
why did their fame not also spread among all people before his name did, in the same way as his?
And why is their praise not also proclaimed to this day as his is? And which sorcerer of all those who have ever lived, barbarian or Greek,
arose as a teacher of such disciples and became the founder of all such laws and teachings as these, which the power of the Savior common to all has displayed?

And who is ever recorded as having performed healings like those our Savior is remembered as performing? And what of his knowledge of the future, and all those predictions, and things like these that are now set forth through those earlier sayings?
Who else in all history, whether before him or after him, is remembered as having accomplished this?
And who promised to do throughout the whole human world what he had foretold in words, and then confirmed his words by deeds?
So that even now, in our own time, the fulfillment of his earlier words can be seen with our own eyes throughout the earth. And whose disciples and eyewitnesses of these events ever, through
the ordeal of fire and iron, sealed the truth of what they testified about their teacher, as did these disciples of our Savior? They endured every humiliation for what they had seen and testified
about him, and bore every kind of torture. Finally, with their own lifeblood they sealed their testimony to what they had testified about him as the Son of God, far from being a sorcerer.
And which sorcerer ever even conceived the idea of forming a congregation of a new people

in his own name—and not merely thinking of it, but also carrying out his plan so that it would not be hidden from the whole human race—and of establishing laws against the error of the many gods, laws

opposed to the ranks of kings, earlier lawgivers, philosophers, poets, and those who discourse about the gods? And who would send out these laws themselves and show them, over a long period of life, to be undefeated and unvanquished?

17. Which sorcerer ever conceived anything like what our Savior conceived? Even if he had conceived it, he probably would not have dared to proclaim it; and even if he had proclaimed it, he probably would not have carried it out.
With one word and one utterance he said to his disciples, “Go and make disciples of all nations
