in my name, and teach them everything that I commanded you.” And he made the deed follow the word.

Immediately, within a short time, all the peoples, Greeks and barbarians alike, were being made disciples. And laws—not in a writing of our Savior, but without writing, at his command—were being sown among all nations,
opposing the ancient worship of many gods: laws that made the Scythians, Persians, and other barbarians chaste, and turned them away from every savage way of life
and lawlessness; laws that overturned the age-old customs among the Jews,

and taught the new and true worship of God. Which of the earlier leaders, then, before the time of our Savior, dared to do such things, so that we might plausibly say of him that he received help from others in this

sorcery? But if there is no one else whom anyone can say was like him, then no human being was the cause of all this excellence in him. It is time, therefore, to acknowledge that a divine nature, foreign to ours,
came into the world: he alone was the first to accomplish these things, which had never before been remembered among human beings.
18. After this, let us ask again whether anyone has ever seen with his own eyes or learned by report that there are sorcerers [?] and makers of potions who practice sorcery without libations,
sacrifices, and the invocation of demons. For it is well known and clear to everyone that all sorcery is ordinarily accomplished through these things. Does anyone, then,

have such an accusation to bring against our Savior, his disciples, or those who to this day conduct their lives according to his teaching? Is it not clear even to the blind that we are prepared for everything opposed
to these things? We would sooner dare to surrender ourselves to death than sacrifice to demons, and we would sooner renounce life than endure being enslaved to demons.
And who does not know how dearly we desire to drive out the whole race of demons by our Savior’s own name and by pure prayers?
Thus our Savior’s word and the teaching that comes from him have made us all far superior to this invisible and unsearchable power,
and have prepared us to be enemies and haters of demons, not their friends and companions, much less their servants and obedient subjects.

How, then, could he who imparted such things to those who obeyed him have himself been a servant of demons? How could he have sacrificed to evil spirits? Or how could he have called upon demons as helpers and supporters?
When all the demons and all the unclean spirits, as though facing one of the torments and punishments proper to their nature, still tremble at his name, withdraw, and flee before his power.
Just as they did long ago, at the time when he lived among human beings, when they could not bear the sight of him.
One after another, from different places, would cry out and say, “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the appointed time to torment us?”
19. But a man whose mind was fixed exclusively on sorcery, and who was wholly occupied with contemptible things—
would he not indeed have been hateful in his conduct, openly disgraceful, corrupt, unjust, godless, and wicked?

And if he were like that, from what source or in what way would he have taught others about worshiping God, or about chastity, or about the knowledge of God, or about the immortal soul, or about righteousness and God’s judgment over everyone?

Would he not instead have been a herald of the opposite of all these things, doing what accompanies wickedness, denying God and God’s providence, and treating God’s judgment and righteousness as though they were
a fable, and laughing at these teachings about virtue and the immortal soul? If, then, things like these were evident
also in the case of this man of ours, there would be nothing to say in reply. But if, in all his words and all his deeds,
he is seen to have called upon God who is above all, the King of all, and to have prepared his disciples to do the same;
and if he himself was chaste and a teacher of chastity; and if he practiced and proclaimed righteousness, truth, mercy, and every virtue; and if he showed how to worship God,

the King of all, how does it not follow from these things that we should in no way suppose that he performed these astonishing deeds by sorcery, but acknowledge that he truly performed them by a hidden and divine power?
[?]. These things, then, answer those who have dared to blaspheme him with godless mouths. But if they change their position and acknowledge concerning him
that he was a teacher of a pure and chaste way of life and introduced the teaching of the worship of God, but did not perform these astonishing deeds, mighty works,
and wonders recorded about him, and that his disciples invented these divine deeds that surpass human ability, it is time to confront them about this accusation too.
Against those who do not believe the testimony of our Savior’s disciples concerning his wondrous deeds.
21. But if they say concerning him that he performed absolutely no wonders or astonishing deeds of the kind to which his disciples testified, but that they invented them,

and that his disciples told lies instead, and for this reason spread stories about his wondrous deeds, let us see whether their argument is persuasive, since they have no explanation to give for why those

disciples and their master went out into the world. For a teacher promises an introduction to some teaching, while the disciples, in turn, are drawn to the teachings and instruction, or to some craft,
and entrust themselves to the teacher. What explanation, then, can anyone give concerning the disciples

of our Savior, regarding their association with him? What compelled them to show this concern for him, and as a teacher of what doctrines did they enroll under him? Or is this clear? For the things they learned from him in full
they also told others, and these are the subjects of philosophy. First, he was a herald of God who is over all, of God’s providence, of righteous judgment, and of the soul

that does not die, of the distinction between the way of life of the good and that of the wicked, and of other related matters recorded in their book. There was also a command concerning the way of life
of philosophy, which he prescribed for them, saying, “Do not acquire gold or silver in your purses, or a bag for the journey,” and other things like these. Instead, they were simply
to entrust themselves to the providence of the Ruler of all and not worry about being in need. And how he exhorted them to practice restraints greater than those Moses commanded!
For the Jews, he laid down the law, “Do not kill,” as for people who found killing easy; likewise, he commanded them not to commit adultery, as people who were reckless and adulterous.
And again, he commanded them not to steal, as people suited to slavery, and not to defraud, as people who were oppressive. But he knew that these others were upright and had no need of these laws.

Rather, they were to value this above everything: that their souls should not be subject to passions, and that they should uproot the springs of evil from deep within their minds, as though pulling them out by the root, and train themselves
to overcome anger and every corrupt desire—that is, not even to become angry, because of the excellence of their souls, which were free from passion, and not to look at a woman with shameful desire.
They were to do the opposite of stealing: to give even their own possessions to those in need. And they were not to boast that they did not defraud others, but rather
that, to those in need—and they were not to boast that they did not defraud others, but rather that they endured without anger those who wanted to defraud them.
Why do I need to gather together all these things that he taught and they learned?
Along with all these things, he advised them to remain so steadfast in truth that they would not need even a truthful oath, much less a false one.
Instead, they were to shape their conduct so that through it they would be seen to be more trustworthy than any oath. They were to limit themselves to “Yes” and speak truthfully.
22. Let us therefore ask whether there is any argument at all concerning those who heard these things and immediately became teachers of these same things to other disciples,
that would lead us to suppose that they invented all the things they testified their master had done.
What, then, is persuasive about supposing that they all lied in complete agreement?
They numbered twelve chosen men and seventy others, who, it is also said, were sent ahead of him, two by two, to every place

and region where he himself was about to go. Yet there is not a single argument that could expose as liars this whole company of people who loved a pure life devoted to the worship of God and disregarded all the members of their households.
In place of their loved ones—I mean their wives, their children, and their entire families—they adopted a life without possessions.
And they brought their testimonies about their master before all humanity in complete agreement, as though speaking with one mouth.
23. This, then, is the first, principal, and true argument. But let us also consider the opposite. Let him be the teacher and them the disciples,

and then, for the sake of argument, let him teach not the things previously mentioned, but their opposites: readily to break the law, to act wickedly, to act unjustly, to oppress, to lie, to lie, to swear oaths, and to do hateful things,
and whatever other evil can be named. All these things are completely alien to our Savior’s teaching; they are contrary to it and marked by insolence and shamelessness. And not
only are they contrary to the women of his community and to his teaching, but also to the way of life handed down to all nations to this day, which is practiced in all his churches.
Nevertheless, even if the argument is false and implausible, let it be granted in accordance with the account that we have [?], so that even on this basis the matters before us may be examined.
Let him, then, teach every kind of wickedness and injustice, and let care be taken above all to conceal them; and let this practice be hidden with still greater cunning
under the guise of preliminary instruction promising a new form of worship. Let them conduct themselves in these ways, and again in ways worse than these, because beforehand
wickedness had ensnared them and was the teaching of his own soul. And let them exalt their master to greatness with invented statements, without shrinking from even a single false statement.

And let them falsely attribute to him all the wonders consisting of astonishing deeds, so that people may admire them too and call them blessed for having been worthy to become disciples of such a man.
24. Come, then, let us see whether, if they really were like this, what they did concerning him could have endured. For they say that evil loves evil, not good.
Where, then, among this great number of people, did this agreement in evil come from? And where did this testimony about them come from, that the undertaking of them all, in complete agreement,
came about? And where did this teaching about the divine orders and the teachings of philosophy come from? And where did this understanding of a virtuous way of life come from? And where

did this instruction in fleeing from evil come from? And where did this knowledge of such teachings and their recording in writing come from? And where did the purity of this conduct and manner of life come from,
which was handed down by them throughout the whole inhabited world? And where did all this power come from?

And where did this courage come from? And where did this confidence come from? And where did this steadfast commitment, lasting until death, come from? But a man who, as someone might say, taught evil and bitter things,
and promised such things—who would have paid him any attention at the outset, even in his thoughts? Unless they say that he was a sorcerer. But his own disciples, whose leader [?]
and were not evil in any way—did these same people persist in these things even after that shameful end, and say that the one among the dead was God, unless they were pointlessly intent on

suffering such things for his sake? And who would ever openly choose punishment for himself without any benefit? For if they had been lovers of possessions and fond of profit, and if their conduct had been depraved and they had been lovers of pleasures,

perhaps it would have been reasonable for us to suppose that they arranged the undertaking for these reasons and risked their lives to the point of death. But if they proclaimed the opposite of these things, crying out openly for all the crowds to hear,
and soon also gave exhortations through instruction in writing,
to flee from every depraved and filthy desire, to turn away from every injustice, and to overcome all passions and the love of money—and when they taught such things to those
who became their disciples, it seems that they themselves did not engage in trade, did not accumulate wealth, and did not share in a life of pleasure and luxury.

Since, then, they did not conduct themselves in any of these ways, how could they endure receiving cruel punishment and retribution for nothing, solely for their testimony about their master, who was no longer alive?
25. Let this be granted: they might have honored him while he was still with them and was associating with them,

and, as someone might say, was misleading them by deception. Why, then, did they call him God even after his death, and much more emphatically then than before? For it is said that while he was among human beings, they even deserted him and denied him
at the time when they were preparing plots against him. But after he departed from among human beings, they preferred to die gladly rather than withdraw their favorable testimony about him.

If, then, they had previously known nothing good in their master—neither a way of life, nor conduct, nor teaching, nor any deed worthy of praise—and had received no benefit from him in any way, but only evil and the deception of people,
how could they so readily die, not because they were accused of anything, but because they testified to those pure and praiseworthy things about him, when each one of them had the opportunity to live
without fear and lead an undisturbed life at home with his loved ones? And how could men who were deceivers and impostors willingly accept death for someone else,
whom they knew with greater certainty than anyone else had, so to speak, in no way been a source of good to them, but a teacher of every evil? For a man who possesses understanding
and virtue might perhaps, as a citizen, sometimes endure an honorable death for a noble victory or for a virtuous man. But someone whose conduct is evil, since he pursues only
this temporary life and the enjoyment of its pleasures, never chooses death over life.

Nor does he endure harsh punishment even for his own loved ones, much less for someone accused of wickedness. How, then, could the disciples of this man who has been mentioned, if he was a deceiver and a sorcerer, and it was not hidden from them that he was such—

Otherwise, would even they, whose souls were held in the hateful grip of wickedness, have endured every torture from their own people and accepted every kind of punishment in return for their testimony about him?
But this is not the nature of wicked people. For I have seen many who, while their companions were alive,

faithfully maintained their friendship and their oath, but the moment those companions died, they dissolved the agreements they had made with one another. As for those sophists who gather in the cities
and publicly boast of their education and the proofs offered in their speeches, we all know very well that they praise the governors of the nations and those who hold
great ruling power, offering them praises as far as the authorities permit them. But the moment their circumstances change, their words change too.
They no longer wish even to mention their former rulers, because they fear those who hold power at the time.
26. If, then, these disciples of our Savior were themselves deceived and were deceivers, add this as well:
they were uneducated and completely untrained. They were also foreigners and understood no language beyond Syriac.
How, after their master had departed from among human beings, did they go out into the whole world and testify to his divinity? What reasoning persuaded them to venture on this, and by what power

did they accomplish what they dared to attempt? Let it be granted that these villagers might go about in their own country and go astray. But that they should be sent to a foreign land and not quietly let the matter rest,
but proclaim to everyone the name of our Savior and his wonderful deeds—and not only that, but also teach his commandments in villages and cities,
and that some of them should disperse throughout the Roman Empire and to this imperial city, some to the land of the Persians, some to the land of the Armenians, and others to the people
of the Parthians, and also to the Scythians, and some even to the ends of the world,

going out and reaching the land of the Indians, while others should cross beyond the ocean to those islands called Britain—I do not think these are things within human power, much less within the power of insignificant and uneducated people, and still less of deceivers and sorcerers.
27. But having found their master to be wicked and deceitful, and having seen with their own eyes the manner of his death, what words could they have used with one another to agree unanimously

to invent stories about him? For they all testified, as though with one mouth, to the cleansing of lepers, the expulsion of demons, the raising of the dead, the restoration of sight to the blind, and the countless other healings he performed.

28. And above all, his resurrection after death, which was revealed to them first. For if these things had not happened and had never been heard of in their own time, how could they have testified as though with one mouth and insisted

that they had happened, standing by their testimony even to death? Or did they perhaps gather together, swear an oath about this, and make an agreement among themselves to invent and falsely report things that had never happened?
And what persuasive words are we to say they used in making this agreement?

Or perhaps words like these: “Friends, that man of yesterday and the day before was a deceiver and a teacher of error who suffered the ultimate punishment before the eyes of us all. What he really was, better
than anyone else, we know exactly, because we were entrusted with his secrets. He appeared pure to many and imagined that he possessed something beyond what most people had.

But he possessed nothing great, nor anything worthy of his standing, unless someone were to mention the deceit and the fault in his conduct, the perverse things he taught us, and this deceptive boasting. In return for these things, come, let us give one another our right hands,
and let us all together make an agreement among ourselves to spread a deception about him unanimously among all humanity.
Let us say that we saw him give sight to the blind—something no one has ever heard of—cleanse lepers, and bring the dead to life. In short,
let us say that he did things we did not see with our own eyes.”
We have not even heard it said with our own ears, yet let us maintain that these things actually happened. But even if his departure was proclaimed otherwise, and he met his death openly,
so that no one could conceal it, let us shamelessly explain this away too, boldly testifying that he rose from the dead and was with us all.

He shared conversation and festive meals with us. Throughout all this, let us preserve this boldness without shame, and let it remain with us so that we stand firm until death. For what does it matter if we die for nothing, without a care?
And what harm is there in receiving distress, lashes, and tortures in our bodies for nothing?
And if we must also suffer imprisonment, humiliation, and oppression for something entirely untrue, let us recklessly endure this too.
Let us all weave our story together in complete agreement and invent it for no benefit, either to ourselves or to those to whom we tell it, nor even
to the one about whom we tell these lies, saying that he is God. Let us spread this falsehood not only among our own people,
but let us also go out to all humanity and fill the whole creation with the things we have attributed to him.
And immediately, starting here, let us lay down laws for all nations that overturn their beliefs about their ancestral gods, beliefs handed down among them from ancient times.
Above all, let us command the Romans not to worship those whom their ancestors considered gods. Let us also move on to the Greeks and proclaim things opposed to the teachings of their wise men.

Let us not leave the Egyptians alone either, but fight against their gods as well. Let us not bring against them what Moses brought upon them long ago, but set the death of our own teacher before them as something terrifying,

and let us overthrow the reputation of their gods, which spread from them among all humanity long ago—not with words and stories, but by the power of our master who was crucified. Then let us go on to another land,
the land of the barbarians, and overturn what all people hold. Let none of us fall short of this purpose.
For what we are daring is no small contest, since no ordinary victories have come our way. Rather, as it seems,
the punishment prescribed by the laws everywhere is plainly chains, torture combs, imprisonment, fire, iron, crosses, and wild beasts. Let us desire these things all the more joyfully.
Let us all share in these sufferings together, since we bear a likeness to our teacher.
For what could be better than this: to be found enemies of God and humanity for no benefit whatever, and to receive no comfort at all?
Let us not even see our loved ones, receive any increase in possessions, or have any hope of anything good at all.
Instead, let us go astray pointlessly and fruitlessly, and lead others astray. For this, they say, is beneficial: to oppose all nations and fight against the gods
whom everyone has acknowledged from ancient times, and to proclaim that our teacher, who died before our very eyes,
is God and the Son of God. Let us be ready to die for him, although we have learned nothing true or beneficial from him.
Let us do this to glorify his name, endure every humiliation and demand for punishment, and accept every form of penalty
for something entirely untrue. For perhaps truth is evil, while falsehood contains something that counteracts evil. For this reason, let us say that he even raised the dead,
cleansed lepers, drove out demons, and performed other miraculous deeds,
although we know of nothing like this about him. Let us invent all these things ourselves and deceive whomever we can.
If, however, anyone is not persuaded, let us instead put ourselves in the place of those whom we have assumed among ourselves to be capable of this deception.
29. Do these arguments seem persuasive to you? Do you still persuade yourself that insignificant, uneducated men invented such things, made an agreement among themselves, and defied Roman authority?
Or how can human nature, which possesses a love of its own life, ever willingly endure death for nothing?
Or how were our Savior’s disciples driven to such an extreme of madness that, although they had seen no miraculous deeds performed by him,
they would all agree together to invent such things, compose false statements about him, and readily die for them?
30. But they did not set out by agreement to proclaim him, nor did they make an arrangement among themselves. Where, then, did this agreement in their testimony about his deeds come from?

Or is it likely that it came from seeing what he had done? For it must be one of two things: either they made an agreement among themselves and invented these things, or they saw them with their own eyes and testified.
If, then, they saw the truth and proclaimed it to everyone, they deserve to be believed when they said of their Savior that he is God, who let them see divine powers, miracles, and deeds
of wonder with their own eyes. But if they saw nothing true among the things that were written, but composed false statements and then joined hands with
one another, swore an oath, and made an agreement to say nothing true, but invented things and testified falsely about their master, how could they actually have been dying
for something that was not true at all? Neither fire, nor iron, nor wild beasts, nor the depths of the sea could make them disown this story they had invented about their master.

31. But what are you saying—that they neither expected nor thought that they would suffer any harm [?] because of this testimony about him, and that this was why they went out fearlessly to proclaim him? Yet it is impossible that they did not expect to suffer every kind of evil.

For they were bringing about the overthrow of the gods of Romans, Greeks, and barbarians alike. The account concerning them itself plainly shows that, after their master’s death, certain enemies of the message who plotted against it

arrested them and first committed them to prison. Then they released them and ordered them not to speak to anyone in the name of Jesus. When they later found them openly teaching the crowds these things about him,
they seized them, flogged them, and sternly ordered them not to teach. Simon Peter answered them, saying, “We must obey God rather than human beings.”
After this, Stephen was stoned to death because he spoke openly in the assembly of the Jews. A severe persecution arose against those who were messengers
for the name of Jesus. Again, on another occasion, when Herod, king of the Jews, killed James the brother of John with the sword, he imprisoned this same Simon Peter in chains,
as is written in the Acts of the Apostles. While they suffered these things, the rest of the disciples endured and persevered in our Savior’s teaching.
They remained steadfast and proclaimed him and his miraculous deeds to everyone all the more. After this, James, whom the long-standing inhabitants of Jerusalem called the Righteous
because of his outstanding virtue, was questioned by the high priest and the teachers of the Jewish people about what he believed concerning Jesus. When he answered them that he is the Son of God,
he too was stoned by them. Simon Peter was crucified upside down in Rome [in Rome], and Paul was put to death.
John was consigned to the island. While they were suffering these things, none of the others departed from his teaching.

They all prayed that things like those already mentioned might happen to them because of their worship of God. For this reason, they testified openly all the more about our Savior and his wonderful deeds.
32. Now, if these were lies, and they had invented them by agreement—

these things that they proclaimed about him—we must marvel at how this entire company maintained their agreement about their fabrication until death, and how not one of them was ever frightened by what happened to those who had been killed before them.
And he withdrew from their fellowship and did not preach against his companions,

or bring to light what they had agreed among themselves. But even the man who was full of love for money and dared to hand him over to his enemies immediately brought punishment upon himself with his own hands.
33. And how is this not astonishing: that wandering, uneducated men, who knew how neither to speak nor to understand anything beyond the
language of their fathers, should not only dare to go out and travel among all the nations, but actually go out and accomplish the task?
And consider how it happened that not one of them ever came forward with a statement contradicting the deeds of their teacher. For if, concerning all
matters that are disputed

and contested in a lawful court, the agreement of witnesses settles the disputed matter, and the law of God says, “Every matter shall be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses,” how should the truth not be established
also through these men—the twelve chosen men, the disciples numbering seventy, and the many thousands besides them—who all together displayed remarkable agreement
and testified to the things done by our Savior? They did this not without suffering, but by enduring tortures, every kind of humiliation, beatings, imprisonments,
and deaths. For this reason they too were accredited by God, who to this day confirms throughout the whole world the message proclaimed through them among all humankind.
34. Consider these things, then, granting them carelessly an unexamined starting point.
For someone might suppose the opposite of the written account and say that the common Savior of all was a teacher, not of words of chastity, but of injustice and violence

and every kind of shamefulness, and that his disciples learned these very things from him and became covetous of everything and worse than all other people. To concede this even for the sake of argument

is utterly improper. It would be like someone bringing an accusation against Moses, who said in the law, “You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, and you shall not bear false witness,”

slandering him and saying that he spoke these things [?] and hypocritically, because he actually wanted his hearers to murder, commit adultery, and do the opposite of the things for which he presented himself as laying down the law,
while outwardly presenting himself as devoted to a pure way of life. There is no shamelessness like this. Likewise, concerning the [?] of the philosophers among the Greeks, someone might speak
slanderously of their austere way of life and all their words, saying that they were and behaved in ways contrary to what was written, while presenting themselves
as devoted to a philosophical way of life. In this way, to put it simply, someone slanders all the writings of the ancients, attacks the truth in them,
and accepts the opposite of what they contain. But just as no one with any sense hesitates
to say that such a person is mad, so also with the words of our Savior and his disciples, if someone overturns the truth in them and tries to impose an interpretation contrary to what he taught
upon him. Nevertheless, this too has been conceded for the sake of argument, so that even with an unexamined acceptance, the opponent’s argument may be seen all the more clearly not to stand.

35. Now that he has been refuted, come, let us also examine the testimony of the divine writings and observe the blameless, truth-loving character of our Savior’s disciples. From this, then, anyone who thinks rightly
judges them worthy of every honor: they admitted that they had been humble men, uneducated in their speech, and they turned to a love of instruction in the worship of God and philosophy.

They loved an austere and difficult way of life, through fasting, abstinence from wine and meat, and many other disciplines of the body, which can be achieved through prayers and petitions to God, and especially through exceptional chastity and holiness of body
and soul. And who would not marvel at them, since for the excellence of wisdom they abstain even from the wives lawfully given to them and are not drawn away by natural desire?
Nor were they enslaved to love for children, for they loved not mortal children, but those who do not die.
And who would not marvel at this way of life of theirs, in which they did not love money? Let us compare this with the fact that they did not flee.

Rather, they loved a teacher who rejected the possession of gold and silver and laid down rules that they should not increase their possessions even to two tunics—a requirement whose hearer might perhaps hesitate because of the severity

of the command. Yet they are seen to have put this saying into practice. For once a lame man, one of those who went around begging for food for some other reason, was asking alms from Simon Peter and his companions.

And since Simon Peter had nothing to give him, he acknowledged that he was free from all possession of silver and gold, saying, “I have no gold or silver.” Then he brought forward the honored name, more precious than anything, and said, “What
I do have, I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, get up and walk.”

36. And when their teacher instructed them about sorrowful things, they looked to him, as when he told them, “In the world you will have affliction,” and again, “You will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice.”
How were they not plainly shown to be sincere and profound in their way of life, since they did not flee from those departures from life, nor pursue
these desirable things? And their master, too, did not entice them through deception, promising them pleasant things and making them his own. Rather, with truthful
and frank speech, he foretold what would happen to them and allowed them to choose such a way of life for themselves. Such, too, were the things he said about the persecutions

that would befall them because of their master's name. He foretold and testified that they would come before governors and be brought before kings, and would endure every punishment and act of vengeance, not because of anything wicked, nor for

any other legitimate reason, but solely because of their testimony about him. We see this happening with our own eyes even now, and we ought to marvel at his prediction. For testimony to the name of our Savior

and confession of him are accustomed to inflame the anger of rulers. Even if someone who confesses Christ has done nothing wicked, they punish and insult him because of his name, as though he were an evildoer worse than all others.

But if someone does not confess his name and denies that he is Christ's disciple, he is immediately released as a free man, even if he has been caught in many wicked acts. And why need I gather many accounts and write about the experiences

of the lives of our Savior's disciples, when what has been said is sufficient for the demonstration before us? Nevertheless, let us add the following to these things, and here bring our discussion of this subject to a fitting close.
37. The apostle Matthew's former way of life was not a virtuous occupation. Rather, he was one of those engaged in tax collecting and extortion.
Not one of the other apostles revealed this to us: neither his fellow apostle John, nor Luke, nor Mark,
the writers of the other Gospels. But Matthew himself wrote about
his own way of life and became his own accuser. Listen, then, to how openly he mentions himself by name in his own account, speaking in this way:
38. “As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax office. He said to him, ‘Follow me.’ And he got up and followed him.

And while he was reclining at table in the house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples.” Again, when he went on afterward and listed the other disciples, he added the designation “tax collector” to himself

and spoke as follows: “The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who was called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector.”
Thus Matthew, through his outstanding humility, showed his truth-loving character and called himself a tax collector.
He did not conceal his former way of life, but counted himself among sinners and listed himself second to his fellow apostle.

For he was paired with Thomas, just as Simon was with Andrew, James with John, and Philip with Bartholomew. He put Thomas first and honored his fellow apostle as his superior, whereas the other evangelists did the opposite.
Listen, then, to Luke: when he mentions Matthew, he does not call him a tax collector. Nor does he place him after Thomas. Rather, knowing that he was a distinguished man, he lists him before him.
After him he brings in Thomas, just as Mark also did. His words are these: “When day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve from among them,
whom he named apostles: Simon, whom he called Peter; Andrew, the brother of James; John; Philip; Bartholomew; Matthew; and Thomas.”
Thus Luke honored Matthew, in keeping with what those who were eyewitnesses and proclaimers of the word from the beginning handed down to him.
Matthew, however, humbly made himself less important, acknowledged that he was a tax collector, and numbered himself second, after his fellow apostle.
39. You will also find John resembling Matthew. For in his own letter he did not even mention himself,
or he called himself “the elder,” but never “apostle” or “evangelist.”
And in the Gospel that he wrote, he mentioned himself as the one whom Jesus loved, but did not identify himself by name.

40. Simon Peter did not even undertake the writing of a Gospel, because of his exceptional reverence [?]. But Mark, who was his acquaintance and disciple [?], is said to have recorded Simon’s words about the deeds of our Savior.
When, in his account, he reached the events in which Jesus asked what people were saying about him and what his disciples themselves thought about him,
and Simon answered him, “You are the Messiah,” he did not write that Jesus gave him an answer or said anything to him, but only that he sternly warned them not to tell anyone this.
Mark wrote these things although he was not near Jesus when he said them. Rather, he heard them from Simon as he taught them. But Simon himself, concerning the things Jesus said to him and about him,
was unwilling to relate them in his own testimony. Matthew shows what these things said to him were in the following words:
“But you, who do you say that I am?” Simon said to him, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”

Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father in heaven. And I too tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.
The bars of Sheol will not overpower it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven,
and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” Although Jesus said all these things to Simon Peter, Mark did not record even one
of them, because Simon apparently did not say these things in his teaching either.
Simon Peter therefore rightly kept silent about these things, and for this reason Mark also left them out. But he proclaimed the events of his denial to everyone.
He had an accusation against himself written down, and that he wept [?] bitterly over it. You will find Mark writing

these things about him: “While Simon was in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s servant girls came to him. When she saw him warming himself, she looked closely at him and said to him, ‘You too were with Jesus the Nazarene.’ But he denied it and said, ‘I do not know or understand what you are saying.’
He went out into the outer courtyard, and a rooster crowed. The girl saw him again and began saying to those standing there, ‘He too is one of them.’
He denied it again. A little later, those standing there again said to Simon, ‘You really are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.’
But he began to curse and say, ‘I do not know this man you are talking about.’ Immediately a rooster crowed
for the second time.” Mark writes these things, and Simon Peter testifies to these things about himself. For all these things in Mark are said to be a record of Simon’s words.

41. Those, then, who decline to tell things that bring them a good reputation, but put into writing the reproaches against themselves so that they will never be forgotten, and record accusations of their own foolishness—these things

which none of those who came afterward would have known if they had not been written down through their own account—how do these not clear them of every impulse of self-love and of false statements, and plainly demonstrate their love of truth?
And let us justly acknowledge that they showed these things willingly. As for those who supposed that the men who displayed such conduct invented things and lied,
and who try to vilify them as deceivers, how can they avoid becoming a laughingstock and being found to be lovers of envy and jealousy and enemies of truth? For how are they not such people—

those who called them impostors and crafty sophists concerning the very things through which they themselves, without deceit or a shameful habit, showed in their account the truthful and pure character of their conduct? They said that they invented things that did not exist

and graciously attributed to their master things that he had not done. It seems to me that it is right to ask them whether we ought to believe the disciples of our Savior or not, and whether we should disbelieve these men alone,
or also all those throughout history, among both Greeks and barbarians, who wrote down a record of the lives and sayings of those who, from time
to time, became renowned for their achievements. If they decide that it is right to believe the others, but that we should disbelieve these men alone, how is their envy not obvious?

32. But what of those who lied about their master and handed down in their writings things that had not happened to him as though they had happened? Did they also lie about those sufferings and those distressing events, and about his betrayal, in a word,

by his disciple, the accusations of those who wronged him, the ridicule and mockery at the trial, the humiliation, the blows to his cheeks, the lashes on his back, the crown of thorns placed on him in contempt, and the garment

of scarlet in which they dressed him, fashioned as a military cloak; and, finally, that he carried his cross, the sign of victory, that he was fastened to it and pierced in his hands and feet, the vinegar they gave him to drink, and that he was struck on the head with a reed,

and that he was reviled by those who were looking at him? Should we suppose that his disciples invented these things too, and the other similar things that are written? Or should we believe that they speak truthfully about these things,
but disbelieve them about the glorious things? And how can this contradictory position stand? For saying that these very same people are truthful and then, in turn, that they lie

is nothing other than making contradictory statements about them. What, then, is the refutation of these claims? For if they had set themselves this aim—to invent things and, through false statements, exalt
their master and adorn him with miracles—they would never have written the things mentioned above against themselves. Nor would they have disclosed to later generations that the one
whose messengers they had become was distressed and sorrowful and troubled in his soul,

or that they abandoned him and fled, or that the chosen one among all the apostles, his disciple, the very Simon Peter who is proclaimed, denied him three times without torture-combs or threats of torture. For even if

others had said these things, would they not have had to deny them, if their sole purpose was to do him a favor through false statements and to make those great claims about themselves and their master?
43. But if they are shown to be lovers of truth in those distressing accounts of theirs about him,
much more are they so in the glorious accounts as well. For why, once they had chosen to lie,
would they have done so about these distressing things, rather than avoiding them, either by silence or by [?] concerning them? For they could not—
those who came afterward—expose the things that had been left unmentioned. For why

did they not disclose and say that Judas, who betrayed him, when he dared to give the kiss that signaled the betrayal, immediately turned to stone; that the right hand of the man who dared to strike him on the cheek immediately withered; and that the high priest

of the Jews was blinded because he was acting together with those who wronged him? And why did they not all lie and say that nothing distressing had really happened to him, but that he had hidden himself from them and laughed at their court?
And those who slandered him were misled by delusions sent from God and thought they had accomplished something against one who was not present. And how was this not more glorious
than inventing that he raised the dead and performed miraculous deeds: to write that nothing human or mortal happened to him,

but that he did everything by divine power and made his ascent to heaven in divine glory? For those who believed their other accounts could not disbelieve these things. Those, therefore, who concealed no truth

about those matters of distress and sorrow—how could they not deserve belief also concerning the rest of the miracles to which they testified about him, being beyond malicious suspicion? Their testimony about our Savior is therefore sufficient.

But nothing prevents us from also making further use of Josephus, the Hebrew witness. In the eighteenth book of his history of the Antiquities of the Jews, while recording the events of Pilate’s time, he mentioned our Savior in these words. Josephus on Christ:
44. Now at that time there was Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is right to call him a human being. For he was a performer of miraculous deeds and a teacher of people,
those who gladly received him in truth. And he gathered many of the Jews and many of the
Gentiles. And he was the Christ. And when Pilate sentenced him to the cross at the [?] of the foremost leaders among us,
those who had loved him from the beginning did not remain silent. For he appeared to them alive again after three days,
the divine prophets having spoken these things and many others about him. From then until now, the people of Christians originating from him have not died out.
45. If, therefore, according to the historian who testifies about him, he was a performer of miraculous deeds, and he made not only twelve apostles
or seventy disciples his followers, but also drew to himself tens of thousands of other Jews and tens of thousands of Gentiles, it is clear that he possessed something greater
than the rest of humanity. For how else could he have drawn to himself, from among Jews and Gentiles,
so many people, unless he had employed miracles, astonishing deeds, and extraordinary teachings? The book of the Acts of the Apostles also testifies that there were many tens of thousands
of Jewish people who were persuaded that he was the Christ of God, the one proclaimed by the prophets. It is also recorded in the history
that there was a great church of Christ in Jerusalem, gathered from among the Jews, until the time of Hadrian’s siege. And it is said that the first
fifteen bishops who served there in succession were Jews, whose names are still recited among the local inhabitants.

Thus these facts also refute every slander against the disciples, since, independently of them and apart from their testimony, people acknowledge that he, the Christ of God, brought many Jews and Gentiles under his authority through the miraculous deeds he performed.

46. You too can perceive the divinity of his power if you consider what he was by nature and how there came to be all this excellence of divine power, whose successful achievements surpassed all description.
For consider that no one had ever before sown his own law and an unfamiliar teaching among all nations, or presented himself to the whole human race as a teacher
of the worship of the one God who is above all. And he chose to use people who were the most rustic and insignificant of all humanity as servants of his will.
And could anyone suppose that he did this without deliberation? For how could those who were not even able to open their mouths
ever have become teachers of even one person, let alone a multitude? And how could they have spoken before crowds,
when they were entirely without education? But perhaps this very thing was a demonstration of the divine will. For he called them, as we have already shown,
and first said, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of people.” And once he had gained them and they had followed him, he breathed divine power into them and filled
them strength and courage; and, as one who truly is the Word of God and the worker of all these miracles, he made them fishers of intelligent and rational souls
and added deeds to that utterance, “Come after me, and I will make you.” At the same time, he made them, as he said, workers and teachers of the worship of his God.
Then he sent them to all the nations throughout the whole creation and showed that they were heralds of his teaching. And who would not marvel, and likewise not
believe in this extraordinary miracle? For none of those men who became distinguished was ever recorded as having accomplished anything like this,
or even as having undertaken anything resembling it. For each one of them was content if he could establish his own promise even in his own land alone
and succeed in confirming among his own single people the laws that seemed good to him. But he employed nothing human or mortal. Consider whether
he did not again utter a truly divine [?] expression in the words he spoke to those disciples of his, whose reach was limited: “Go and make disciples of all nations.”
And his disciples might reasonably have answered their master in this way: “How can we do this? For how shall we preach to the Romans?
And how shall we speak to the Egyptians? And what language shall we use with the Greeks, we who have been brought up with the Syriac language alone? And the Persians and Armenians
and Chaldeans and Scythians and Indians, and the other nations called barbarians—how shall we persuade them to turn away from the gods of their fathers

and worship the one Creator of all? What excellence of speech shall we rely on to undertake this? Or what hope of victory shall we have, when we dare to lay down laws for all nations contrary to the laws established from ancient times
concerning their gods? And what power do we have to rely on, so that we may succeed in this daring undertaking?” These, then, were the things that the disciples

of our Savior either said or thought. And with a single addition to his words, their master himself gave them a great solution to the matters about which they were uncertain, saying, “You will prevail in my name.”
For he did not simply and indiscriminately command them to go and make disciples of all nations, but with that important addition which he expressed by saying, “In my name.” For the power of his name
is so great, as the apostle said: “God gave him a name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and beneath the earth.”
Thus he appropriately revealed the excellence of the secret power in his name, which was hidden from many, and added the expression, “In my name.”
Then he also foretold precisely what was to come, saying, “This gospel of mine must be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations.”
Now this statement was spoken at that time in a corner of the earth, where only those nearby could hear. And how could they have believed him when he said this,
unless they had gained evidence of the truth of his words from other divine deeds performed by him?

For when you consider this, you must acknowledge that what he said was trustworthy. For when he commanded, no one questioned him; instead, they relied on his direction and, in accordance with his promises, made disciples of the whole human
race. They went out from their own land to all the nations, and within a short time his words were seen fulfilled in deeds. Thus, within a short time, his gospel was proclaimed
throughout the whole creation as a testimony to all nations. Both barbarians and Greeks received writings about the common Savior of all in their ancestral scripts and their ancestral language.
47. Yet one may reasonably be uncertain about what the manner
of teaching employed by our Savior’s disciples was. Did they perhaps enter the centers of cities and then cry out in the middle of the marketplaces,
raising their voices and calling to those they encountered, and then speaking with the people? And what exactly was the message they spoke to the people?
so that it might seem that the listeners were persuaded by it. But how could men with no experience in speaking address the people?
And they were far removed from any education. Or why, then, did they not speak in an assembly, but instead speak with the few who received them?
What words, then, and what kinds of expressions did they use to persuade their listeners?
For their struggle was no small one, since they did not deny the shameful death of the one they proclaimed.
For even if they had concealed this and had not acknowledged before everyone what things, and how much, he suffered at the hands of the Jews,

and had brought forward only the splendid and glorious things—I mean his astonishing deeds, his miraculous works, and his philosophical teachings—even then it would not have been easy to make those who heard

readily agree with their words, because their speech was unfamiliar. They were only now hearing new things from men who had nothing worthy of acceptance as true to serve as evidence for what they were saying.
48. But suppose that what has just been said was persuasive: that they once proclaimed the one whose messengers they became to be God, who appeared in a human body and is nothing else

in his nature but the Word of God; that for this reason he performed all these wonders and mighty deeds, yet at another time endured their opposites—dishonor and insults—and finally the shameful punishment of the cross,
which is imposed on those whose deeds are the worst of all humanity. Who would not laugh at them [?], as though they were saying contradictory things? And whose mind could have been so stonelike

that he would readily believe them when they said that after his death they had seen him risen from the dead—the very one who could not help himself even while he was among the living? And who would ever be persuaded by those uneducated, insignificant men when they said, “The practices
of your fathers you must despise; the [?] of the wise men of old you must reject; and you must be persuaded by us alone.
And these commandments were given by the one who was crucified, for he alone is the beloved and only Son of the one God who alone is above all.”
49. Therefore, out of love for the truth, when I examine the matter for myself, I see in it no convincing power, nor
anything great or worthy of belief, nor anything persuasive enough to convince even one uneducated person, much less wise and eloquent people.
But then again, when I consider the power of the message and the outcome of their deeds—how they persuaded many tens of thousands,
and how congregations of tens of thousands of people were gathered by those insignificant villagers,
and were established not in hidden and unknown places, but especially in great cities,

in imperial Rome itself, I mean, and in Alexandria and Antioch, throughout Egypt and Libya, in Europe and Asia, in villages and other places, and among all nations—then again I am compelled by necessity

to hasten to seek the cause and acknowledge that they undertook this bold venture only through divine power greater than human power, and through the help of the one who said to them, “Go and make disciples of all nations in my name.”

And when he said this to them, he added a promise by which they were prepared to take courage and readily devote themselves to what they had been commanded. For he said to them, “Look, I am with you all
the days until the end of the world.” It is also said that he breathed the Holy Spirit into them and gave them divine power to perform wonders, when he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.”
And on another occasion he said to them, “Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, and cast out demons. You received freely; give freely.”

[?]. You too, then, see how their message took hold. For the book of their Acts also bears witness to these astonishing things and agrees with them, as it records concerning them how, through miraculous deeds performed in the name of Jesus
by them, those who were nearby and saw were enlightened. Those who saw were apparently astonished first through the deeds.
And then they made it easy for them to ask who this was, by whose power and in whose name the miracle had happened.

And then, when they taught, they found that their hearers had already come to faith before receiving their teaching. For they had not been persuaded by words; rather, deeds had prepared them beforehand.
They made it easy for them to accept what was being said. Indeed, some people soon offered them sacrifices and drink offerings as though they were gods, it is said.
They thought that one of them was Hermes and the other Zeus. And all this was astonishing
to their minds—the demonstration provided by miraculous deeds. And with them in this state, everything that was being proclaimed about our Savior was now accepted quickly and easily. And concerning

his resurrection from the dead, they did not testify with mere words unsupported by demonstrations. Rather, they persuaded people through their own hands and actions, displaying the deeds of someone alive.
51. And if they proclaimed that he is God and the Son of God, and that before coming among human beings he was with his Father,
how did they not meet with still greater opposition over this, with people thinking it impossible and unbelievable? For they readily reasoned
that it was impossible to regard these deeds that were taking place as human deeds rather than God's, even if no one expressly said so.

52. This, then, and nothing else, was the question being investigated: by what power were our Savior's disciples believed by those who first heard them? How did they persuade Greeks and non-Greeks alike to reflect on him as the Word
of God? And how did they establish a school for the worship of God Most High in the midst of cities and in every village? Who would not marvel at this too, and consider within
himself and recognize that this was no human achievement: never at any earlier time had the many nations of the whole world come under a single Roman authority, but only from the time of our Savior.

For at the very time when he came among human beings, Roman power also happened to grow. At that time Augustus became the first sole ruler of many nations, and in his time Cleopatra was defeated and the Ptolemaic succession in Egypt came to an end.
For from that time until now, that ancient kingdom, established in Egypt from what one might call humanity's earliest stock, was uprooted.

And from that same time the Jewish nation became subject to the Romans, as did the Syrians, the [?], the Macedonians, the Bithynians, the Greeks, and, to sum it up, all the rest of those under Roman authority.
Who would not acknowledge that this did not happen apart from our Savior's divine teaching, when considering that it would not have been easy for his disciples to set out and travel
in foreign lands while all the nations were divided against one another and had no dealings with one another because of the many governors in every place and every city?
But with these removed, without fear and swiftly,

and with ease, they completed the journey that lay before them. God Most High had first established peace and restrained the anger of the demon worshipers in the cities through fear of the great empire.
For consider: if there had been nothing to restrain those who were infatuated with the error of many gods from fighting against Christ's teaching,
you would perhaps have seen mutual disturbances, persecutions, and serious wars in every city and every village, if the demon worshipers had possessed authority over us.
But as things stand, this too is the work of God Most High: through great fear of the mighty empire he subjects the enemies of his word. For he desires it to grow every day
and flourish among all humanity. Yet again, so that it should not be thought that it took hold through the rulers' neglect rather than through the surpassing power of God,

whenever one of the tyrants was stirred to wickedness and resolved to fight against the word of Christ, the God of all allowed him too to carry out his will, both to demonstrate the steadfastness of those devoted
to the worship of God, and at the same time so that it might be clearly apparent to everyone that the continued existence of the word does not depend on human will.
But by God's own power, and in an instant. Who would not marvel at the things that regularly happen at times like these?
For those champions of the worship of God, whose virtue had previously been hidden from people, were at that time revealed to everyone and were seen adorned with victories from God.
But those enemies of the worship of God were paying the penalties they deserved, as blows were sent against them from God and their entire bodies were ravaged by severe, incurable sufferings.
Thus they were soon driven even to confess their wickedness against our Savior.
And all the rest, those who were worthy of the divine name and boast that their thoughts are concerned with the things of Christ, within a short time

were trained through trials and demonstrated the purity and clarity of their minds. Then they regained their freedom, and God soon visited them. Through them the Savior makes the word shine forth in greatness every day.
The writing of the five books of Eusebius of Caesarea is complete,
which are called The Divine Manifestation.
